paragraphs: This paper addresses the dependence between separating characters and recognizing them. A character classifier needs an appropriate image region, yet deciding where that region begins and ends can require knowing the character. Touching characters and gaps within a character make a pipeline based on separating images before recognition especially vulnerable.

The proposed COISR approach combines the two decisions in one neural network. In its first version, a backpropagation network scans a field of characters and learns whether its window is centered on one character or lies between characters. When centered on a character, it also identifies that character. Tests on hand-printed digits produce reported very low error rates.

A second version, COISR-SACCADE, additionally learns movements that take the input window from one character to the next. This avoids the exhaustive scanning required by the first version. The shared contribution is to make position and identity decisions cooperate within a learned system, while the second version also incorporates how the system moves through the character field.
summary.tldr: COISR jointly learns character location and identity, with a second version learning window movements to avoid exhaustive scanning.

title: Recognizing Overlapping Hand-Printed Characters by Centered-Object Integrated Segmentation and Recognition

abstract: We have trained networks of E - II units with short-range connec(cid:173) tions to simulate simple cellular automata that exhibit complex or chaotic behaviour. Three levels of learning are possible (in decreas(cid:173) ing order of difficulty): learning the underlying automaton rule, learning asymptotic dynamical behaviour, and learning to extrap(cid:173) olate the training history. The levels of learning achieved with and without weight sharing for different automata provide new insight into their dynamics.

paragraphs: The authors train neural networks with short-range connections to simulate simple cellular automata whose behavior can be complex or chaotic. The central question is what successful learning of such a system actually means. A network may reproduce observed behavior without having acquired the underlying rule that generates all of the automaton's updates.

The paper distinguishes three levels of success, ordered from hardest to easiest: recovering the automaton rule, capturing its long-run dynamics, and extending the history seen during training. This separates learning a generating mechanism from learning broader behavioral properties or continuing a particular observed sequence. The distinction gives different meanings to apparently successful predictions.

The authors examine which levels are achieved for different automata, both with and without weight sharing. These comparisons provide insight into the automata's dynamics as well as the networks' learning. The study therefore uses neural simulation as an investigative tool: the kind of structure a network manages to learn helps characterize the dynamical system being simulated.
summary.tldr: Neural simulations of cellular automata distinguish learning an underlying rule from learning long-run behavior or extending observed histories.

title: Learning Cellular Automaton Dynamics with Neural Networks

abstract: One of the fundamental properties that both neural networks and the central nervous system share is the ability to learn and gener(cid:173) alize from examples. While this property has been studied exten(cid:173) sively in the neural network literature it has not been thoroughly explored in human perceptual and motor learning. We have chosen a coordinate transformation system-the visuomotor map which transforms visual coordinates into motor coordinates-to study the generalization effects of learning new input-output pairs. Using a paradigm of computer controlled altered visual feedback, we have studied the generalization of the visuomotor map subsequent to both local and context-dependent remappings. A local remapping of one or two input-output pairs induced a significant global, yet decaying, change in the visuomotor map, suggesting a representa(cid:173) tion for the map composed of units with large functional receptive fields. Our study of context-dependent remappings indicated that a single point in visual space can be mapped to two different fin(cid:173) ger locations depending on a context variable-the starting point of the movement. Furthermore, as the context is varied there is a gradual shift between the two remappings, consistent with two visuomotor modules being learned and gated smoothly with the context.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people generalize when learning a changed relationship between visual locations and movements. Using computer-controlled alterations of visual feedback, the authors modify selected input-output relationships in the visuomotor map. They then examine how those changes affect other locations and how learning depends on the movement’s starting point.

Changing only one or two relationships produces a significant change across the map, with the effect diminishing away from the remapped locations. The authors interpret this broad but decaying generalization as evidence for representational units with large functional receptive fields. A local learning experience therefore influences a wider range of movements.

The context-dependent experiments show that one visual location can become associated with two finger locations, depending on where the movement begins. As the starting context changes, behavior shifts gradually between the learned mappings. This is consistent with two visuomotor modules whose influence is smoothly controlled by context. Together, the findings use generalization patterns to infer possible computational organization underlying movement learning.
summary.tldr: Visuomotor remapping spreads beyond trained locations and shifts smoothly with context, suggesting broad representations and context-gated modules.

title: Computational Structure of coordinate transformations: A generalization study

abstract: With the rapid expansion of computer networks during the past few years, security has become a crucial issue for modern computer systems. A good way to detect illegitimate use is through monitoring unusual user activity. Methods of intrusion detection based on hand-coded rule sets or predicting commands on-line are laborous to build or not very reliable. This paper proposes a new way of applying neural networks to detect intrusions. We believe that a user leaves a 'print' when using the system; a neural network can be used to learn this print and identify each user much like detectives use thumbprints to place people at crime scenes. If a user's behavior does not match hislher print, the system administrator can be alerted of a possible security breech. A backpropagation neural network called NNID (Neural Network Intrusion Detector) was trained in the identification task and tested experimentally on a system of 10 users. The system was 96% accurate in detecting unusual activity, with 7% false alarm rate. These results suggest that learning user profiles is an effective way for detecting intrusions.

paragraphs: This paper approaches intrusion detection by learning the characteristic behavior of individual computer users. Its premise is that a user's activity leaves a recognizable behavioral signature. If activity associated with that user no longer matches the learned signature, the system can alert an administrator to a possible security breach.

The proposed system, NNID, uses a neural network trained with backpropagation to identify users from their behavior. User identification becomes the basis for detecting unusual activity: the detector looks for a mismatch between observed behavior and the expected user profile. This provides a learned alternative to constructing hand-coded detection rules or relying on online command prediction.

The authors test NNID on a system with ten users and report 96% accuracy in detecting unusual activity, alongside a 7% false alarm rate. The two figures capture useful detection and the accompanying burden of incorrect alerts. The results support learning user profiles as an intrusion-detection approach, with alerts indicating possible breaches that warrant attention rather than establishing intrusion by themselves.
summary.tldr: A neural network learns user behavior profiles to flag unusual activity, reporting 96% detection accuracy and a 7% false alarm rate.

title: Intrusion Detection with Neural Networks

Its ﬁnal goal is to be able to generalize, i.e. infer new instances of these relations among the con- cepts. paragraphs: The paper introduces Linear Relational Embedding, or LRE, for learning representations of concepts from examples of relations between them. Its aim is to infer additional relationships from a limited set of known facts. In a family domain, for example, the desired behavior is to use given kinship relationships to infer another relationship that was not explicitly supplied.

LRE represents each concept as a learned vector and represents relationships as linear transformations between those vectors. For binary relations, the data can be written as triples containing two concepts and their relation. The inference task is then to complete a missing concept when the other concept and the relation are given. This makes relational prediction depend on the learned geometry of the representations.

On a family-relationship task, the authors report better generalization than any previously published method. They also show that LRE can effectively produce compact distributed representations for recursive structures of varying sizes, including trees and lists. The contribution connects learning relational facts with representing hierarchical data through a common vector-based approach.
summary.tldr: LRE learns concept vectors and linear relations to infer missing facts and compactly represent recursive structures.

title: Learning Hierarchical Structures with Linear Relational Embedding

abstract: We present a new multiple-instance (MI) learning technique (EM(cid:173) DD) that combines EM with the diverse density (DD) algorithm. EM-DD is a general-purpose MI algorithm that can be applied with boolean or real-value labels and makes real-value predictions. On the boolean Musk benchmarks, the EM-DD algorithm without any tuning significantly outperforms all previous algorithms. EM-DD is relatively insensitive to the number of relevant attributes in the data set and scales up well to large bag sizes. Furthermore, EM(cid:173) DD provides a new framework for MI learning, in which the MI problem is converted to a single-instance setting by using EM to estimate the instance responsible for the label of the bag.

paragraphs: In multiple-instance learning, a label applies to a bag of instances, leaving uncertainty about which instance accounts for that label. EM-DD addresses this uncertainty by combining expectation-maximization with the diverse density algorithm. It is designed as a general-purpose method that accepts Boolean or real-valued labels and produces real-valued predictions.

The central move is to use EM to estimate the instance responsible for each bag's label. With that assignment estimated, the learning problem can be treated in a single-instance setting. This gives the method a broader conceptual role: it supplies a framework for translating bag-level supervision into a form that more directly identifies the examples driving the labels.

On the Boolean Musk benchmarks, the authors report that EM-DD significantly outperforms all previous algorithms without tuning. They also report relative insensitivity to the number of relevant attributes and good scaling to large bags. These findings support the method's practical value in the evaluated setting, alongside its stated ability to handle more than Boolean labels.
summary.tldr: EM-DD estimates which instance explains a bag's label, combining EM and diverse density to improve multiple-instance learning.

title: EM-DD: An Improved Multiple-Instance Learning Technique

abstract: Cortical synaptic plasticity depends on the relative timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes and also on the temporal pattern of presynaptic spikes and of postsynaptic spikes. We study the hypothesis that cortical synap- tic plasticity does not associate individual spikes, but rather whole ﬁr- ing episodes, and depends only on when these episodes start and how long they last, but as little as possible on the timing of individual spikes. Here we present the mathematical background for such a study. Stan- dard methods from hidden Markov models are used to deﬁne what “ﬁr- ing episodes” are. Estimating the probability of being in such an episode requires not only the knowledge of past spikes, but also of future spikes. We show how to construct a causal learning rule, which depends only on past spikes, but associates pre- and postsynaptic ﬁring episodes as if it also knew future spikes. We also show that this learning rule agrees with some features of synaptic plasticity in superﬁcial layers of rat visual cortex (Froemke and Dan, Nature 416:433, 2002).

paragraphs: The paper studies the hypothesis that cortical synaptic plasticity associates whole firing episodes rather than individual spikes. Under this view, the start and duration of an episode matter most, while the precise timing of spikes within it matters as little as possible. This offers a way to account for sensitivity to temporal patterns on both sides of a synapse.

Hidden Markov model methods give firing episodes a mathematical definition. A difficulty is that estimating whether a neuron is in an episode uses information from both earlier and later spikes. A learning mechanism operating in real time has access only to the past, so the authors must reconcile episode-based inference with a causal update rule.

They construct a rule that uses past spikes while associating presynaptic and postsynaptic episodes as though future spikes were also available. The rule agrees with some observed features of plasticity in superficial layers of rat visual cortex. This provides partial empirical agreement for the mathematical construction, while the episode-based account remains the hypothesis being investigated.
summary.tldr: A hidden Markov model yields a causal plasticity rule that associates firing episodes and agrees with some rat visual-cortex observations.

title: Hidden Markov Model of Cortical Synaptic Plasticity: Derivation of the Learning Rule

abstract: Chemical reaction networks by which individual cells gather and process information about their chemical environments have been dubbed “signal transduction” networks. Despite this suggestive terminology, there have been few attempts to analyze chemical signaling systems with the quantitative tools of information theory. Gradient sensing in the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum is a well characterized signal transduction system in which a cell estimates the direction of a source of diffusing chemoattractant molecules based on the spatiotemporal sequence of ligand-receptor binding events at the cell membrane. Using Monte Carlo techniques (MCell) we construct a simulation in which a collection of individual ligand particles undergoing Brownian diffusion in a three-dimensional volume interact with receptors on the surface of a static amoeboid cell. Adapting a method for estimation of spike train entropies described by Victor (originally due to Kozachenko and Leonenko), we estimate lower bounds on the mutual information between the transmitted signal (direction of ligand source) and the received signal (spatiotemporal pattern of receptor binding/unbinding events). Hence we provide a quantitative framework for addressing the question: how much could the cell know, and when could it know it? We show that the time course of the mutual information between the cell’s surface receptors and the (unknown) gradient direction is consistent with experimentally measured cellular response times. We find that the acquisition of directional information depends strongly on the time constant at which the intracellular response is filtered.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much information a cell can obtain about the direction of a chemical source, and how quickly that information becomes available. Its example is the amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, which senses chemical gradients through molecules binding to and leaving receptors on its surface. The emphasis is on quantifying the information carried by those events.

The authors simulate individual molecules diffusing through a three-dimensional volume and interacting with receptors on a stationary amoeboid cell. They adapt an entropy-estimation method to estimate lower bounds on the mutual information between source direction and the spatial and temporal pattern of receptor events. These bounds quantify information available in the receptor activity, without claiming an exact measurement of everything the cell knows.

The estimated information develops over time in a way consistent with experimentally measured cellular response times. The authors also find that directional information acquisition depends strongly on the time constant used to filter the intracellular response. This connects sensing performance to how the response is processed over time, as well as to the receptor events themselves.
summary.tldr: Simulated receptor activity yields lower bounds on how quickly an amoeba can acquire information about a chemical source’s direction.

title: An Information Theoretic Framework for Eukaryotic Gradient Sensing

abstract: Current computational models of bottom-up and top-down components of atten- tion are predictive of eye movements across a range of stimuli and of simple, ﬁxed visual tasks (such as visual search for a target among distractors). How- ever, to date there exists no computational framework which can reliably mimic human gaze behavior in more complex environments and tasks, such as driving a vehicle through traﬃc. Here, we develop a hybrid computational/behavioral framework, combining simple models for bottom-up salience and top-down rel- evance, and looking for changes in the predictive power of these components at diﬀerent critical event times during 4.7 hours (500,000 video frames) of observers playing car racing and ﬂight combat video games. This approach is motivated by our observation that the predictive strengths of the salience and relevance mod- els exhibit reliable temporal signatures during critical event windows in the task sequence—for example, when the game player directly engages an enemy plane in a ﬂight combat game, the predictive strength of the salience model increases signiﬁcantly, while that of the relevance model decreases signiﬁcantly. Our new framework combines these temporal signatures to implement several event detec- tors. Critically, we ﬁnd that an event detector based on fused behavioral and stim- ulus information (in the form of the model’s predictive strength) is much stronger than detectors based on behavioral information alone (eye position) or image in- formation alone (model prediction maps). This approach to event detection, based on eye tracking combined with computational models applied to the visual input, may have useful applications as a less-invasive alternative to other event detection approaches based on neural signatures derived from EEG or fMRI recordings.

paragraphs: This paper detects critical visual events by examining how well attention models predict where people look over time. It combines a bottom-up model of visual salience with a top-down model of task relevance. The analysis covers 4.7 hours of people playing car-racing and flight-combat games, providing complex tasks in which attention changes around important events.

The key signal is the changing agreement between model predictions and observed gaze. During direct engagement with an enemy aircraft, for example, the salience model becomes significantly more predictive while the relevance model becomes significantly less predictive. Such temporal patterns provide signatures that the framework combines into several event detectors.

A detector using this combination of behavior and visual input is much stronger than detectors using eye position alone or model prediction maps alone. The finding shows that model-to-human agreement carries useful event information beyond either source separately. The authors suggest that this approach may offer a less-invasive alternative to event detection using EEG or fMRI signatures; that application remains a proposed possibility.
summary.tldr: Changes in how attention models predict human gaze provide useful signatures for detecting critical events in video games.

title: Congruence between model and human attention reveals unique signatures of critical visual events

abstract: When we have several related tasks, solving them simultaneously is shown to be more effective than solving them individually. This approach is called multi-task learning (MTL) and has been studied extensively. Existing approaches to MTL often treat all the tasks as \emph{uniformly related to each other and the relatedness of the tasks is controlled globally. For this reason, the existing methods can lead to undesired solutions when some tasks are not highly related to each other, and some pairs of related tasks can have significantly different solutions. In this paper, we propose a novel MTL algorithm that can overcome these problems. Our method makes use of a task network, which describes the relation structure among tasks. This allows us to deal with intricate relation structures in a systematic way. Furthermore, we control the relatedness of the tasks locally, so all pairs of related tasks are guaranteed to have similar solutions. We apply the above idea to support vector machines (SVMs) and show that the optimization problem can be cast as a second order cone program, which is convex and can be solved efficiently. The usefulness of our approach is demonstrated through simulations with protein super-family classification and ordinal regression problems.

title: Multi-Task Learning via Conic Programming

abstract: We describe, analyze, and experiment with a new framework for empirical loss minimization with regularization. Our algorithmic framework alternates between two phases. On each iteration we first perform an {\em unconstrained} gradient descent step. We then cast and solve an instantaneous optimization problem that trades off minimization of a regularization term while keeping close proximity to the result of the first phase. This yields a simple yet effective algorithm for both batch penalized risk minimization and online learning. Furthermore, the two phase approach enables sparse solutions when used in conjunction with regularization functions that promote sparsity, such as $\ell_1$. We derive concrete and very simple algorithms for minimization of loss functions with $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, $\ell_2^2$, and $\ell_\infty$ regularization. We also show how to construct efficient algorithms for mixed-norm $\ell_1/\ell_q$ regularization. We further extend the algorithms and give efficient implementations for very high-dimensional data with sparsity. We demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework in experiments with synthetic and natural datasets.

This paper develops a framework that separates those responsibilities into two successive operations. The separation gives a common algorithmic structure for both batch learning from a dataset and online learning as examples arrive.

Each iteration first takes an unconstrained gradient step to reduce the loss. A second optimization then balances reducing the regularization penalty against remaining close to the first step's result. This second phase gives the regularizer a direct role in shaping the update. When the penalty encourages sparsity, such as the L1 penalty, the approach can produce sparse solutions.

The authors derive simple algorithms for several penalties, including L1, L2, squared L2, and the infinity norm. They also develop efficient methods for mixed norms and implementations suited to very high-dimensional sparse data. Analysis and experiments on synthetic and natural datasets demonstrate the framework's potential across these different regularized learning settings.
summary.tldr: Alternating a gradient step with a regularization-focused optimization provides efficient algorithms for batch, online, and sparse learning.

title: Efficient Learning using Forward-Backward Splitting

abstract: Probabilistic models of natural images are usually evaluated by measuring performance on rather indirect tasks, such as denoising and inpainting. A more direct way to evaluate a generative model is to draw samples from it and to check whether statistical properties of the samples match the statistics of natural images. This method is seldom used with high-resolution images, because current models produce samples that are very different from natural images, as assessed by even simple visual inspection. We investigate the reasons for this failure and we show that by augmenting existing models so that there are two sets of latent variables, one set modelling pixel intensities and the other set modelling image-specific pixel covariances, we are able to generate high-resolution images that look much more realistic than before. The overall model can be interpreted as a gated MRF where both pair-wise dependencies and mean intensities of pixels are modulated by the states of latent variables. Finally, we confirm that if we disallow weight-sharing between receptive fields that overlap each other, the gated MRF learns more efficient internal representations, as demonstrated in several recognition tasks.

paragraphs: A model can perform well at denoising or filling missing image regions without generating convincing images itself. This paper focuses on the more direct test of drawing samples and examining whether they resemble natural images. It investigates why existing models produce high-resolution samples whose shortcomings are apparent even through visual inspection.

The proposed modification introduces two sets of hidden variables. One models pixel intensities, while the other models the image-specific covariances that describe how pixels vary together. The resulting model can be understood as a gated Markov random field: hidden-variable states modulate both average pixel intensities and pairwise pixel dependencies.

With this augmentation, the authors report substantially more realistic high-resolution samples. They also examine how parameters are shared across overlapping receptive fields. Disallowing that weight sharing produces more efficient internal representations, as demonstrated on several recognition tasks. The findings concern both the appearance of generated images and the usefulness of the representations learned within the model.
summary.tldr: Separate latent variables for pixel intensities and image-specific covariances produce more realistic high-resolution image samples.

title: Generating more realistic images using gated MRF's

abstract: Storing a new pattern in a palimpsest memory system comes at the cost of interfering with the memory traces of previously stored items. Knowing the age of a pattern thus becomes critical for recalling it faithfully. This implies that there should be a tight coupling between estimates of age, as a form of familiarity, and the neural dynamics of recollection, something which current theories omit. Using a normative model of autoassociative memory, we show that a dual memory system, consisting of two interacting modules for familiarity and recollection, has best performance for both recollection and recognition. This finding provides a new window onto actively contentious psychological and neural aspects of recognition memory.

This paper argues that an estimate of age, treated as a form of familiarity, should be closely connected to the neural dynamics that reconstruct the remembered pattern.

The authors investigate this connection using a normative model of autoassociative memory. Their proposed dual system contains interacting modules for familiarity and recollection. The important feature is the interaction: information about a pattern's age is coupled to the process of retrieving it, addressing a relationship the authors say existing theories omit.

Within the model, the dual system gives the best performance for both recollection and recognition. This is a result about the modeled memory system, providing a theoretical reason for distinct but cooperating memory functions. It offers a perspective on psychological and neural debates about recognition by connecting the division of labor to interference caused by storing new memories.
summary.tldr: A memory model finds that interacting familiarity and recollection modules best handle retrieval when new memories interfere with old ones.

title: Two is better than one: distinct roles for familiarity and recollection in retrieving palimpsest memories

abstract: Learning problems such as logistic regression are typically formulated as pure optimization problems defined on some loss function. We argue that this view ignores the fact that the loss function depends on stochastically generated data which in turn determines an intrinsic scale of precision for statistical estimation. By considering the statistical properties of the update variables used during the optimization (e.g. gradients), we can construct frequentist hypothesis tests to determine the reliability of these updates. We utilize subsets of the data for computing updates, and use the hypothesis tests for determining when the batch-size needs to be increased. This provides computational benefits and avoids overfitting by stopping when the batch-size has become equal to size of the full dataset. Moreover, the proposed algorithms depend on a single interpretable parameter – the probability for an update to be in the wrong direction – which is set to a single value across all algorithms and datasets. In this paper, we illustrate these ideas on three L1 regularized coordinate algorithms: L1 -regularized L2 -loss SVMs, L1 -regularized logistic regression, and the Lasso, but we emphasize that the underlying methods are much more generally applicable.

The authors use the statistical properties of update quantities, such as gradients, to assess whether proposed optimization steps are reliable.

This connects computational effort to the evidence available for an update direction. These examples demonstrate the approach, while the authors argue that the underlying statistical testing principle has broader applicability.
summary.tldr: Hypothesis tests assess optimization-update reliability and adapt batch sizes to reduce computation while respecting statistical precision.

title: Statistical Tests for Optimization Efficiency

abstract: The sum-product network (SPN) is a recently-proposed deep model consisting of a network of sum and product nodes, and has been shown to be competitive with state-of-the-art deep models on certain difficult tasks such as image completion. Designing an SPN network architecture that is suitable for the task at hand is an open question. We propose an algorithm for learning the SPN architecture from data. The idea is to cluster variables (as opposed to data instances) in order to identify variable subsets that strongly interact with one another. Nodes in the SPN network are then allocated towards explaining these interactions. Experimental evidence shows that learning the SPN architecture significantly improves its performance compared to using a previously-proposed static architecture.

paragraphs: Sum-product networks are deep models assembled from sum and product nodes. Although they had shown competitive performance on tasks such as image completion, choosing a suitable network architecture remained an open problem. This paper addresses that design decision by learning the architecture from the data.

The key step is to cluster variables according to their interactions. Grouping variables identifies subsets whose relationships deserve to be represented together. The algorithm then allocates network nodes toward explaining those interactions. Architecture selection is therefore guided by relationships within the modeled data, giving the network a structure tailored to the dependencies the learning procedure discovers.

Experiments show a significant performance improvement over a previously proposed static architecture. This supports the value of learning the network’s organization in addition to using the sum-product modeling framework itself. The reported comparison concerns the learned architecture and that static alternative; it does not establish superiority over every deep model. The main contribution is a concrete, data-driven strategy for deciding where an SPN should devote its representational structure.
summary.tldr: Clustering interacting variables guides sum-product network architecture learning and improves performance over a fixed architecture in experiments.

title: Learning the Architecture of Sum-Product Networks Using Clustering on Variables

abstract: The recently introduced continuous Skip-gram model is an efficient method for learning high-quality distributed vector representations that capture a large number of precise syntactic and semantic word relationships. In this paper we present several improvements that make the Skip-gram model more expressive and enable it to learn higher quality vectors more rapidly. We show that by subsampling frequent words we obtain significant speedup, and also learn higher quality representations as measured by our tasks. We also introduce Negative Sampling, a simplified variant of Noise Contrastive Estimation (NCE) that learns more accurate vectors for frequent words compared to the hierarchical softmax. An inherent limitation of word representations is their indifference to word order and their inability to represent idiomatic phrases. For example, the meanings of Canada'' and "Air'' cannot be easily combined to obtain "Air Canada''. Motivated by this example, we present a simple and efficient method for finding phrases, and show that their vector representations can be accurately learned by the Skip-gram model. "

The authors introduce a simple, efficient phrase-discovery method and show that Skip-gram can accurately learn vectors for the resulting phrases. This extends the units represented by the model, allowing an idiomatic phrase to have its own representation instead of relying only on separate word vectors.
summary.tldr: Frequent-word subsampling, Negative Sampling, and phrase discovery improve the speed, quality, and expressiveness of Skip-gram representations.

title: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality

abstract: In the high-dimensional regression model a response variable is linearly related to $p$ covariates, but the sample size $n$ is smaller than $p$. We assume that only a small subset of covariates is `active' (i.e., the corresponding coefficients are non-zero), and consider the model-selection problem of identifying the active covariates. A popular approach is to estimate the regression coefficients through the Lasso ($\ell_1$-regularized least squares). This is known to correctly identify the active set only if the irrelevant covariates are roughly orthogonal to the relevant ones, as quantified through the so called `irrepresentability' condition. In this paper we study the `Gauss-Lasso' selector, a simple two-stage method that first solves the Lasso, and then performs ordinary least squares restricted to the Lasso active set. We formulate `generalized irrepresentability condition' (GIC), an assumption that is substantially weaker than irrepresentability. We prove that, under GIC, the Gauss-Lasso correctly recovers the active set.

paragraphs: In high-dimensional regression, there are more candidate covariates than observations. This paper assumes that only a small subset truly has nonzero coefficients and asks how to identify it. The goal is model selection: recovering the active variables, rather than merely obtaining predictions from a fitted regression.

Lasso is a common approach, but identifying the active set requires an irrepresentability condition restricting the relationship between relevant and irrelevant covariates. The paper studies the Gauss-Lasso selector, which first fits Lasso and then performs ordinary least squares using the variables selected by Lasso. This creates a two-stage route to identifying the active set.

The authors formulate a generalized irrepresentability condition that is substantially weaker than the original condition. Under this assumption, they prove that Gauss-Lasso correctly recovers the active variables. The result expands the conditions under which recovery can be guaranteed for the two-stage method. Its force comes from weakening a structural assumption while retaining a model-selection guarantee, with that guarantee still conditional on the generalized requirement.
summary.tldr: Gauss-Lasso recovers active regression variables under a generalized irrepresentability condition that is substantially weaker than the usual one.

title: Model Selection for High-Dimensional Regression under the Generalized Irrepresentability Condition

abstract: Even with the advent of more sophisticated, data-hungry methods, boosted decision trees remain extraordinarily successful for fast rigid object detection, achieving top accuracy on numerous datasets. While effective, most boosted detectors use decision trees with orthogonal (single feature) splits, and the topology of the resulting decision boundary may not be well matched to the natural topology of the data. Given highly correlated data, decision trees with oblique (multiple feature) splits can be effective. Use of oblique splits, however, comes at considerable computational expense. Inspired by recent work on discriminative decorrelation of HOG features, we instead propose an efficient feature transform that removes correlations in local neighborhoods. The result is an overcomplete but locally decorrelated representation ideally suited for use with orthogonal decision trees. In fact, orthogonal trees with our locally decorrelated features outperform oblique trees trained over the original features at a fraction of the computational cost. The overall improvement in accuracy is dramatic: on the Caltech Pedestrian Dataset, we reduce false positives nearly tenfold over the previous state-of-the-art.

title: Local Decorrelation For Improved Pedestrian Detection

abstract: We study the problem of low-rank tensor factorization in the presence of missing data. We ask the following question: how many sampled entries do we need, to efficiently and exactly reconstruct a tensor with a low-rank orthogonal decomposition? We propose a novel alternating minimization based method which iteratively refines estimates of the singular vectors. We show that under certain standard assumptions, our method can recover a three-mode $n\times n\times n$ dimensional rank-$r$ tensor exactly from $O(n^{3/2} r^5 \log^4 n)$ randomly sampled entries. In the process of proving this result, we solve two challenging sub-problems for tensors with missing data. First, in analyzing the initialization step, we prove a generalization of a celebrated result by Szemer\'edie et al. on the spectrum of random graphs. Next, we prove global convergence of alternating minimization with a good initialization. Simulations suggest that the dependence of the sample size on dimensionality $n$ is indeed tight.

summary.tldr: An alternating-minimization method exactly recovers orthogonally decomposable tensors from limited random entries under specified assumptions.

title: Provable Tensor Factorization with Missing Data

abstract: We study the performance of standard online learning algorithms when the feedback is delayed by an adversary. We show that \texttt{online-gradient-descent} and \texttt{follow-the-perturbed-leader} achieve regret $O(\sqrt{D})$ in the delayed setting, where $D$ is the sum of delays of each round's feedback. This bound collapses to an optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ bound in the usual setting of no delays (where $D = T$). Our main contribution is to show that standard algorithms for online learning already have simple regret bounds in the most general setting of delayed feedback, making adjustments to the analysis and not to the algorithms themselves. Our results help affirm and clarify the success of recent algorithms in optimization and machine learning that operate in a delayed feedback model.

paragraphs: Online learning involves making decisions before receiving all the information needed to evaluate them. This paper studies the harder situation in which an adversary controls feedback delays. The question is how much those delays worsen regret, the measure used to compare the learner’s accumulated performance with a reference decision.

The authors analyze online gradient descent and follow-the-perturbed-leader. They show that these standard algorithms achieve regret O(sqrt(D)), where D sums the delays associated with the rounds’ feedback. Under the paper’s convention, ordinary immediate feedback gives D = T, so the bound becomes the optimal O(sqrt(T)) dependence on the number of rounds.

The main change is to the analysis, rather than to the algorithms themselves. This establishes that familiar methods already have simple regret guarantees in the general delayed-feedback setting studied. The result also clarifies why algorithms operating with delayed information can succeed: their performance can be bounded in terms of the accumulated delay, making its effect explicit.
summary.tldr: Standard online learning algorithms achieve O(sqrt(D)) regret under adversarial feedback delays without algorithmic modifications.

title: Online Learning with Adversarial Delays

abstract: Rodents navigating in a well-known environment can rapidly learn and revisit observed reward locations, often after a single trial. While the mechanism for rapid path planning is unknown, the CA3 region in the hippocampus plays an important role, and emerging evidence suggests that place cell activity during hippocampal preplay periods may trace out future goal-directed trajectories. Here, we show how a particular mapping of space allows for the immediate generation of trajectories between arbitrary start and goal locations in an environment, based only on the mapped representation of the goal. We show that this representation can be implemented in a neural attractor network model, resulting in bump--like activity profiles resembling those of the CA3 region of hippocampus. Neurons tend to locally excite neurons with similar place field centers, while inhibiting other neurons with distant place field centers, such that stable bumps of activity can form at arbitrary locations in the environment. The network is initialized to represent a point in the environment, then weakly stimulated with an input corresponding to an arbitrary goal location. We show that the resulting activity can be interpreted as a gradient ascent on the value function induced by a reward at the goal location. Indeed, in networks with large place fields, we show that the network properties cause the bump to move smoothly from its initial location to the goal, around obstacles or walls. Our results illustrate that an attractor network with hippocampal-like attributes may be important for rapid path planning.

The network is initialized to represent a point in the environment, then weakly stimulated with an input corresponding to an arbitrary goal location. Indeed, in networks with large place fields, we show that the network properties cause the bump to move smoothly from its initial location to the goal, around obstacles or walls. Our results illustrate that an attractor network with hippocampal-like attributes may be important for rapid path planning.

paragraphs: Rodents can quickly learn and return to rewarding locations in familiar environments. This paper develops a possible neural mechanism for that ability, motivated by hippocampal activity that may represent future routes. The starting point is a spatial mapping that supports immediate trajectory generation between arbitrary starting and goal locations using the mapped goal representation.

The mapping is implemented in an attractor network whose activity forms localized bumps. Neurons associated with nearby locations tend to excite one another, while those associated with distant locations inhibit one another. These interactions support stable activity bumps resembling patterns in the hippocampal CA3 region. A bump initially represents one location, and weak stimulation specifies a goal.

The resulting activity can be interpreted as climbing a value function generated by reward at the goal. For networks with large place fields, the bump moves smoothly toward the goal around walls or obstacles. This demonstrates a model-based mechanism for rapid planning and suggests a possible role for hippocampal-like attractor dynamics, without establishing that rodents necessarily use this mechanism.
summary.tldr: A hippocampal-like attractor network can generate goal-directed paths through mazes through the movement of localized neural activity.

title: Attractor Network Dynamics Enable Preplay and Rapid Path Planning in Maze–like Environments

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering a signal observed in Gaussian noise. If the set of signals is convex and compact, and can be specified beforehand, one can use classical linear estimators that achieve a risk within a constant factor of the minimax risk. However, when the set is unspecified, designing an estimator that is blind to the hidden structure of the signal remains a challenging problem. We propose a new family of estimators to recover signals observed in Gaussian noise. Instead of specifying the set where the signal lives, we assume the existence of a well-performing linear estimator. Proposed estimators enjoy exact oracle inequalities and can be efficiently computed through convex optimization. We present several numerical illustrations that show the potential of the approach.

paragraphs: Recovering a signal from Gaussian noise is easier when its possible structure can be specified in advance. For a known convex, compact signal set, classical linear estimators can achieve risk within a constant factor of the minimax risk. The challenge considered here is recovery when that signal set is unspecified.

The paper proposes a family of estimators that does not require an explicit description of where the signal lives. Instead, it assumes that a well-performing linear estimator exists. This shifts the needed prior information from a declared structural set to the existence of an effective estimation rule, while leaving the proposed method blind to the hidden signal structure.

The estimators satisfy exact oracle inequalities, providing formal comparisons to the relevant oracle performance, and can be computed efficiently through convex optimization. Numerical illustrations show the approach's potential. The contribution combines a stated replacement assumption with both statistical guarantees and a tractable computation method, addressing how useful recovery remains possible without specifying the signal's structural class beforehand.
summary.tldr: Convexly computable estimators recover signals in Gaussian noise without a specified structural set, assuming a good linear estimator exists.

title: Structure-Blind Signal Recovery

abstract: In this work we propose a novel interpretation of residual networks showing that they can be seen as a collection of many paths of differing length. Moreover, residual networks seem to enable very deep networks by leveraging only the short paths during training. To support this observation, we rewrite residual networks as an explicit collection of paths. Unlike traditional models, paths through residual networks vary in length. Further, a lesion study reveals that these paths show ensemble-like behavior in the sense that they do not strongly depend on each other. Finally, and most surprising, most paths are shorter than one might expect, and only the short paths are needed during training, as longer paths do not contribute any gradient. For example, most of the gradient in a residual network with 110 layers comes from paths that are only 10-34 layers deep. Our results reveal one of the key characteristics that seem to enable the training of very deep networks: Residual networks avoid the vanishing gradient problem by introducing short paths which can carry gradient throughout the extent of very deep networks.

This paper makes that interpretation explicit by rewriting the network in terms of those paths. The perspective separates the total depth of the architecture from the depths of the routes through which information and training gradients travel.

A lesion study finds ensemble-like behavior: the paths do not strongly depend on one another. The training analysis further finds that short paths carry the useful gradients, while longer paths contribute none in the reported observations. In a 110-layer residual network, most of the gradient comes from paths only 10 to 34 layers deep.

These findings suggest an explanation for why very deep residual networks can be trained successfully. Short routes allow gradients to travel throughout a deep architecture without relying on equally deep chains of computation. The paper identifies this as a key characteristic that appears to avoid the vanishing-gradient problem. Its ensemble interpretation concerns the behavior of paths within a residual network, rather than asserting that those paths are separately trained models.
summary.tldr: Residual-network experiments suggest that short, ensemble-like paths carry the gradients that enable training very deep architectures.

title: Residual Networks Behave Like Ensembles of Relatively Shallow Networks

abstract: We present an intriguing discovery related to Random Fourier Features: replacing multiplication by a random Gaussian matrix with multiplication by a properly scaled random orthogonal matrix significantly decreases kernel approximation error. We call this technique Orthogonal Random Features (ORF), and provide theoretical and empirical justification for its effectiveness. Motivated by the discovery, we further propose Structured Orthogonal Random Features (SORF), which uses a class of structured discrete orthogonal matrices to speed up the computation. The method reduces the time cost from $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ to $\mathcal{O}(d \log d)$, where $d$ is the data dimensionality, with almost no compromise in kernel approximation quality compared to ORF. Experiments on several datasets verify the effectiveness of ORF and SORF over the existing methods. We also provide discussions on using the same type of discrete orthogonal structure for a broader range of kernels and applications.

Replacing a Gaussian random matrix with a properly scaled random orthogonal matrix substantially reduces kernel approximation error. The authors call this approach Orthogonal Random Features, or ORF.

SORF uses structured discrete orthogonal matrices, reducing computation from quadratic in the data dimension to the dimension multiplied by its logarithm.

The authors report that this speed improvement comes with almost no loss of kernel approximation quality relative to ORF. Experiments on several datasets support the effectiveness of both methods compared with existing approaches. The contribution links more accurate random feature construction with faster computation, and the paper also discusses potential uses of the discrete orthogonal structure for other kernels and applications.
summary.tldr: Orthogonal random transformations improve kernel approximation, while a structured version accelerates computation with almost no loss of approximation quality.

title: Orthogonal Random Features

abstract: We analyze the clustering problem through a flexible probabilistic model that aims to identify an optimal partition on the sample X1,...,Xn. We perform exact clustering with high probability using a convex semidefinite estimator that interprets as a corrected, relaxed version of K-means. The estimator is analyzed through a non-asymptotic framework and showed to be optimal or near-optimal in recovering the partition. Furthermore, its performances are shown to be adaptive to the problem’s effective dimension, as well as to K the unknown number of groups in this partition. We illustrate the method’s performances in comparison to other classical clustering algorithms with numerical experiments on simulated high-dimensional data.

Its target is exact clustering: identifying the partition itself with high probability. This gives the analysis a concrete statistical objective, beyond simply producing groups that look compact under an optimization criterion.

The proposed estimator uses convex semidefinite optimization and can be understood as a corrected relaxation of K-means. The authors analyze it with finite-sample guarantees, rather than relying only on what happens as the dataset grows indefinitely. Within their model and analysis, the estimator achieves optimal or nearly optimal performance for recovering the partition.

A central result is adaptivity to both the effective dimension of the problem and the unknown number of groups. This connects the recovery guarantees to the problem's underlying complexity while accommodating uncertainty about how many clusters exist. Numerical experiments on simulated high-dimensional data compare the method with classical clustering algorithms and illustrate its performance alongside the theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: A convex relaxation of K-means provides strong partition-recovery guarantees that adapt to effective dimension and an unknown number of clusters.

title: Adaptive Clustering through Semidefinite Programming

abstract: In neuropsychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia or depression, there is often a disruption in the way that regions of the brain synchronize with one another. To facilitate understanding of network-level synchronization between brain regions, we introduce a novel model of multisite low-frequency neural recordings, such as local field potentials (LFPs) and electroencephalograms (EEGs). The proposed model, named Cross-Spectral Factor Analysis (CSFA), breaks the observed signal into factors defined by unique spatio-spectral properties. These properties are granted to the factors via a Gaussian process formulation in a multiple kernel learning framework. In this way, the LFP signals can be mapped to a lower dimensional space in a way that retains information of relevance to neuroscientists. Critically, the factors are interpretable. The proposed approach empirically allows similar performance in classifying mouse genotype and behavioral context when compared to commonly used approaches that lack the interpretability of CSFA. We also introduce a semi-supervised approach, termed discriminative CSFA (dCSFA). CSFA and dCSFA provide useful tools for understanding neural dynamics, particularly by aiding in the design of causal follow-up experiments.

This paper introduces Cross-Spectral Factor Analysis, or CSFA, for multisite low-frequency recordings such as local field potentials and EEGs. Disrupted synchronization in disorders including schizophrenia and depression motivates the need for interpretable descriptions of these networks.

CSFA decomposes recorded signals into factors with distinct spatial and spectral properties. A Gaussian-process formulation within a multiple-kernel-learning framework gives the factors this structure. The resulting lower-dimensional representation retains information relevant to neuroscientists while making its components interpretable in terms of patterns across locations and frequencies.

In the reported experiments, CSFA achieves similar performance to commonly used, less interpretable approaches when classifying mouse genotype and behavioral context. The authors also introduce a semi-supervised extension called discriminative CSFA. Together, the methods are presented as tools for understanding neural dynamics and helping design causal follow-up experiments; the classification results demonstrate usefulness alongside the interpretability of the representation.
summary.tldr: CSFA extracts interpretable spatial-frequency factors from neural recordings while retaining competitive classification performance in the reported experiments.

title: Cross-Spectral Factor Analysis

abstract: Greedy optimization methods such as Matching Pursuit (MP) and Frank-Wolfe (FW) algorithms regained popularity in recent years due to their simplicity, effectiveness and theoretical guarantees. MP and FW address optimization over the linear span and the convex hull of a set of atoms, respectively. In this paper, we consider the intermediate case of optimization over the convex cone, parametrized as the conic hull of a generic atom set, leading to the first principled definitions of non-negative MP algorithms for which we give explicit convergence rates and demonstrate excellent empirical performance. In particular, we derive sublinear (O(1/t)) convergence on general smooth and convex objectives, and linear convergence (O(e^{-t})) on strongly convex objectives, in both cases for general sets of atoms. Furthermore, we establish a clear correspondence of our algorithms to known algorithms from the MP and FW literature. Our novel algorithms and analyses target general atom sets and general objective functions, and hence are directly applicable to a large variety of learning settings.

paragraphs: Greedy optimization methods construct solutions using elements of a set, called atoms. Matching Pursuit works over their linear span, while Frank-Wolfe works over their convex hull. This paper studies the intermediate setting of a convex cone: solutions are formed from nonnegative combinations of atoms, without requiring those coefficients to sum to one.

The authors develop principled nonnegative Matching Pursuit algorithms and establish explicit convergence rates. For general smooth convex objectives, they derive an O(1/t) rate, where t counts iterations. For strongly convex objectives, they obtain a linear rate expressed as O(e⁻ᵗ). The stronger objective assumption therefore supports a faster convergence guarantee in their analysis.

The results cover general atom sets, and the paper explains how the new algorithms correspond to existing Matching Pursuit and Frank-Wolfe methods. It also reports strong empirical performance. The contribution gives cone-constrained optimization a clear place within this family of greedy methods, supplying both algorithms and theoretical rates that can apply across a variety of learning settings.
summary.tldr: Nonnegative Matching Pursuit algorithms optimize over convex cones with explicit convergence guarantees for convex and strongly convex objectives.

title: Greedy Algorithms for Cone Constrained Optimization with Convergence Guarantees

abstract: Low-rank approximation is a common tool used to accelerate kernel methods: the $n \times n$ kernel matrix $K$ is approximated via a rank-$k$ matrix $\tilde K$ which can be stored in much less space and processed more quickly. In this work we study the limits of computationally efficient low-rank kernel approximation. We show that for a broad class of kernels, including the popular Gaussian and polynomial kernels, computing a relative error $k$-rank approximation to $K$ is at least as difficult as multiplying the input data matrix $A \in R^{n \times d}$ by an arbitrary matrix $C \in R^{d \times k}$. Barring a breakthrough in fast matrix multiplication, when $k$ is not too large, this requires $\Omega(nnz(A)k)$ time where $nnz(A)$ is the number of non-zeros in $A$. This lower bound matches, in many parameter regimes, recent work on subquadratic time algorithms for low-rank approximation of general kernels [MM16,MW17], demonstrating that these algorithms are unlikely to be significantly improved, in particular to $O(nnz(A))$ input sparsity runtimes. At the same time there is hope: we show for the first time that $O(nnz(A))$ time approximation is possible for general radial basis function kernels (e.g., the Gaussian kernel) for the closely related problem of low-rank approximation of the kernelized dataset.

paragraphs: Kernel methods often become cheaper when their large kernel matrix is replaced by a low-rank approximation. This paper asks how quickly that approximation can be computed, particularly whether runtime can scale only with the number of nonzero entries in the original data. Such input-sparsity time would make sparse data especially valuable.

For a broad kernel class, including Gaussian and polynomial kernels, the authors show that relative-error rank-k approximation is at least as hard as multiplying the data matrix by an arbitrary matrix with k columns. Without a breakthrough in fast matrix multiplication, this implies an Ω(nnz(A)k) runtime requirement when k is not too large. It matches existing bounds in many parameter regimes.

The paper also distinguishes approximating the kernel matrix from approximating the kernelized dataset. For the latter problem, it establishes input-sparsity-time approximation for general radial basis function kernels, including Gaussian kernels. Thus, the negative result is conditional and task-specific, while the positive result shows that a closely related approximation target can permit substantially faster computation.
summary.tldr: Conditional lower bounds restrict fast kernel-matrix approximation, while approximating the kernelized dataset can achieve input-sparsity time.

title: Is Input Sparsity Time Possible for Kernel Low-Rank Approximation?

abstract: The stunning empirical successes of neural networks currently lack rigorous theoretical explanation. What form would such an explanation take, in the face of existing complexity-theoretic lower bounds? A first step might be to show that data generated by neural networks with a single hidden layer, smooth activation functions and benign input distributions can be learned efficiently. We demonstrate here a comprehensive lower bound ruling out this possibility: for a wide class of activation functions (including all currently used), and inputs drawn from any logconcave distribution, there is a family of one-hidden-layer functions whose output is a sum gate that are hard to learn in a precise sense: any statistical query algorithm (which includes all known variants of stochastic gradient descent with any loss function) needs an exponential number of queries even using tolerance inversely proportional to the input dimensionality. Moreover, this hard family of functions is realizable with a small (sublinear in dimension) number of activation units in the single hidden layer. The lower bound is also robust to small perturbations of the true weights. Systematic experiments illustrate a phase transition in the training error as predicted by the analysis.

These results constrain a possible general explanation of neural-network success: shallow networks and benign input distributions alone do not guarantee efficient learning within this algorithmic framework. The claim concerns a hard family, rather than every network in the covered classes.
summary.tldr: Even small one-hidden-layer networks can require exponentially many statistical queries to learn under logconcave inputs.

title: On the Complexity of Learning Neural Networks

abstract: An explosion of high-throughput DNA sequencing in the past decade has led to a surge of interest in population-scale inference with whole-genome data. Recent work in population genetics has centered on designing inference methods for relatively simple model classes, and few scalable general-purpose inference techniques exist for more realistic, complex models. To achieve this, two inferential challenges need to be addressed: (1) population data are exchangeable, calling for methods that efficiently exploit the symmetries of the data, and (2) computing likelihoods is intractable as it requires integrating over a set of correlated, extremely high-dimensional latent variables. These challenges are traditionally tackled by likelihood-free methods that use scientific simulators to generate datasets and reduce them to hand-designed, permutation-invariant summary statistics, often leading to inaccurate inference. In this work, we develop an exchangeable neural network that performs summary statistic-free, likelihood-free inference. Our framework can be applied in a black-box fashion across a variety of simulation-based tasks, both within and outside biology. We demonstrate the power of our approach on the recombination hotspot testing problem, outperforming the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Population genetics needs methods that can infer biological structure from large collections of genome data. Two obstacles make this difficult: the ordering of sampled population members should not matter, and calculating a likelihood requires accounting for correlated hidden variables in an extremely large space. These obstacles become especially important when moving beyond relatively simple biological models.

The paper develops an exchangeable neural network for inference using simulated data. Its architecture exploits the symmetry associated with reordering population samples, while its likelihood-free approach avoids the difficult likelihood calculation. It also removes the need to reduce datasets to manually designed summary statistics, a traditional step that can lead to inaccurate inference.

The framework is intended for use across different simulation-based tasks, including applications outside biology. On recombination hotspot testing, the authors report performance beyond the state of the art. This result supports the approach on that task: respecting the structure of population data while learning directly from simulations can improve inference without requiring hand-designed summaries.
summary.tldr: An exchangeable neural network performs simulation-based population genetic inference without hand-designed summary statistics and improves recombination hotspot testing.

title: A Likelihood-Free Inference Framework for Population Genetic Data using Exchangeable Neural Networks

abstract: Monte-Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) has been successfully applied to very large POMDPs, a standard model for stochastic sequential decision-making problems. However, many real-world problems inherently have multiple goals, where multi-objective formulations are more natural. The constrained POMDP (CPOMDP) is such a model that maximizes the reward while constraining the cost, extending the standard POMDP model. To date, solution methods for CPOMDPs assume an explicit model of the environment, and thus are hardly applicable to large-scale real-world problems. In this paper, we present CC-POMCP (Cost-Constrained POMCP), an online MCTS algorithm for large CPOMDPs that leverages the optimization of LP-induced parameters and only requires a black-box simulator of the environment. In the experiments, we demonstrate that CC-POMCP converges to the optimal stochastic action selection in CPOMDP and pushes the state-of-the-art by being able to scale to very large problems.

paragraphs: Decision-making under uncertainty often involves maximizing reward while keeping a separate cost within a constraint. Constrained partially observable Markov decision processes express this combination. The paper addresses the difficulty of solving large instances when existing methods require an explicit environment model, a requirement that can make large real-world applications hard to handle.

The proposed algorithm, CC-POMCP, uses online Monte Carlo tree search and needs only a black-box simulator of the environment. It combines simulation-based search with optimization of parameters induced by a linear program. This supplies a way to address the reward objective and cost constraint within a planning method designed for large constrained problems.

In experiments, CC-POMCP converges to optimal stochastic action selection and scales to very large problems. The convergence statement is presented as an experimental finding. The results support the usefulness of combining simulator-based planning with cost constraints, extending the reach of constrained partially observable decision-making beyond methods that depend on an explicit model.
summary.tldr: CC-POMCP uses simulator-based tree search to handle large partially observable planning problems with reward objectives and cost constraints.

title: Monte-Carlo Tree Search for Constrained POMDPs

abstract: People belong to multiple communities, words belong to multiple topics, and books cover multiple genres; overlapping clusters are commonplace. Many existing overlapping clustering methods model each person (or word, or book) as a non-negative weighted combination of "exemplars" who belong solely to one community, with some small noise. Geometrically, each person is a point on a cone whose corners are these exemplars. This basic form encompasses the widely used Mixed Membership Stochastic Blockmodel of networks and its degree-corrected variants, as well as topic models such as LDA. We show that a simple one-class SVM yields provably consistent parameter inference for all such models, and scales to large datasets. Experimental results on several simulated and real datasets show our algorithm (called SVM-cone) is both accurate and scalable.

paragraphs: Many datasets require overlapping groups: a person can belong to several communities, and a word can relate to several topics. This paper studies models that represent each item as a nonnegative weighted combination of exemplars belonging to only one group, with a small amount of noise. Those weights describe the item's mixed membership.

The shared structure has a geometric interpretation: the data form a cone whose corners correspond to the exemplars. This formulation encompasses mixed-membership network models, their degree-corrected variants, and topic models such as LDA. The authors use that common geometry to develop one inference approach that applies across these different model families.

Their algorithm, SVM-cone, uses a simple one-class support vector machine and provides provably consistent parameter inference for models of the stated form. Experiments on simulated and real datasets support both accuracy and scalability. The contribution is a unifying computational route: recovering overlapping memberships through shared geometric structure rather than designing an unrelated inference procedure for every application.
summary.tldr: SVM-cone uses shared cone geometry to provide scalable, provably consistent inference for several overlapping-cluster model families.

title: Overlapping Clustering Models, and One (class) SVM to Bind Them All

abstract: We consider general Gaussian latent tree models in which the observed variables are not restricted to be leaves of the tree. Extending related recent work, we give a full semi-algebraic description of the set of covariance matrices of any such model. In other words, we find polynomial constraints that characterize when a matrix is the covariance matrix of a distribution in a given latent tree model. However, leveraging these constraints to test a given such model is often complicated by the number of constraints being large and by singularities of individual polynomials, which may invalidate standard approximations to relevant probability distributions. Illustrating with the star tree, we propose a new testing methodology that circumvents singularity issues by trading off some statistical estimation efficiency and handles cases with many constraints through recent advances on Gaussian approximation for maxima of sums of high-dimensional random vectors. Our test avoids the need to maximize the possibly multimodal likelihood function of such models and is applicable to models with larger number of variables. These points are illustrated in numerical experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies Gaussian models whose dependence structure forms a tree containing both observed and hidden variables. Unlike a more restricted setup, observed variables may appear inside the tree as well as at its leaves. The authors characterize exactly which covariance matrices are compatible with any given model of this kind through polynomial equalities and inequalities.

Turning that mathematical characterization into a statistical test creates two difficulties. There may be many constraints to check, and singularities in individual polynomials can undermine standard distributional approximations. Illustrated using a star-shaped tree, the proposed testing approach avoids these singularity problems by accepting some loss of statistical estimation efficiency.

To accommodate large collections of constraints, the method uses Gaussian approximations for maxima of sums of high-dimensional random vectors. It also avoids maximizing a likelihood function that may have multiple peaks. Numerical experiments illustrate these benefits and applicability to models with more variables, connecting the algebraic description to a practical testing strategy.
summary.tldr: Polynomial covariance constraints enable tests of Gaussian latent tree models that address singularities and large numbers of constraints.

title: Algebraic tests of general Gaussian latent tree models

abstract: Most graph kernels are an instance of the class of R-Convolution kernels, which measure the similarity of objects by comparing their substructures. Despite their empirical success, most graph kernels use a naive aggregation of the final set of substructures, usually a sum or average, thereby potentially discarding valuable information about the distribution of individual components. Furthermore, only a limited instance of these approaches can be extended to continuously attributed graphs. We propose a novel method that relies on the Wasserstein distance between the node feature vector distributions of two graphs, which allows to find subtler differences in data sets by considering graphs as high-dimensional objects, rather than simple means. We further propose a Weisfeiler--Lehman inspired embedding scheme for graphs with continuous node attributes and weighted edges, enhance it with the computed Wasserstein distance, and thus improve the state-of-the-art prediction performance on several graph classification tasks.

paragraphs: Graph kernels often compare graphs through their component substructures and combine those comparisons using a sum or average. This aggregation can discard information about how components are distributed. The paper proposes comparing distributions of node feature vectors, aiming to retain distinctions that a simple aggregate may overlook.

The method uses Wasserstein distance to compare those distributions across graphs. It also introduces a Weisfeiler–Lehman-inspired embedding scheme that accommodates continuous node attributes and weighted edges. Combining the embeddings with the distributional comparison extends the approach to graph information that only a limited subset of earlier kernel methods could handle.

The authors report improved state-of-the-art predictive performance on several graph-classification tasks. The stated benefit comes from representing graphs through richer collections of node features and comparing their distributions, allowing subtler differences to influence similarity. This connects the representation of local graph information with the way that information is aggregated into a comparison between whole graphs, and the classification results provide empirical support for that combination.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein comparisons of node-feature distributions improve reported graph classification while supporting continuous attributes and weighted edges.

title: Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Graph Kernels

abstract: Sparse subspace clustering (SSC) represents each data point as a sparse linear combination of other data points in the dataset. In the representation learning step SSC finds a lower dimensional representation of data points, while in the spectral clustering step data points are clustered according to the underlying subspaces. However, both steps suffer from high computational and memory complexity, preventing the application of SSC to large-scale datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Selective Sampling-based Scalable Sparse Subspace Clustering (S5C) algorithm which selects subsamples based on the approximated subgradients and linearly scales with the number of data points in terms of time and memory requirements. Along with the computational advantages, we derive theoretical guarantees for the correctness of S5C. Our theoretical result presents novel contribution for SSC in the case of limited number of subsamples. Extensive experimental results demonstrate effectiveness of our approach.
