paragraphs: Sparse subspace clustering represents each data point using a sparse linear combination of other points, then uses spectral clustering to group points by their underlying subspaces. Both representation learning and clustering can require substantial computation and memory. Those costs limit how readily the method can be applied to large datasets.

Selective Sampling-based Scalable Sparse Subspace Clustering, or S5C, addresses this by selecting subsamples using approximate subgradients. The selection mechanism is central to reducing the amount of data involved in the expensive parts of the procedure. The resulting method scales linearly with the number of data points in both time and memory requirements.

The authors also derive correctness guarantees, contributing theory for sparse subspace clustering when only a limited number of subsamples is available. Experiments provide additional evidence of effectiveness. The significance is the combination of scalable resource requirements and theoretical support for the sampling approach: reducing the computational burden is accompanied by analysis of whether the resulting clustering procedure remains correct in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: S5C uses approximate-subgradient-based subsampling to make sparse subspace clustering scale linearly in time and memory, with correctness guarantees.

title: Selective Sampling-based Scalable Sparse Subspace Clustering

abstract: Multi-simulator training has contributed to the recent success of Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL) by stabilizing learning and allowing for higher training throughputs. In this work, we propose Gossip-based Actor-Learner Architectures (GALA) where several actor-learners (such as A2C agents) are organized in a peer-to-peer communication topology, and exchange information through asynchronous gossip in order to take advantage of a large number of distributed simulators. We prove that GALA agents remain within an epsilon-ball of one-another during training when using loosely coupled asynchronous communication. By reducing the amount of synchronization between agents, GALA is more computationally efficient and scalable compared to A2C, its fully-synchronous counterpart. GALA also outperforms A2C, being more robust and sample efficient. We show that we can run several loosely coupled GALA agents in parallel on a single GPU and achieve significantly higher hardware utilization and frame-rates than vanilla A2C at comparable power draws.

paragraphs: Using many simulators can stabilize reinforcement learning and increase the rate at which training experience is produced. Coordinating all of that work can also introduce synchronization costs. Gossip-based Actor-Learner Architectures, or GALA, organize multiple actor-learners in a peer-to-peer network so that they exchange information asynchronously while using distributed simulators.

The approach reduces the need for agents to move through training in lockstep. A theoretical result shows that the agents remain within an epsilon-sized neighborhood of one another during training despite loosely coupled asynchronous communication. This establishes a form of bounded agreement: reducing synchronization need not mean that the learners drift arbitrarily far apart.

Compared with fully synchronous A2C, the paper reports better computational efficiency and scalability, alongside stronger robustness and sample efficiency. It also demonstrates multiple loosely coupled agents running on one GPU, with higher utilization and frame rates at comparable power draws. These findings link the communication design to both learning performance and more effective use of available hardware.
summary.tldr: GALA uses asynchronous peer-to-peer communication to keep reinforcement learners close while improving learning and hardware efficiency over synchronous A2C.

title: Gossip-based Actor-Learner Architectures for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep generative models (DGMs) have shown promise in image generation. However, most of the existing methods learn a model by simply optimizing a divergence between the marginal distributions of the model and the data, and often fail to capture rich structures, such as attributes of objects and their relationships, in an image. Human knowledge is a crucial element to the success of DGMs to infer these structures, especially in unsupervised learning. In this paper, we propose amortized structural regularization (ASR), which adopts posterior regularization (PR) to embed human knowledge into DGMs via a set of structural constraints. We derive a lower bound of the regularized log-likelihood in PR and adopt the amortized inference technique to jointly optimize the generative model and an auxiliary recognition model for inference efficiently. Empirical results show that ASR outperforms the DGM baselines in terms of inference performance and sample quality.

paragraphs: Matching the overall distribution of generated images to observed images does not necessarily capture object attributes or relationships. This paper addresses that structural gap by incorporating human knowledge into deep generative models. The knowledge takes the form of constraints describing structure that the model should account for, including in unsupervised learning.

Amortized structural regularization uses posterior regularization to introduce those constraints. The authors derive a lower bound on the regularized log-likelihood, giving them an objective for training. They also use amortized inference to jointly optimize the generator and an auxiliary recognition model. The recognition model supports efficient inference, making the structural approach practical to optimize alongside the generative model.

The empirical results show better inference performance and sample quality than the deep generative baselines evaluated. These two outcomes address related but distinct goals: recovering useful underlying structure and producing better generated images. The findings support using explicit structural knowledge during learning when matching marginal image distributions alone fails to capture the relationships of interest.
summary.tldr: Amortized structural regularization incorporates human-defined constraints into generative models, improving reported inference and image sample quality.

title: Multi-objects Generation with Amortized Structural Regularization

abstract: Multi-sample, importance-weighted variational autoencoders (IWAE) give tighter bounds and more accurate uncertainty estimates than variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained with a standard single-sample objective. However, IWAEs scale poorly: as the latent dimensionality grows, they require exponentially many samples to retain the benefits of importance weighting. While sequential Monte-Carlo (SMC) can address this problem, it is prohibitively slow because the resampling step imposes sequential structure which cannot be parallelised, and moreover, resampling is non-differentiable which is problematic when learning approximate posteriors. To address these issues, we developed tensor Monte-Carlo (TMC) which gives exponentially many importance samples by separately drawing $K$ samples for each of the $n$ latent variables, then averaging over all $K^n$ possible combinations. While the sum over exponentially many terms might seem to be intractable, in many cases it can be computed efficiently as a series of tensor inner-products. We show that TMC is superior to IWAE on a generative model with multiple stochastic layers trained on the MNIST handwritten digit database, and we show that TMC can be combined with standard variance reduction techniques.

paragraphs: Importance-weighted variational autoencoders use multiple samples to obtain tighter bounds and more accurate uncertainty estimates. Their sample requirements can grow exponentially with latent dimensionality. Sequential Monte Carlo can address this difficulty, but its resampling step introduces sequential computation and is non-differentiable, creating obstacles for speed and learning approximate posteriors.

Tensor Monte Carlo draws K samples separately for each of n latent variables and averages over all K to the power n combinations. This creates exponentially many combinations from a much smaller collection of individual draws. In many cases, the resulting sum can be evaluated efficiently through a sequence of tensor inner products. That computational qualification is central to making the construction useful.

The paper demonstrates better performance than IWAE on an MNIST generative model with multiple stochastic layers. It also shows compatibility with standard variance-reduction techniques. The approach offers a way to exploit many importance-sample combinations through structured computation, with the reported experiment supporting its usefulness for a multilayer latent-variable model.
summary.tldr: Tensor Monte Carlo combines per-variable samples into exponentially many importance-sample combinations that can often be evaluated efficiently with tensor operations.

title: Tensor Monte Carlo: Particle Methods for the GPU era

abstract: Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED) is a principled framework for making efficient use of limited experimental resources. Unfortunately, its applicability is hampered by the difficulty of obtaining accurate estimates of the expected information gain (EIG) of an experiment. To address this, we introduce several classes of fast EIG estimators by building on ideas from amortized variational inference. We show theoretically and empirically that these estimators can provide significant gains in speed and accuracy over previous approaches. We further demonstrate the practicality of our approach on a number of end-to-end experiments.

To address this, we introduce several classes of fast EIG estimators by building on ideas from amortized variational inference. We show theoretically and empirically that these estimators can provide significant gains in speed and accuracy over previous approaches. We further demonstrate the practicality of our approach on a number of end-to-end experiments.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimal experimental design aims to make limited experimental resources more informative. A central quantity is expected information gain, which expresses how much an experiment is expected to teach us. Accurately estimating that quantity can be difficult enough to restrict the practical use of the design framework.

This paper introduces several classes of fast information-gain estimators based on ideas from amortized variational inference. The contribution targets the calculation needed to assess candidate experiments. Improving this calculation matters because experiment selection depends on estimates that are both informative and affordable to compute, especially when experimental resources themselves are constrained.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that their estimators can substantially improve speed and accuracy over previous approaches. They also demonstrate the method in multiple end-to-end experiments, supporting its practicality within the full design process. The stated result is that these estimators can make Bayesian experimental design more usable by improving a central computational step; it is not a claim that every estimator improves every experimental setting.
summary.tldr: Variational information-gain estimators can make Bayesian experimental design faster and more accurate, with theoretical and end-to-end empirical support.

title: Variational Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design

abstract: Nearest neighbor is a popular nonparametric method for classification and regression with many appealing properties. In the big data era, the sheer volume and spatial/temporal disparity of big data may prohibit centrally processing and storing the data. This has imposed considerable hurdle for nearest neighbor predictions since the entire training data must be memorized. One effective way to overcome this issue is the distributed learning framework. Through majority voting, the distributed nearest neighbor classifier achieves the same rate of convergence as its oracle version in terms of the regret, up to a multiplicative constant that depends solely on the data dimension. The multiplicative difference can be eliminated by replacing majority voting with the weighted voting scheme. In addition, we provide sharp theoretical upper bounds of the number of subsamples in order for the distributed nearest neighbor classifier to reach the optimal convergence rate. It is interesting to note that the weighted voting scheme allows a larger number of subsamples than the majority voting one. Our findings are supported by numerical studies.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor prediction relies on retaining training data, which becomes difficult when datasets are large or spread across locations and times. This paper analyzes distributed nearest-neighbor classification as a way to address that obstacle. The central question is how combining predictions from subsamples affects statistical accuracy compared with an oracle version.

With majority voting, the distributed classifier achieves the oracle's convergence rate in regret, up to a multiplicative constant depending only on data dimension. Replacing majority voting with weighted voting eliminates that multiplicative difference. The aggregation rule therefore matters even when both approaches attain the same broad convergence-rate behavior.

The authors also derive sharp upper bounds on how many subsamples can be used while preserving the optimal convergence rate. Weighted voting permits more subsamples than majority voting under these bounds. Numerical studies support the theoretical findings. The results explain both the statistical cost of distribution and how weighted aggregation allows a greater degree of splitting without losing the optimal rate.
summary.tldr: Weighted voting removes an oracle-comparison penalty in distributed nearest-neighbor classification and permits more subsamples while retaining optimal convergence.

title: Statistical Guarantees of Distributed Nearest Neighbor Classification

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular approach to optimize expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions. A significant challenge in BO is to scale to high-dimensional parameter spaces while retaining sample efficiency. A solution considered in existing literature is to embed the high-dimensional space in a lower-dimensional manifold, often via a random linear embedding. In this paper, we identify several crucial issues and misconceptions about the use of linear embeddings for BO. We study the properties of linear embeddings from the literature and show that some of the design choices in current approaches adversely impact their performance. We show empirically that properly addressing these issues significantly improves the efficacy of linear embeddings for BO on a range of problems, including learning a gait policy for robot locomotion.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings of a black-box function when evaluating each candidate is expensive. As the number of parameters increases, retaining efficiency in the number of evaluations becomes difficult. One proposed remedy is to conduct the search through a lower-dimensional representation, often constructed using a random linear embedding.

This paper reexamines how such embeddings are used. The authors study properties of existing approaches and identify important issues and misconceptions, showing that some design choices reduce performance. This shifts attention from the general promise of dimensionality reduction to the particular choices involved in building an embedding-based optimization method.

The authors then address those issues and evaluate the resulting approach on a range of problems, including learning a gait policy for robot locomotion. Their experiments show substantial improvements in the effectiveness of linear embeddings for Bayesian optimization. The findings suggest that the practical value of an embedding depends strongly on its design and use: correcting problematic choices can improve performance while retaining the underlying strategy of searching through a lower-dimensional representation.
summary.tldr: Revisiting problematic design choices substantially improves linear-embedding Bayesian optimization on evaluated problems, including robot gait learning.

title: Re-Examining Linear Embeddings for High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

abstract: A classic problem in machine learning and data analysis is to partition the vertices of a network in such a way that vertices in the same set are densely connected and vertices in different sets are loosely connected. In practice, the most popular approaches rely on local search algorithms; not only for the ease of implementation and the efficiency, but also because of the accuracy of these methods on many real world graphs. For example, the Louvain algorithm -- a local search based algorithm -- has quickly become the method of choice for clustering in social networks. However, explaining the success of these methods remains an open problem: in the worst-case, the runtime can be up to \Omega(n^2), much worse than what is typically observed in practice, and no guarantee on the quality of its output can be established. The goal of this paper is to shed light on the inner-workings of Louvain; only if we understand Louvain, can we rely on it and further improve it. To achieve this goal, we study the behavior of Louvain in the famous two-bloc Stochastic Block Model, which has a clear ground-truth and serves as the standard testbed for graph clustering algorithms. We provide valuable tools for the analysis of Louvain, but also for many other combinatorial algorithms. For example, we show that the probability for a node to have more edges towards its own community is 1/2 + \Omega( \min( \Delta(p-q)/\sqrt{np},1 )) in the SBM(n,p,q), where \Delta is the imbalance. Note that this bound is asymptotically tight and useful for the analysis of a wide range of algorithms (Louvain, Kernighan-Lin, Simulated Annealing etc).

paragraphs: Louvain is a popular local-search algorithm for finding network communities: groups with dense internal connections and looser connections between groups. Its practical success is difficult to explain through worst-case analysis, which permits slow runtimes and provides no general output-quality guarantee. This paper studies its behavior in a structured probabilistic setting.

The authors use the two-block stochastic block model, where the planted communities provide a known reference for analyzing clustering. They develop tools for understanding Louvain and other combinatorial algorithms. One result gives an asymptotically tight bound on the probability that a node has more edges toward its own community, expressing the advantage above one-half through imbalance and the model's connection probabilities.

This local probability calculation helps quantify the information available to algorithms making decisions from connections. The authors identify its usefulness for Louvain, Kernighan-Lin, simulated annealing, and related analyses. The contribution described is a set of tools for explaining behavior under the stochastic block model, addressing the gap between pessimistic worst-case reasoning and the success of local search in practice.
summary.tldr: Analysis in the two-block stochastic block model develops tight probabilistic tools for understanding Louvain and other local-search algorithms.

title: On the Power of Louvain in the Stochastic Block Model

abstract: We investigate a new problem of detecting hands and recognizing their physical contact state in unconstrained conditions. This is a challenging inference task given the need to reason beyond the local appearance of hands. The lack of training annotations indicating which object or parts of an object the hand is in contact with further complicates the task. We propose a novel convolutional network based on Mask-RCNN that can jointly learn to localize hands and predict their physical contact to address this problem. The network uses outputs from another object detector to obtain locations of objects present in the scene. It uses these outputs and hand locations to recognize the hand's contact state using two attention mechanisms. The first attention mechanism is based on the hand and a region's affinity, enclosing the hand and the object, and densely pools features from this region to the hand region. The second attention module adaptively selects salient features from this plausible region of contact. To develop and evaluate our method's performance, we introduce a large-scale dataset called ContactHands, containing unconstrained images annotated with hand locations and contact states. The proposed network, including the parameters of attention modules, is end-to-end trainable. This network achieves approximately 7% relative improvement over a baseline network that was built on the vanilla Mask-RCNN architecture and trained for recognizing hand contact states.

paragraphs: Recognizing whether a hand is making physical contact requires reasoning about its surroundings as well as its appearance. This paper studies joint hand detection and contact-state recognition in unconstrained images. The task is further complicated by the absence of training annotations specifying exactly which object, or part of an object, a hand touches.

The proposed network builds on Mask-RCNN and uses another object detector to locate objects in the scene. Two attention mechanisms connect this contextual information to the detected hands. One pools features from a region enclosing a hand and an object according to their affinity. The other adaptively selects salient features from the plausible contact region. The resulting network, including its attention components, is trainable end to end.

The authors introduce ContactHands, a large-scale dataset annotated with hand locations and contact states, to develop and evaluate the method. Their network achieves approximately 7% relative improvement over a vanilla Mask-RCNN-based contact-recognition baseline. This result supports using object context and selective attention to improve contact-state recognition in the tested images.
summary.tldr: A hand-detection network uses object context and two attention mechanisms to improve physical-contact recognition.

title: Detecting Hands and Recognizing Physical Contact in the Wild

abstract: Emergentism and pragmatics are two research fields that study the dynamics of linguistic communication along quite different timescales and intelligence levels. From the perspective of multi-agent reinforcement learning, they correspond to stochastic games with reinforcement training and stage games with opponent awareness, respectively. Given that their combination has been explored in linguistics, in this work, we combine computational models of short-term mutual reasoning-based pragmatics with long-term language emergentism. We explore this for agent communication in two settings, referential games and Starcraft II, assessing the relative merits of different kinds of mutual reasoning pragmatics models both empirically and theoretically. Our results shed light on their importance for making inroads towards getting more natural, accurate, robust, fine-grained, and succinct utterances.

From the perspective of multi-agent reinforcement learning, they correspond to stochastic games with reinforcement training and stage games with opponent awareness, respectively. Given that their combination has been explored in linguistics, in this work, we combine computational models of short-term mutual reasoning-based pragmatics with long-term language emergentism. We explore this for agent communication in two settings, referential games and Starcraft II, assessing the relative merits of different kinds of mutual reasoning pragmatics models both empirically and theoretically. Our results shed light on their importance for making inroads towards getting more natural, accurate, robust, fine-grained, and succinct utterances.

paragraphs: The paper brings together two perspectives on communication between learning agents. Emergent language concerns how a communication system develops through repeated training. Pragmatic reasoning concerns how agents interpret and choose messages in a particular interaction while considering one another. These processes operate on different timescales, but both can influence whether a message succeeds.

The authors combine computational models of short-term mutual reasoning with long-term language emergence. In the reinforcement-learning view used here, the long-term process involves stochastic games and reinforcement training, while pragmatic interaction involves stage games with awareness of the other agent. The combination lets communication be shaped both by accumulated learning and by reasoning about the current partner.

The study examines referential games and StarCraft II, comparing different mutual-reasoning models through empirical and theoretical analysis. The results highlight the relevance of pragmatics for progress toward communication that is more natural, accurate, robust, detailed, and concise. The contribution is evidence about the relative merits of these reasoning models, supporting their role in improving emergent language.
summary.tldr: Combining immediate reasoning about communication partners with long-term language learning offers a promising route toward better agent utterances.

title: Incorporating Pragmatic Reasoning Communication into Emergent Language

abstract: We consider the theory of regression on a manifold using reproducing kernel Hilbert space methods. Manifold models arise in a wide variety of modern machine learning problems, and our goal is to help understand the effectiveness of various implicit and explicit dimensionality-reduction methods that exploit manifold structure. Our first key contribution is to establish a novel nonasymptotic version of the Weyl law from differential geometry. From this we are able to show that certain spaces of smooth functions on a manifold are effectively finite-dimensional, with a complexity that scales according to the manifold dimension rather than any ambient data dimension. Finally, we show that given (potentially noisy) function values taken uniformly at random over a manifold, a kernel regression estimator (derived from the spectral decomposition of the manifold) yields minimax-optimal error bounds that are controlled by the effective dimension.

This paper studies regression on such a manifold using reproducing kernel Hilbert space methods. Its aim is to explain why methods that exploit manifold structure can benefit from the lower-dimensional organization of the problem.

The first contribution is a nonasymptotic version of Weyl's law from differential geometry. The authors use it to show that certain spaces of smooth functions on a manifold are effectively finite-dimensional. Their complexity scales with the dimension of the manifold, rather than the ambient dimension used to describe the data.

Those bounds are controlled by the effective dimension. The result connects geometric structure to statistical difficulty under the stated sampling setup, providing a theoretical explanation for the value of exploiting intrinsic dimension in regression.
summary.tldr: Manifold regression can achieve minimax-optimal error bounds governed by intrinsic effective dimension under uniformly sampled observations.

title: Sample complexity and effective dimension for regression on manifolds

abstract: Modern neural network performance typically improves as model size increases. A recent line of research on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) of over-parameterized networks indicates that the improvement with size increase is a product of a better conditioned loss landscape. In this work, we investigate a form of over-parameterization achieved through ensembling, where we define collegial ensembles (CE) as the aggregation of multiple independent models with identical architectures, trained as a single model. We show that the optimization dynamics of CE simplify dramatically when the number of models in the ensemble is large, resembling the dynamics of wide models, yet scale much more favorably. We use recent theoretical results on the finite width corrections of the NTK to perform efficient architecture search in a space of finite width CE that aims to either minimize capacity, or maximize trainability under a set of constraints. The resulting ensembles can be efficiently implemented in practical architectures using group convolutions and block diagonal layers. Finally, we show how our framework can be used to analytically derive optimal group convolution modules originally found using expensive grid searches, without having to train a single model.

This paper investigates another way to increase model capacity: aggregate several independent networks with identical architectures and train their combination as one model. The authors call this construction a collegial ensemble.

As the number of component models becomes large, the ensemble's optimization dynamics simplify and resemble those of wide networks, while scaling more favorably. Depending on the constraints, the search can aim to reduce capacity or improve trainability.

This connects an analysis of learning dynamics to concrete architecture choices, making theory useful for designing the structure before training begins.
summary.tldr: Collegial ensembles combine identical network architectures into one trainable model and use optimization theory to guide efficient architecture design.

title: Collegial Ensembles

abstract: In this paper we study the training dynamics for gradient flow on over-parametrized tensor decomposition problems. Empirically, such training process often first fits larger components and then discovers smaller components, which is similar to a tensor deflation process that is commonly used in tensor decomposition algorithms. We prove that for orthogonally decomposable tensor, a slightly modified version of gradient flow would follow a tensor deflation process and recover all the tensor components. Our proof suggests that for orthogonal tensors, gradient flow dynamics works similarly as greedy low-rank learning in the matrix setting, which is a first step towards understanding the implicit regularization effect of over-parametrized models for low-rank tensors.

paragraphs: The paper studies the training dynamics of over-parameterized tensor decomposition under gradient flow. Empirically, this process often captures larger tensor components before finding smaller ones. That ordering resembles deflation, a decomposition strategy that recovers components progressively. The authors investigate when this observed pattern can be supported by a mathematical result.

For orthogonally decomposable tensors, they prove that a slightly modified gradient-flow procedure follows a deflation process and recovers every tensor component. Both the orthogonal structure and the modification to gradient flow belong to the stated result. The proof gives a precise setting in which progressive component discovery is more than an empirical observation.

The analysis suggests a connection to greedy low-rank learning in matrices: optimization dynamics can uncover structure in an ordered way even in an over-parameterized representation. The authors present this as a first step toward understanding implicit regularization for low-rank tensors. Its significance is the link between the path taken during training and the structured decomposition ultimately recovered.
summary.tldr: For orthogonally decomposable tensors, a modified gradient flow provably recovers components through a deflation-like process.

title: Understanding Deflation Process in Over-parametrized Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Supervised Pix2Pix and unsupervised Cycle-consistency are two modes that dominate the field of medical image-to-image translation. However, neither modes are ideal. The Pix2Pix mode has excellent performance. But it requires paired and well pixel-wise aligned images, which may not always be achievable due to respiratory motion or anatomy change between times that paired images are acquired. The Cycle-consistency mode is less stringent with training data and works well on unpaired or misaligned images. But its performance may not be optimal. In order to break the dilemma of the existing modes, we propose a new unsupervised mode called RegGAN for medical image-to-image translation. It is based on the theory of "loss-correction". In RegGAN, the misaligned target images are considered as noisy labels and the generator is trained with an additional registration network to fit the misaligned noise distribution adaptively. The goal is to search for the common optimal solution to both image-to-image translation and registration tasks. We incorporated RegGAN into a few state-of-the-art image-to-image translation methods and demonstrated that RegGAN could be easily combined with these methods to improve their performances. Such as a simple CycleGAN in our mode surpasses latest NICEGAN even though using less network parameters. Based on our results, RegGAN outperformed both Pix2Pix on aligned data and Cycle-consistency on misaligned or unpaired data. RegGAN is insensitive to noises which makes it a better choice for a wide range of scenarios, especially for medical image-to-image translation tasks in which well pixel-wise aligned data are not available. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Kid-Liet/Reg-GAN.

Motion or anatomical changes can make that requirement difficult to satisfy. Cycle-consistency methods accept unpaired or misaligned images, but the abstract describes their translation performance as potentially less satisfactory.

RegGAN addresses this tradeoff by treating target-image misalignment as noise in the training labels. Alongside the image generator, it trains a registration network that adaptively accounts for that misalignment. Drawing on loss-correction theory, the approach seeks a shared solution to translation and registration, allowing the training objective to account for spatial disagreement between images.

summary.tldr: RegGAN jointly learns image translation and registration by treating misalignment as label noise, improving results across the reported medical imaging settings.

title: Breaking the Dilemma of Medical Image-to-image Translation

abstract: In bandit multiple hypothesis testing, each arm corresponds to a different null hypothesis that we wish to test, and the goal is to design adaptive algorithms that correctly identify large set of interesting arms (true discoveries), while only mistakenly identifying a few uninteresting ones (false discoveries). One common metric in non-bandit multiple testing is the false discovery rate (FDR). We propose a unified, modular framework for bandit FDR control that emphasizes the decoupling of exploration and summarization of evidence. We utilize the powerful martingale-based concept of "e-processes" to ensure FDR control for arbitrary composite nulls, exploration rules and stopping times in generic problem settings. In particular, valid FDR control holds even if the reward distributions of the arms could be dependent, multiple arms may be queried simultaneously, and multiple (cooperating or competing) agents may be querying arms, covering combinatorial semi-bandit type settings as well. Prior work has considered in great detail the setting where each arm's reward distribution is independent and sub-Gaussian, and a single arm is queried at each step. Our framework recovers matching sample complexity guarantees in this special case, and performs comparably or better in practice. For other settings, sample complexities will depend on the finer details of the problem (composite nulls being tested, exploration algorithm, data dependence structure, stopping rule) and we do not explore these; our contribution is to show that the FDR guarantee is clean and entirely agnostic to these details.

paragraphs: Bandit multiple testing combines two decisions: which possibilities to investigate next, and which ones have enough evidence to count as discoveries. Each arm represents a hypothesis. The statistical challenge is to find many genuine discoveries while controlling the false discovery rate, which concerns the proportion of reported discoveries that are mistaken.

The paper separates exploration from evidence assessment in a modular framework. Its central tool is an e-process, a martingale-based way of accumulating statistical evidence. This construction supports false discovery rate control across arbitrary composite null hypotheses, exploration strategies, and stopping times. It also accommodates dependent rewards, simultaneous queries to several arms, and multiple agents collecting observations.

In the previously studied setting of independent, sub-Gaussian rewards with one arm queried at a time, the framework matches existing sample complexity guarantees and performs comparably or better empirically. Its broader result concerns validity, not a universal sampling budget. Outside that special setting, the number of observations needed depends on the hypotheses, exploration strategy, dependence, and stopping rule; the paper does not analyze those sample complexities.
summary.tldr: A modular framework separates adaptive exploration from evidence assessment to control false discoveries across a broad range of bandit testing settings.

title: A unified framework for bandit multiple testing

abstract: We introduce the dueling teams problem, a new online-learning setting in which the learner observes noisy comparisons of disjoint pairs of $k$-sized teams from a universe of $n$ players. The goal of the learner is to minimize the number of duels required to identify, with high probability, a Condorcet winning team, i.e., a team which wins against any other disjoint team (with probability at least $1/2$).Noisy comparisons are linked to a total order on the teams. We formalize our model by building upon the dueling bandits setting (Yue et al. 2012) and provide several algorithms, both for stochastic and deterministic settings. For the stochastic setting, we provide a reduction to the classical dueling bandits setting, yielding an algorithm that identifies a Condorcet winning team within $\mathcal{O}((n + k \log (k)) \frac{\max(\log\log n, \log k)}{\Delta^2})$ duels, where $\Delta$ is a gap parameter. For deterministic feedback, we additionally present a gap-independent algorithm that identifies a Condorcet winning team within $\mathcal{O}(nk\log(k)+k^5)$ duels.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a learning problem in which feedback compares whole teams rather than individual players. Each duel involves two disjoint teams of k players drawn from n available players. The learner seeks a Condorcet winning team: one whose probability of winning against every disjoint opponent is at least one half.

The challenge is to identify such a team with high probability using few comparisons. The model links noisy comparison outcomes to a total ordering of teams. For stochastic feedback, the authors reduce the problem to classical dueling bandits and derive a comparison bound depending on the number of players, team size, and a gap parameter. Its inverse-square dependence on that gap makes the guarantee sensitive to how distinguishable the comparisons are.

For deterministic feedback, the paper provides an additional algorithm with a bound of order nk log k plus k to the fifth power, independent of a gap parameter. The contribution establishes algorithms and comparison guarantees for collective choices when observations arrive only through team-level contests.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and comparison guarantees for identifying a winning team from noisy or deterministic contests between disjoint teams.

title: Dueling Bandits with Team Comparisons

abstract: Human reasoning can be understood as an interplay between two systems: the intuitive and associative ("System 1") and the deliberative and logical ("System 2"). Neural sequence models---which have been increasingly successful at performing complex, structured tasks---exhibit the advantages and failure modes of System 1: they are fast and learn patterns from data, but are often inconsistent and incoherent. In this work, we seek a lightweight, training-free means of improving existing System 1-like sequence models by adding System 2-inspired logical reasoning. We explore several variations on this theme in which candidate generations from a neural sequence model are examined for logical consistency by a symbolic reasoning module, which can either accept or reject the generations. Our approach uses neural inference to mediate between the neural System 1 and the logical System 2. Results in robust story generation and grounded instruction-following show that this approach can increase the coherence and accuracy of neurally-based generations.

This paper approaches that problem through the idea of two complementary reasoning systems: one that recognizes patterns and proposes responses, and another that evaluates them logically. The goal is a lightweight way to improve existing sequence models without additional training.

The authors explore several arrangements in which a neural model produces candidate generations and a symbolic reasoning module checks their logical consistency. The symbolic component can accept or reject a candidate. Neural inference mediates between the sequence model and the logical module, providing the connection needed for the two kinds of processing to work together.

Evaluations address robust story generation and grounded instruction-following. The results show that this combination can improve coherence and accuracy in generated outputs. Its practical significance lies in adding a reasoning-based check around an existing generator through a training-free approach. The evidence supports improvements on the evaluated tasks, while the framework describes a broader way to combine learned generation with explicit consistency checks.
summary.tldr: A training-free combination of neural generation and symbolic consistency checks improves coherence and accuracy in story generation and instruction-following tests.

title: Improving Coherence and Consistency in Neural Sequence Models with Dual-System, Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

abstract: This paper studies model-based bandit and reinforcement learning (RL) with nonlinear function approximations. We propose to study convergence to approximate local maxima because we show that global convergence is statistically intractable even for one-layer neural net bandit with a deterministic reward. For both nonlinear bandit and RL, the paper presents a model-based algorithm, Virtual Ascent with Online Model Learner (ViOlin), which provably converges to a local maximum with sample complexity that only depends on the sequential Rademacher complexity of the model class. Our results imply novel global or local regret bounds on several concrete settings such as linear bandit with finite or sparse model class, and two-layer neural net bandit. A key algorithmic insight is that optimism may lead to over-exploration even for two-layer neural net model class. On the other hand, for convergence to local maxima, it suffices to maximize the virtual return if the model can also reasonably predict the gradient and Hessian of the real return.

It shows that guaranteeing global convergence can be statistically intractable even for a one-layer neural network bandit with deterministic rewards. That finding motivates approximate local maxima as a more attainable target for the analysis.

For reaching local maxima, maximizing the model's virtual return is sufficient if the model also predicts the real return's gradient and Hessian reasonably well. This condition connects successful local improvement to learning both the slope and curvature of the true objective.
summary.tldr: ViOlin provides local-convergence guarantees for nonlinear model-based learning by exploiting predicted return geometry.

title: Provable Model-based Nonlinear Bandit and Reinforcement Learning: Shelve Optimism, Embrace Virtual Curvature

abstract: Real-world datasets often have missing values associated with complex generative processes, where the cause of the missingness may not be fully observed. This is known as missing not at random (MNAR) data. However, many imputation methods do not take into account the missingness mechanism, resulting in biased imputation values when MNAR data is present. Although there are a few methods that have considered the MNAR scenario, their model's identifiability under MNAR is generally not guaranteed. That is, model parameters can not be uniquely determined even with infinite data samples, hence the imputation results given by such models can still be biased. This issue is especially overlooked by many modern deep generative models. In this work, we fill in this gap by systematically analyzing the identifiability of generative models under MNAR. Furthermore, we propose a practical deep generative model which can provide identifiability guarantees under mild assumptions, for a wide range of MNAR mechanisms. Our method demonstrates a clear advantage for tasks on both synthetic data and multiple real-world scenarios with MNAR data.

paragraphs: Missing values can depend on causes that are not fully observed, a situation called missing not at random. Filling in such values without accounting for the missingness mechanism can introduce bias. The paper examines a deeper issue: even a model that represents missingness may not have parameters that can be uniquely recovered from the available observations.

This property, called identifiability, matters because collecting indefinitely more samples does not resolve ambiguity between indistinguishable parameter settings. The authors systematically analyze identifiability for generative models under missing-not-at-random conditions. They highlight that this issue can persist in modern deep generative approaches, despite their ability to represent complex data.

The paper then proposes a practical deep generative model with identifiability guarantees under assumptions described as mild, covering a wide range of missingness mechanisms. Experiments show advantages on synthetic data and several real-world scenarios with missing-not-at-random data. The contribution combines an analysis of what can be recovered from incomplete observations with a model designed to satisfy those recovery conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes identifiability under missing-not-at-random data and develops a deep imputation model with conditional identifiability guarantees.

title: Identifiable Generative models for Missing Not at Random Data Imputation

abstract: Recent works leveraging learning to enhance sampling have shown promising results, in particular by designing effective non-local moves and global proposals. However, learning accuracy is inevitably limited in regions where little data is available such as in the tails of distributions as well as in high-dimensional problems. In the present paper we study an Explore-Exploit Markov chain Monte Carlo strategy ($\operatorname{Ex^2MCMC}$) that combines local and global samplers showing that it enjoys the advantages of both approaches. We prove $V$-uniform geometric ergodicity of $\operatorname{Ex^2MCMC}$ without requiring a uniform adaptation of the global sampler to the target distribution. We also compute explicit bounds on the mixing rate of the Explore-Exploit strategy under realistic conditions. Moreover, we propose an adaptive version of the strategy ($\operatorname{FlEx^2MCMC}$) where a normalizing flow is trained while sampling to serve as a proposal for global moves. We illustrate the efficiency of $\operatorname{Ex^2MCMC}$ and its adaptive version on classical sampling benchmarks as well as in sampling high-dimensional distributions defined by Generative Adversarial Networks seen as Energy Based Models.

Moreover, we propose an adaptive version of the strategy ($\operatorname{FlEx^2MCMC}$) where a normalizing flow is trained while sampling to serve as a proposal for global moves. paragraphs: Learned sampling methods can propose large moves through a probability distribution, but their accuracy is limited where training data are scarce, including distribution tails and high-dimensional settings. This paper studies an Explore-Exploit MCMC strategy that combines local sampling with global proposals. The aim is to benefit from both types of movement.

For this combined strategy, called Ex²MCMC, the authors prove a geometric convergence property in a weighted sense. The result does not require the global sampler to match the target distribution uniformly. They also derive explicit bounds on mixing speed under stated realistic conditions. These guarantees address a central concern with learned global proposals: imperfect coverage need not prevent the combined method from having rigorous convergence behavior.

An adaptive version, FlEx²MCMC, trains a normalizing flow during sampling and uses it to propose global moves. The authors illustrate both methods on standard sampling benchmarks and high-dimensional distributions derived from generative adversarial networks treated as energy-based models. The work combines theoretical guarantees with demonstrations of the local-global sampling design.
summary.tldr: Ex²MCMC combines local and global sampling with convergence guarantees that do not require a uniformly accurate global proposal.

title: Local-Global MCMC kernels: the best of both worlds

abstract: In this paper, we study the gyrovector space structure (gyro-structure) of matrix manifolds. Our work is motivated by the success of hyperbolic neural networks (HNNs) that have demonstrated impressive performance in a variety of applications. At the heart of HNNs is the theory of gyrovector spaces that provides a powerful tool for studying hyperbolic geometry. Here we focus on two matrix manifolds, i.e., Symmetric Positive Definite (SPD) and Grassmann manifolds, and consider connecting the Riemannian geometry of these manifolds with the basic operations, i.e., the binary operation and scalar multiplication on gyrovector spaces. Our work reveals some interesting facts about SPD and Grassmann manifolds. First, SPD matrices with an Affine-Invariant (AI) or a Log-Euclidean (LE) geometry have rich structure with strong connection to hyperbolic geometry. The authors connect the Riemannian geometry of these spaces with a binary operation and scalar multiplication. summary.tldr: The paper develops gyrovector-related structures on positive definite matrices and linear subspaces, connecting their geometry to learning applications.

title: The Gyro-Structure of Some Matrix Manifolds

abstract: Neural tangent kernel (NTK) is a powerful tool to analyze training dynamics of neural networks and their generalization bounds. The study on NTK has been devoted to typical neural network architectures, but it is incomplete for neural networks with Hadamard products (NNs-Hp), e.g., StyleGAN and polynomial neural networks (PNNs). In this work, we derive the finite-width NTK formulation for a special class of NNs-Hp, i.e., polynomial neural networks. We prove their equivalence to the kernel regression predictor with the associated NTK, which expands the application scope of NTK. Based on our results, we elucidate the separation of PNNs over standard neural networks with respect to extrapolation and spectral bias. Our two key insights are that when compared to standard neural networks, PNNs can fit more complicated functions in the extrapolation regime and admit a slower eigenvalue decay of the respective NTK, leading to a faster learning towards high-frequency functions. Besides, our theoretical results can be extended to other types of NNs-Hp, which expand the scope of our work. Our empirical results validate the separations in broader classes of NNs-Hp, which provide a good justification for a deeper understanding of neural architectures.

paragraphs: Elementwise multiplication, also called a Hadamard product, appears in neural architectures whose training behavior is not fully covered by standard neural tangent kernel analyses. The paper studies polynomial neural networks as a particular class of these architectures. Its aim is to explain how multiplication affects extrapolation and the kinds of functions learned during training.

The authors derive a finite-width neural tangent kernel for polynomial networks and prove equivalence to regression using the associated kernel. This creates a mathematical route for comparing polynomial networks with standard neural networks. Their analysis shows that polynomial networks can fit more complicated functions outside the training regime and that their kernels have more slowly decaying eigenvalues.

That spectral property leads to faster learning of high-frequency functions in the analysis. The authors also explain that their theoretical results can extend to other networks with Hadamard products. Empirical results support the identified distinctions in broader architectural classes, linking the use of multiplication to specific differences in extrapolation and learning behavior.
summary.tldr: A neural tangent kernel analysis explains how polynomial networks can extrapolate more complex functions and learn high-frequency functions faster than standard networks.

title: Extrapolation and Spectral Bias of Neural Nets with Hadamard Product: a Polynomial Net Study

abstract: We study the dynamics and implicit bias of gradient flow (GF) on univariate ReLU neural networks with a single hidden layer in a binary classification setting. We show that when the labels are determined by the sign of a target network with $r$ neurons, with high probability over the initialization of the network and the sampling of the dataset, GF converges in direction (suitably defined) to a network achieving perfect training accuracy and having at most $\mathcal{O}(r)$ linear regions, implying a generalization bound. Unlike many other results in the literature, under an additional assumption on the distribution of the data, our result holds even for mild over-parameterization, where the width is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(r)$ and independent of the sample size.

paragraphs: A ReLU network with one input and one hidden layer represents a piecewise-linear function. Its effective complexity depends on how many linear regions the learned function uses. This paper studies whether gradient flow, a continuous-time form of gradient-based training, favors a relatively simple function in a binary classification problem.

The result assumes that labels come from the sign of a target network containing r neurons. With high probability over both initialization and dataset sampling, gradient flow converges in a suitably defined direction to a network with perfect training accuracy and at most O(r) linear regions. That bound on the learned function's regions also yields a generalization bound.

Under an additional assumption on the data distribution, the result holds with only mild overparameterization: network width scales roughly with r, up to logarithmic factors, independently of sample size. The finding links successful fitting and controlled function complexity in this specific setting. Its guarantee concerns directional convergence under the stated labeling and distribution conditions.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, gradient flow learns a perfectly fitting univariate ReLU classifier with only O(r) linear regions.

title: On the Effective Number of Linear Regions in Shallow Univariate ReLU Networks: Convergence Guarantees and Implicit Bias

abstract: We study reinforcement learning (RL) in settings where observations are high-dimensional, but where an RL agent has access to abstract knowledge about the structure of the state space, as is the case, for example, when a robot is tasked to go to a specific room in a building using observations from its own camera, while having access to the floor plan. We formalize this setting as transfer reinforcement learning from an "abstract simulator," which we assume is deterministic (such as a simple model of moving around the floor plan), but which is only required to capture the target domain's latent-state dynamics approximately up to unknown (bounded) perturbations (to account for environment stochasticity). Crucially, we assume no prior knowledge about the structure of observations in the target domain except that they can be used to identify the latent states (but the decoding map is unknown). Under these assumptions, we present an algorithm, called TASID, that learns a robust policy in the target domain, with sample complexity that is polynomial in the horizon, and independent of the number of states, which is not possible without access to some prior knowledge. In synthetic experiments, we verify various properties of our algorithm and show that it empirically outperforms transfer RL algorithms that require access to "full simulators" (i.e., those that also simulate observations).

paragraphs: An agent may receive complicated observations while already knowing something about the environment's underlying structure. The paper illustrates this with a robot that sees through a camera but has a building's floor plan. It asks how such abstract knowledge can reduce the experience needed to learn a useful policy.

The authors formalize that knowledge as a deterministic abstract simulator. It need only approximate latent-state transitions up to unknown bounded perturbations, allowing for stochasticity in the target environment. The observations must identify latent states, but the agent does not know the mapping from observations to those states. Thus, the simulator provides structural guidance without having to generate realistic observations.

Under these assumptions, TASID learns a robust target-domain policy with sample complexity polynomial in the horizon and independent of the number of states. The paper notes that this independence is unavailable without some prior knowledge. Synthetic experiments verify properties of the algorithm and show it outperforming compared transfer methods that require full simulators capable of generating observations as well as dynamics.
summary.tldr: TASID uses approximate abstract dynamics to learn robust policies with state-count-independent sample complexity under stated latent-state assumptions.

title: Provably sample-efficient RL with side information about latent dynamics

abstract: We initiate the study of dynamic regret minimization for goal-oriented reinforcement learning modeled by a non-stationary stochastic shortest path problem with changing cost and transition functions.We start by establishing a lower bound $\Omega((B_{\star} SAT_{\star}(\Delta_c + B_{\star}^2\Delta_P))^{1/3}K^{2/3})$, where $B_{\star}$ is the maximum expected cost of the optimal policy of any episode starting from any state, $T_{\star}$ is the maximum hitting time of the optimal policy of any episode starting from the initial state, $SA$ is the number of state-action pairs, $\Delta_c$ and $\Delta_P$ are the amount of changes of the cost and transition functions respectively, and $K$ is the number of episodes.The different roles of $\Delta_c$ and $\Delta_P$ in this lower bound inspire us to design algorithms that estimate costs and transitions separately.Specifically, assuming the knowledge of $\Delta_c$ and $\Delta_P$, we develop a simple but sub-optimal algorithm and another more involved minimax optimal algorithm (up to logarithmic terms).These algorithms combine the ideas of finite-horizon approximation [Chen et al., 2021b], special Bernstein-style bonuses of the MVP algorithm [Zhang et al., 2020], adaptive confidence widening [Wei and Luo, 2021], as well as some new techniques such as properly penalizing long-horizon policies.Finally, when $\Delta_c$ and $\Delta_P$ are unknown, we develop a variant of the MASTER algorithm [Wei and Luo, 2021] and integrate the aforementioned ideas into it to achieve $\widetilde{O}(\min\{B_{\star} S\sqrt{ALK}, (B_{\star}^2S^2AT_{\star}(\Delta_c+B_{\star}\Delta_P))^{1/3}K^{2/3}\})$ regret, where $L$ is the unknown number of changes of the environment.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning to reach a goal when both action costs and environment transitions can change between episodes. It models the task as a non-stationary stochastic shortest path problem and measures dynamic regret, which accounts for the changing optimal behavior. The aim is to characterize how difficult adaptation is and design algorithms that approach that difficulty limit.

The authors first prove a lower bound involving the number of episodes, state-action pairs, optimal-policy costs and hitting times, and the amounts of cost and transition change. These two kinds of change affect the bound differently, motivating separate estimation of costs and transitions. When their total variation amounts are known, the paper gives a simple suboptimal algorithm and a more involved minimax-optimal algorithm up to logarithmic factors.

The algorithms combine finite-horizon approximation, confidence adjustments, exploration bonuses, and penalties for long-horizon policies. When variation amounts are unknown, a modified MASTER approach provides a separate regret guarantee. This distinguishes near-optimal learning with known change budgets from adaptation without that knowledge.
summary.tldr: New regret bounds and algorithms characterize goal-oriented learning under changing costs and transitions, with near-optimality when change budgets are known.

title: Near-Optimal Goal-Oriented Reinforcement Learning in Non-Stationary Environments

abstract: Dynamic pricing is a fast-moving research area in machine learning and operations management. A lot of work has been done for this problem with known noise. In this paper, we consider a contextual dynamic pricing problem under a linear customer valuation model with an unknown market noise distribution $F$. This problem is very challenging due to the difficulty in balancing three tangled tasks of revenue-maximization, estimating the linear valuation parameter $\theta_{0}$, and learning the nonparametric $F$. To address this issue, we develop a novel {\it Explore-then-UCB} (ExUCB) strategy that includes an exploration for $\theta_{0}$-learning and a followed UCB procedure of joint revenue-maximization and $F$-learning. Under Lipschitz and 2nd-order smoothness assumptions on $F$, ExUCB is the first approach to achieve the $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret rate. Under the Lipschitz assumption only, ExUCB matches the best existing regret of $\tilde{O}(T^{3/4})$ and is computationally more efficient. Furthermore, for regret lower bounds under the nonparametric $F$, not much work has been done beyond only assuming Lipschitz. To fill this gap, we provide the first $\tilde{\Omega}(T^{3/5})$ lower bound under Lipschitz and 2nd-order smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper studies pricing when customer value depends linearly on observed context, but market noise has an unknown distribution. A pricing strategy must simultaneously earn revenue, estimate the linear valuation parameters, and learn that noise distribution without specifying a fixed parametric form. These objectives interact because the prices chosen also affect what the seller learns.

Explore-then-UCB separates part of this challenge into stages. It first explores to estimate the valuation parameters, then uses an upper-confidence-bound procedure to combine revenue seeking with learning the noise distribution. Under Lipschitz continuity and second-order smoothness of that distribution, its regret grows at rate T^(2/3), up to logarithmic factors.

With Lipschitz continuity alone, the method matches the best existing T^(3/4) regret rate while improving computational efficiency. The authors also establish a T^(3/5) lower bound, up to logarithmic factors, under the stronger smoothness assumptions. This supplies a benchmark for unavoidable difficulty, although the stated upper and lower rates do not coincide.
summary.tldr: Explore-then-UCB improves contextual pricing regret under smooth unknown noise and establishes a new lower bound for that setting.

title: Contextual Dynamic Pricing with Unknown Noise: Explore-then-UCB Strategy and Improved Regrets

abstract: While significant theoretical progress has been achieved, unveiling the generalization mystery of overparameterized neural networks still remains largely elusive. In this paper, we study the generalization behavior of shallow neural networks (SNNs) by leveraging the concept of algorithmic stability. We consider gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to train SNNs, for both of which we develop consistent excess risk bounds by balancing the optimization and generalization via early-stopping. As compared to existing analysis on GD, our new analysis requires a relaxed overparameterization assumption and also applies to SGD. The key for the improvement is a better estimation of the smallest eigenvalues of the Hessian matrices of the empirical risks and the loss function along the trajectories of GD and SGD by providing a refined estimation of their iterates.

paragraphs: This paper studies why shallow neural networks trained with gradient methods can generalize beyond their training data. It uses algorithmic stability, which connects sensitivity to changes in training data with generalization behavior. The analysis covers both gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent, two common ways to update network parameters.

For both methods, the authors derive consistent excess-risk bounds by using early stopping to balance optimization progress against generalization. The stopping decision is therefore part of the theoretical guarantee. Compared with previous gradient-descent analysis, the new results require a weaker overparameterization assumption and extend the treatment to stochastic gradient descent.

The improvement comes from tracking the optimization iterates more precisely. That refined control gives better estimates of the smallest eigenvalues of Hessian matrices associated with the empirical risk and loss along the training trajectories. These curvature estimates strengthen the stability analysis. The result is a more permissive theoretical account of generalization for the shallow networks studied, explicitly connecting network size assumptions, training dynamics, and when training stops.
summary.tldr: A refined stability analysis gives early-stopping generalization guarantees for shallow networks under a weaker overparameterization assumption.

title: Stability and Generalization Analysis of Gradient Methods for Shallow Neural Networks

abstract: We consider distributed convex optimization problems in the regime when the communication between the server and the workers is expensive in both uplink and downlink directions. We develop a new and provably accelerated method, which we call 2Direction, based on fast bidirectional compressed communication and a new bespoke error-feedback mechanism which may be of independent interest. Indeed, we find that the EF and EF21-P mechanisms (Seide et al., 2014; Gruntkowska et al., 2023) that have considerable success in the design of efficient non-accelerated methods are not appropriate for accelerated methods. In particular, we prove that 2Direction improves the previous state-of-the-art communication complexity $\widetilde{\Theta}\left(K \times \left(\frac{L}{\alpha \mu} + \frac{L_{\max} \omega}{n \mu} + \omega\right)\right)$ (Gruntkowska et al., 2023) to $\widetilde{\Theta}(K \times (\sqrt{\frac{L (\omega + 1)}{\alpha \mu}} + \sqrt{\frac{L_{\max} \omega^2}{n \mu}} + \frac{1}{\alpha} + \omega))$ in the $\mu$--strongly-convex setting, where $L$ and $L_{\max}$ are smoothness constants, $n$ is \# of workers, $\omega$ and $\alpha$ are compression errors of the Rand$K$ and Top$K$ sparsifiers (as examples), $K$ is \# of coordinates/bits that the server and workers send to each other. Moreover, our method is the first that improves upon the communication complexity of the vanilla accelerated gradient descent method (AGD). We obtain similar improvements in the general convex regime as well. Finally, our theoretical findings are corroborated by experimental evidence.

paragraphs: Distributed training can become expensive when workers must repeatedly exchange information with a central server. This paper studies convex optimization when communication is costly in both directions. Its method, 2Direction, combines compressed messages with acceleration, aiming to reduce the communication needed to solve the optimization problem.

The central technical ingredient is a new error-feedback mechanism for handling compression errors. The authors find that two existing mechanisms, EF and EF21-P, which have worked well for non-accelerated methods, are unsuitable for accelerated methods. Their replacement is designed specifically to make bidirectional compression compatible with acceleration.

For strongly convex problems, the paper proves improved communication complexity, replacing some previous dependencies with square-root expressions while accounting for compression quality, smoothness, and worker count. It also reports improvements for general convex problems and identifies 2Direction as the first method to improve on vanilla accelerated gradient descent's communication complexity. Experiments support the theoretical results. The contribution concerns communication efficiency within these optimization settings, with a mechanism tailored to that objective.
summary.tldr: 2Direction combines acceleration, bidirectional compression, and a new error-feedback mechanism to improve communication complexity in distributed convex optimization.

title: 2Direction: Theoretically Faster Distributed Training with Bidirectional Communication Compression

abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT [Khattab et al., 2020] allow token-level interactions between queries and documents, and hence achieve state of the art on many information retrieval benchmarks. However, their non-linear scoring function cannot be scaled to millions of documents, necessitating a three-stage process for inference: retrieving initial candidates via token retrieval, accessing all token vectors, and scoring the initial candidate documents. The non-linear scoring function is applied over all token vectors of each candidate document, making the inference process complicated and slow. In this paper, we aim to simplify the multi-vector retrieval by rethinking the role of token retrieval. We present XTR, ConteXtualized Token Retriever, which introduces a simple, yet novel, objective function that encourages the model to retrieve the most important document tokens first. The improvement to token retrieval allows XTR to rank candidates only using the retrieved tokens rather than all tokens in the document, and enables a newly designed scoring stage that is two-to-three orders of magnitude cheaper than that of ColBERT. On the popular BEIR benchmark, XTR advances the state-of-the-art by 2.8 nDCG@10 without any distillation. Detailed analysis confirms our decision to revisit the token retrieval stage, as XTR demonstrates much better recall of the token retrieval stage compared to ColBERT.

paragraphs: Multi-vector search models compare queries and documents through token-level representations, enabling detailed matching. Their scoring can be expensive at large scale. In the process described here, token retrieval first finds candidate documents, after which all token vectors for each candidate are accessed and used to compute its final score.

XTR changes the training objective so that the first retrieval stage preferentially returns the most important document tokens. Better token selection then allows candidates to be ranked using only the retrieved tokens. This connects retrieval and scoring more tightly: the initial stage gathers evidence that is useful enough to support the final ranking without accessing every token representation in each candidate.

The resulting scoring stage is reported to be two to three orders of magnitude cheaper than ColBERT's. On BEIR, XTR improves the state of the art by 2.8 nDCG@10 without distillation. Further analysis finds substantially better token-retrieval recall than ColBERT. The findings show that improving which tokens are retrieved can simultaneously simplify scoring and improve ranking quality in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: XTR learns to retrieve important document tokens first, enabling cheaper scoring and stronger retrieval performance.

title: Rethinking the Role of Token Retrieval in Multi-Vector Retrieval

abstract: To ensure secure and dependable mobility in environments shared by humans and robots, social navigation robots should possess the capability to accurately perceive and predict the trajectories of nearby pedestrians. In this paper, we present a novel dataset of pedestrian trajectories, referred to as Social Interactive Trajectory (SiT) dataset, which can be used to train pedestrian detection, tracking, and trajectory prediction models needed to design social navigation robots. Our dataset includes sequential raw data captured by two 3D LiDARs and five cameras covering a 360-degree view, two inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors, and real-time kinematic positioning (RTK), as well as annotations including 2D & 3D boxes, object classes, and object IDs. Thus far, various human trajectory datasets have been introduced to support the development of pedestrian motion forecasting models. Our SiT dataset differs from these datasets in the following two respects. First, whereas the pedestrian trajectory data in other datasets was obtained from static scenes, our data was collected while the robot navigates in a crowded environment, capturing human-robot interactive scenarios in motion. Second, our dataset has been carefully organized to facilitate training and evaluation of end-to-end prediction models encompassing 3D detection, 3D multi-object tracking, and trajectory prediction. This design allows for an end-to-end unified modular approach across different tasks. We have introduced a comprehensive benchmark for assessing models across all aforementioned tasks, and have showcased the performance of multiple baseline models as part of our evaluation. Our dataset provides a strong foundation for future research in pedestrian trajectory prediction, which could expedite the development of safe and agile social navigation robots. The SiT dataset, devkit, and pre-trained models are publicly released at: https://spalaboratory.github.io/SiT

Our dataset provides a strong foundation for future research in pedestrian trajectory prediction, which could expedite the development of safe and agile social navigation robots. The SiT dataset, devkit, and pre-trained models are publicly released at: https://spalaboratory.github.io/SiT

paragraphs: Social navigation robots need to detect nearby people, track them, and predict where they will move. SiT is a pedestrian-trajectory dataset designed to support this connected set of tasks. Its recordings were collected while a robot moved through crowded environments, capturing interactions between pedestrians and a moving robot.

The dataset includes sequential measurements from two 3D LiDARs, five cameras providing a full surrounding view, two inertial sensors, and real-time kinematic positioning. Annotations include two-dimensional and three-dimensional boxes, object categories, and identifiers. These complementary data types support following objects over time and relating their trajectories to the robot's changing surroundings.

SiT is organized for training and evaluating a unified pipeline spanning 3D detection, multi-object tracking, and trajectory prediction. The authors provide a benchmark covering these tasks and evaluate multiple baseline models. They also release the dataset, development tools, and pretrained models publicly. The contribution is a shared resource for studying pedestrian prediction in moving human-robot interactions, with potential to support safer and more agile navigation.
summary.tldr: SiT provides sensor recordings and annotations from a moving robot to benchmark pedestrian detection, tracking, and trajectory prediction.

title: SiT Dataset: Socially Interactive Pedestrian Trajectory Dataset for Social Navigation Robots

abstract: Photos serve as a way for humans to record what they experience in their daily lives, and they are often regarded as trustworthy sources of information. However, there is a growing concern that the advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) technology may produce fake photos, which can create confusion and diminish trust in photographs. This study aims to comprehensively evaluate agents for distinguishing state-of-the-art AI-generated visual content. Our study benchmarks both human capability and cutting-edge fake image detection AI algorithms, using a newly collected large-scale fake image dataset Fake2M. In our human perception evaluation, titled HPBench, we discovered that humans struggle significantly to distinguish real photos from AI-generated ones, with a misclassification rate of 38.7\%. Along with this, we conduct the model capability of AI-Generated images detection evaluation MPBench and the top-performing model from MPBench achieves a 13\% failure rate under the same setting used in the human evaluation.We hope that our study can raise awareness of the potential risks of AI-generated images and facilitate further research to prevent the spread of false information. More information can refer to https://github.com/Inf-imagine/Sentry.
