paragraphs: This paper evaluates how well people and automated detectors distinguish real photographs from AI-generated images. Its motivation is that realistic synthetic imagery can confuse viewers and weaken trust in photographs. The authors introduce Fake2M, a large-scale fake-image dataset, to support a systematic evaluation of both human and model capabilities.

The human evaluation, HPBench, finds a misclassification rate of 38.7%. The model evaluation, MPBench, tests fake-image detection algorithms; its best-performing model has a 13% failure rate under the same setting used for the human evaluation. This shared setting makes the reported human and model results directly relevant to the same detection challenge.

The findings show substantial difficulty for human observers and remaining errors even for the strongest tested detector. They provide benchmark evidence about detection performance in the evaluated setting, helping characterize the problem posed by convincing generated images. The authors intend the dataset and evaluations to raise awareness and support further research aimed at limiting the spread of false information.
summary.tldr: Fake2M-based evaluations find substantial human difficulty detecting AI-generated images and a 13% failure rate for the best tested detector.

title: Seeing is not always believing: Benchmarking Human and Model Perception of AI-Generated Images

abstract: In self-supervised representation learning, Siamese networks are a natural architecture for learning transformation-invariance by bringing representations of positive pairs closer together. But it is prone to collapse into a degenerate solution. To address the issue, in contrastive learning, a contrastive loss is used to prevent collapse by moving representations of negative pairs away from each other. But it is known that algorithms with negative sampling are not robust to a reduction in the number of negative samples. So, on the other hand, there are algorithms that do not use negative pairs. Many positive-only algorithms adopt asymmetric network architecture consisting of source and target encoders as a key factor in coping with collapse. By exploiting the asymmetric architecture, we introduce a methodology to implicitly incorporate the idea of contrastive learning. As its implementation, we present a novel method guided stop-gradient. We apply our method to benchmark algorithms SimSiam and BYOL and show that our method stabilizes training and boosts performance. We also show that the algorithms with our method work well with small batch sizes and do not collapse even when there is no predictor. The code is available in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Self-supervised Siamese networks learn by bringing representations of related views closer together. A central danger is collapse, where the learned representations become degenerate. Contrastive methods counter this by separating negative pairs, but their performance can be sensitive to having fewer negatives. Positive-only methods often instead rely on asymmetry between source and target encoders.

This paper uses that asymmetric architecture to incorporate the idea of contrastive learning implicitly. Its implementation, guided stop-gradient, changes how the learning process uses the source–target arrangement. The contribution connects the motivation behind contrastive learning with the architecture used by positive-only methods, offering a way to address collapse within that setting.

The authors apply guided stop-gradient to SimSiam and BYOL. They report more stable training and better performance for both benchmark algorithms. The resulting methods also work well with small batches and avoid collapse even when the predictor is absent. These findings show that the proposed mechanism can support useful representations under the specific architectural and batch-size variations evaluated.
summary.tldr: Guided stop-gradient introduces implicit contrastive learning into asymmetric networks, improving SimSiam and BYOL while resisting collapse.

title: Implicit Contrastive Representation Learning with Guided Stop-gradient

abstract: Systems of interacting objects often evolve under the influence of underlying field effects that govern their dynamics, yet previous works have abstracted away from such effects, and assume that systems evolve in a vacuum. In this work, we focus on discovering these fields, and infer them from the observed dynamics alone, without directly observing them. We theorize the presence of latent force fields, and propose neural fields to learn them. Since the observed dynamics constitute the net effect of local object interactions and global field effects, recently popularized equivariant networks are inapplicable, as they fail to capture global information. To address this, we propose to disentangle local object interactions --which are SE(3) equivariant and depend on relative states-- from external global field effects --which depend on absolute states. We model the interactions with equivariant graph networks, and combine them with neural fields in a novel graph network that integrates field forces. Our experiments show that we can accurately discover the underlying fields in charged particles settings, traffic scenes, and gravitational n-body problems, and effectively use them to learn the system and forecast future trajectories.

paragraphs: Observed motion can reflect both interactions among objects and a shared external field. A model that accounts only for object interactions can miss this global influence. This paper aims to recover underlying force fields from trajectories alone, without directly observing the fields responsible for part of the motion.

The method separates local interactions, which depend on relative states, from external field effects, which depend on absolute states. Equivariant graph networks model the local component, respecting how those interactions transform under rotations and translations. Neural fields represent the global component. A combined graph network incorporates both contributions when modeling the system's dynamics.

This separation addresses the inability of the discussed equivariant interaction models to capture the needed global information. Experiments in charged-particle systems, traffic scenes, and gravitational n-body problems show accurate recovery of underlying fields. The recovered fields also help the model learn system behavior and forecast future trajectories. The results support modeling global influences explicitly when the observed motion combines environmental effects with interactions among individual objects.
summary.tldr: Combining neural fields with equivariant graph networks recovers hidden global influences from motion and improves trajectory modeling.

title: Latent Field Discovery in Interacting Dynamical Systems with Neural Fields

abstract: Recent advances in constrained reinforcement learning (RL) have endowed reinforcement learning with certain safety guarantees. However, deploying existing constrained RL algorithms in continuous control tasks with general hard constraints remains challenging, particularly in those situations with non-convex hard constraints. Inspired by the generalized reduced gradient (GRG) algorithm, a classical constrained optimization technique, we propose a reduced policy optimization (RPO) algorithm that combines RL with GRG to address general hard constraints. RPO partitions actions into basic actions and nonbasic actions following the GRG method and outputs the basic actions via a policy network. Subsequently, RPO calculates the nonbasic actions by solving equations based on equality constraints using the obtained basic actions. The policy network is then updated by implicitly differentiating nonbasic actions with respect to basic actions. Additionally, we introduce an action projection procedure based on the reduced gradient and apply a modified Lagrangian relaxation technique to ensure inequality constraints are satisfied. To the best of our knowledge, RPO is the first attempt that introduces GRG to RL as a way of efficiently handling both equality and inequality hard constraints. It is worth noting that there is currently a lack of RL environments with complex hard constraints, which motivates us to develop three new benchmarks: two robotics manipulation tasks and a smart grid operation control task. With these benchmarks, RPO achieves better performance than previous constrained RL algorithms in terms of both cumulative reward and constraint violation. We believe RPO, along with the new benchmarks, will open up new opportunities for applying RL to real-world problems with complex constraints.

paragraphs: Continuous control becomes difficult when actions must satisfy hard constraints, especially non-convex ones. Reduced Policy Optimization combines reinforcement learning with the generalized reduced gradient method from constrained optimization. Its aim is to handle equality and inequality constraints within the action-generation and learning process, rather than relying only on a conventional constrained reinforcement learning formulation.

RPO partitions each action into basic and nonbasic components. A policy network produces the basic components, and equations derived from equality constraints determine the remaining ones. Training uses implicit differentiation to account for how the solved components change with the network's outputs. A reduced-gradient projection procedure and modified Lagrangian relaxation address inequality constraints.

The authors also introduce three benchmarks because existing reinforcement learning environments offer limited coverage of complex hard constraints. These comprise two robotic manipulation tasks and a smart grid control task. On those benchmarks, RPO improves both cumulative reward and constraint violation relative to previous constrained reinforcement learning algorithms. The work therefore contributes both a constraint-aware optimization method and environments for evaluating it.
summary.tldr: RPO combines reinforcement learning with reduced-gradient optimization to handle hard action constraints and improves results on three new benchmarks.

title: Reduced Policy Optimization for Continuous Control with Hard Constraints

abstract: Soft prompt tuning achieves superior performances across a wide range of few-shot tasks. However, the performances of prompt tuning can be highly sensitive to the initialization of the prompts. We have also empirically observed that conventional prompt tuning methods cannot encode and learn sufficient task-relevant information from prompt tokens. In this work, we develop an information-theoretic framework that formulates soft prompt tuning as maximizing the mutual information between prompts and other model parameters (or encoded representations). This novel view helps us to develop a more efficient, accurate and robust soft prompt tuning method, InfoPrompt. With this framework, we develop two novel mutual information based loss functions, to (i) explore proper prompt initialization for the downstream tasks and learn sufficient task-relevant information from prompt tokens and (ii) encourage the output representation from the pretrained language model to be more aware of the task-relevant information captured in the learnt prompts. Extensive experiments validate that InfoPrompt can significantly accelerate the convergence of the prompt tuning and outperform traditional prompt tuning methods. Finally, we provide a formal theoretical result to show that a gradient descent type algorithm can be used to train our mutual information loss.

paragraphs: Soft prompt tuning adapts a language model using learned prompt tokens, but its performance can depend strongly on how those tokens are initialized. The authors also observe that conventional methods may fail to learn enough task-relevant information in the prompts. InfoPrompt addresses both issues through an information-theoretic formulation of prompt learning.

The framework treats tuning as maximizing mutual information between prompts and other model parameters or encoded representations. It introduces two losses with complementary roles. One supports suitable initialization and helps prompt tokens learn task-relevant information; the other encourages the pretrained model’s output representation to reflect the information captured by those learned prompts.

Experiments show that InfoPrompt can converge significantly faster and outperform traditional prompt-tuning methods. The paper also provides a theoretical result showing that a gradient-descent-type algorithm can train the proposed mutual-information loss. The contribution connects what the prompts learn with how that information appears in the model’s representations, while supplying both experimental evidence and a formal basis for optimizing the objective.
summary.tldr: InfoPrompt uses mutual-information objectives to improve soft-prompt initialization, task information, and convergence in the reported experiments.

title: InfoPrompt: Information-Theoretic Soft Prompt Tuning for Natural Language Understanding

abstract: Bilevel optimization has recently regained interest owing to its applications in emerging machine learning fields such as hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and reinforcement learning. Recent results have shown that simple alternating (implicit) gradient-based algorithms can match the convergence rate of single-level gradient descent (GD) when addressing bilevel problems with a strongly convex lower-level objective. However, it remains unclear whether this result can be generalized to bilevel problems beyond this basic setting. In this paper, we first introduce a stationary metric for the considered bilevel problems, which generalizes the existing metric, for a nonconvex lower-level objective that satisfies the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. We then propose a Generalized ALternating mEthod for bilevel opTimization (GALET) tailored to BLO with convex PL LL problem and establish that GALET achieves an $\epsilon$-stationary point for the considered problem within $\tilde{\cal O}(\epsilon^{-1})$ iterations, which matches the iteration complexity of GD for single-level smooth nonconvex problems.

In this paper, we first introduce a stationary metric for the considered bilevel problems, which generalizes the existing metric, for a nonconvex lower-level objective that satisfies the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links two optimization problems: the upper problem depends on the solution of a lower one. This structure appears in hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, and reinforcement learning. Prior results showed that simple alternating gradient methods can match the convergence rate of ordinary gradient descent when the lower objective is strongly convex. The paper asks how far that result extends.

The authors first introduce a generalized measure of stationarity for problems whose lower objective may be nonconvex but satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. This gives a way to describe progress toward an appropriate stationary solution in a broader setting. They then propose GALET, an alternating algorithm tailored specifically to a convex lower problem satisfying that condition.

For that convex PL setting, GALET reaches an epsilon-stationary point within roughly inverse-epsilon iterations, up to logarithmic factors. This matches the stated iteration complexity of gradient descent for smooth, nonconvex single-level problems. The distinction between the broader stationarity definition and the narrower algorithmic guarantee matters: the abstract does not extend GALET's guarantee to every nonconvex PL lower objective.
summary.tldr: GALET matches a single-level gradient-descent iteration rate for bilevel problems with a convex PL lower objective.

title: An Alternating Optimization Method for Bilevel Problems under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz Condition

abstract: The recent progress in text-to-image models pretrained on large-scale datasets has enabled us to generate various images as long as we provide a text prompt describing what we want. Nevertheless, the availability of these models is still limited when we expect to generate images that fall into a specific domain either hard to describe or just unseen to the models. In this work, we propose DomainGallery, a few-shot domain-driven image generation method which aims at finetuning pretrained Stable Diffusion on few-shot target datasets in an attribute-centric manner. Specifically, DomainGallery features prior attribute erasure, attribute disentanglement, regularization and enhancement. These techniques are tailored to few-shot domain-driven generation in order to solve key issues that previous works have failed to settle. Extensive experiments are given to validate the superior performance of DomainGallery on a variety of domain-driven generation scenarios.

paragraphs: Text-to-image models can generate many kinds of images from written descriptions, but a prompt may not adequately specify a particular visual domain. The desired domain may be difficult to describe or absent from the model’s prior experience. DomainGallery tackles this situation by adapting pretrained Stable Diffusion using a small target dataset.

The method organizes fine-tuning around attributes rather than relying only on a verbal description of the domain. Its components include erasing prior attributes, separating attributes, regularizing the adaptation, and enhancing attributes. Together, these operations are designed for the specific difficulties of domain-driven generation from few examples. The target examples provide the adaptation signal for visual characteristics that prompting alone may not capture.

The authors report extensive experiments showing superior performance across a variety of domain-driven generation scenarios. The finding supports attribute-focused fine-tuning as a way to adapt an existing image generator to narrowly specified visual data. The contribution concerns learning a target domain from limited examples; it does not require that users first find a complete textual description of that domain.
summary.tldr: DomainGallery adapts Stable Diffusion to visual domains represented by few examples through attribute-focused fine-tuning.

title: DomainGallery: Few-shot Domain-driven Image Generation by Attribute-centric Finetuning

abstract: Mobile device operation tasks are increasingly becoming a popular multi-modal AI application scenario. Current Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), constrained by their training data, lack the capability to function effectively as operation assistants. Instead, MLLM-based agents, which enhance capabilities through tool invocation, are gradually being applied to this scenario. However, the two major navigation challenges in mobile device operation tasks — task progress navigation and focus content navigation — are difficult to effectively solve under the single-agent architecture of existing work. This is due to the overly long token sequences and the interleaved text-image data format, which limit performance. To address these navigation challenges effectively, we propose Mobile-Agent-v2, a multi-agent architecture for mobile device operation assistance. The architecture comprises three agents: planning agent, decision agent, and reflection agent. The planning agent condenses lengthy, interleaved image-text history operations and screens summaries into a pure-text task progress, which is then passed on to the decision agent. This reduction in context length makes it easier for decision agent to navigate the task progress. To retain focus content, we design a memory unit that updates with task progress by decision agent. Additionally, to correct erroneous operations, the reflection agent observes the outcomes of each operation and handles any mistake accordingly. Experimental results indicate that Mobile-Agent-v2 achieves over a 30% improvement in task completion compared to the single-agent architecture of Mobile-Agent. The code is open-sourced at https://github.com/X-PLUG/MobileAgent.

paragraphs: A mobile assistant must keep track of what it has already accomplished and which screen content remains relevant. Long histories mixing screenshots and text make both tasks difficult for a single multimodal agent. Mobile-Agent-v2 addresses this navigation problem by distributing responsibility among planning, decision, and reflection agents.

The planning agent converts the operation history and screen summaries into a concise, text-only account of task progress. The decision agent uses that account to choose subsequent actions, reducing the amount of mixed visual and textual history it must process. A memory unit retains relevant content and is updated as the task advances, helping preserve information that would otherwise be lost during summarization.

The reflection agent examines the outcome of each operation and responds to mistakes. Together, these components separate progress tracking, action selection, and error handling while maintaining shared task context. Experiments report more than a 30% improvement in task completion over the single-agent Mobile-Agent architecture. This supports the value of coordinated roles and explicit memory for the evaluated mobile-operation tasks.
summary.tldr: Mobile-Agent-v2 coordinates planning, decision, and reflection agents to improve task tracking, relevant-content memory, and mobile-operation completion.

title: Mobile-Agent-v2: Mobile Device Operation Assistant with Effective Navigation via Multi-Agent Collaboration

abstract: Offline optimization has recently emerged as an increasingly popular approach to mitigate the prohibitively expensive cost of online experimentation. The key idea is to learn a surrogate of the black-box function that underlines the target experiment using a static (offline) dataset of its previous input-output queries. Such an approach is, however, fraught with an out-of-distribution issue where the learned surrogate becomes inaccurate outside the offline data regimes. To mitigate this, existing offline optimizers have proposed numerous conditioning techniques to prevent the learned surrogate from being too erratic. Nonetheless, such conditioning strategies are often specific to particular surrogate or search models, which might not generalize to a different model choice. This motivates us to develop a model-agnostic approach instead, which incorporates a notion of model sharpness into the training loss of the surrogate as a regularizer. Our approach is supported by a new theoretical analysis demonstrating that reducing surrogate sharpness on the offline dataset provably reduces its generalized sharpness on unseen data. Our analysis extends existing theories from bounding generalized prediction loss (on unseen data) with loss sharpness to bounding the worst-case generalized surrogate sharpness with its empirical estimate on training data, providing a new perspective on sharpness regularization. Our extensive experimentation on a diverse range of optimization tasks also shows that reducing surrogate sharpness often leads to significant improvement, marking (up to) a noticeable 9.6% performance boost. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/cuong-dm/IGNITE.

paragraphs: Offline optimization uses past experiment results to learn a surrogate for an expensive black-box function. The surrogate then guides optimization without requiring new experiments during learning. A central difficulty is that its predictions can become unreliable outside the regions represented in the fixed dataset, potentially misleading the search.

The authors propose adding a sharpness regularizer to the surrogate's training loss. Their approach is intended to work across model choices, addressing the specificity of earlier conditioning methods. The theoretical analysis connects reduced sharpness on the offline dataset with reduced generalized sharpness on unseen data, bounding worst-case generalized sharpness through an empirical estimate.

This shifts the theoretical focus from prediction-loss bounds to control of how sharply the learned surrogate behaves beyond its training examples. Experiments across diverse optimization tasks show that reducing surrogate sharpness often improves performance, with gains reaching 9.6%. The reported benefit is therefore both theoretical and empirical: the regularizer has a justification related to unseen-data behavior and produces useful improvements in the tested optimization settings.
summary.tldr: Regularizing surrogate sharpness offers a model-agnostic way to improve offline optimization, with theoretical support and reported gains of up to 9.6%.

title: Incorporating Surrogate Gradient Norm to Improve Offline Optimization Techniques

abstract: Entity alignment (EA) aims to merge two knowledge graphs (KGs) by identifying equivalent entity pairs. While existing methods heavily rely on human-generated labels, it is prohibitively expensive to incorporate cross-domain experts for annotation in real-world scenarios. The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents new avenues for automating EA with annotations, inspired by their comprehensive capability to process semantic information. However, it is nontrivial to directly apply LLMs for EA since the annotation space in real-world KGs is large. LLMs could also generate noisy labels that may mislead the alignment. To this end, we propose a unified framework, LLM4EA, to effectively leverage LLMs for EA. Specifically, we design a novel active learning policy to significantly reduce the annotation space by prioritizing the most valuable entities based on the entire inter-KG and intra-KG structure. Moreover, we introduce an unsupervised label refiner to continuously enhance label accuracy through in-depth probabilistic reasoning. We iteratively optimize the policy based on the feedback from a base EA model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the advantages of LLM4EA on four benchmark datasets in terms of effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency.

While existing methods heavily rely on human-generated labels, it is prohibitively expensive to incorporate cross-domain experts for annotation in real-world scenarios. The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) presents new avenues for automating EA with annotations, inspired by their comprehensive capability to process semantic information. However, it is nontrivial to directly apply LLMs for EA since the annotation space in real-world KGs is large. LLMs could also generate noisy labels that may mislead the alignment. To this end, we propose a unified framework, LLM4EA, to effectively leverage LLMs for EA. Specifically, we design a novel active learning policy to significantly reduce the annotation space by prioritizing the most valuable entities based on the entire inter-KG and intra-KG structure. Moreover, we introduce an unsupervised label refiner to continuously enhance label accuracy through in-depth probabilistic reasoning. We iteratively optimize the policy based on the feedback from a base EA model. Extensive experiments demonstrate the advantages of LLM4EA on four benchmark datasets in terms of effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency.

paragraphs: Entity alignment identifies entries in two knowledge graphs that refer to the same entity, enabling the graphs to be merged. Human labels can be costly because annotation may require expertise across domains. LLM4EA investigates using language models to supply annotations while addressing two obstacles: the large space of possible matches and errors in generated labels.

The framework uses an active-learning policy to prioritize valuable entities for annotation. That policy considers relationships both within each graph and across the two graphs, reducing the annotation space. An unsupervised label-refinement component then uses probabilistic reasoning to improve label accuracy, rather than treating every language-model annotation as reliable.

The process is iterative: feedback from an underlying entity-alignment model helps improve the selection policy. Experiments on four benchmark datasets report advantages in effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency. The approach matters because it treats annotation selection and annotation quality as connected problems. Language-model semantic knowledge becomes part of a feedback-driven alignment system that explicitly accounts for noisy labels.
summary.tldr: LLM4EA combines selective language-model annotation, probabilistic label refinement, and alignment-model feedback to match entities across knowledge graphs.

title: Entity Alignment with Noisy Annotations from Large Language Models

abstract: Species range maps (SRMs) are essential tools for research and policy-making in ecology, conservation, and environmental management. However, traditional SRMs rely on the availability of environmental covariates and high-quality observational data, both of which can be challenging to obtain due to geographic inaccessibility and resource constraints. We propose a novel approach combining millions of citizen science species observations with textual descriptions from Wikipedia, covering habitat preferences and range descriptions for tens of thousands of species. Our framework maps location, species, and text descriptions into a common space, facilitating the learning of rich spatial covariates at a global scale and enabling zero-shot range estimation from textual descriptions. Evaluated on held-out species, our zero-shot SRMs significantly outperform baselines and match the performance of SRMs obtained using tens of observations. Our approach also acts as a strong prior when combined with observational data, resulting in more accurate range estimation with less data. We present extensive quantitative and qualitative analyses of the learned representations in the context of range estimation and other spatial tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Species range maps estimate where a species occurs and support conservation, ecology, and environmental decisions. Traditional approaches depend on environmental measurements and reliable observations, which can be difficult to obtain in inaccessible or poorly resourced regions. This paper investigates how written descriptions can complement observations when estimating geographic ranges.

The framework combines millions of citizen science observations with Wikipedia descriptions of habitat preferences and geographic ranges for tens of thousands of species. It represents locations, species, and text in a common space. This shared representation learns spatial information globally and allows a range estimate to be produced from a species description without observations of that species.

On held-out species, these zero-shot estimates significantly outperform baselines and match estimates built from tens of observations. When observations are available, the language-informed representation also supplies a strong prior, improving range estimation with less data. Quantitative and qualitative analyses examine both range estimation and other spatial tasks. Together, the findings show how descriptive knowledge can support prediction for species with scarce observational records.
summary.tldr: A shared representation of species, locations, and text enables useful range maps from descriptions and improves estimates when observations are scarce.

title: Combining Observational Data and Language for Species Range Estimation

abstract: We present the ShareGPT4Video series, aiming to facilitate the video understanding of large video-language models (LVLMs) and the video generation of text-to-video models (T2VMs) via dense and precise captions. The series comprises: 1) ShareGPT4Video, 40K GPT4V annotated dense captions of videos with various lengths and sources, developed through carefully designed data filtering and annotating strategy. 2) ShareCaptioner-Video, an efficient and capable captioning model for arbitrary videos, with 4.8M high-quality aesthetic videos annotated by it. 3) ShareGPT4Video-8B, a simple yet superb LVLM that reached SOTA performance on three advancing video benchmarks. To achieve this, taking aside the non-scalable costly human annotators, we find using GPT4V to caption video with a naive multi-frame or frame-concatenation input strategy leads to less detailed and sometimes temporal-confused results. We argue the challenge of designing a high-quality video captioning strategy lies in three aspects: 1) Inter-frame precise temporal change understanding. 2) Intra-frame detailed content description. 3) Frame-number scalability for arbitrary-length videos. To this end, we meticulously designed a differential video captioning strategy, which is stable, scalable, and efficient for generating captions for videos with arbitrary resolution, aspect ratios, and length. Based on it, we construct ShareGPT4Video, which contains 40K high-quality videos spanning a wide range of categories, and the resulting captions encompass rich world knowledge, object attributes, camera movements, and crucially, detailed and precise temporal descriptions of events. Based on ShareGPT4Video, we further develop ShareCaptioner-Video, a superior captioner capable of efficiently generating high-quality captions for arbitrary videos. We annotated 4.8M aesthetically appealing videos by it and verified their effectiveness on a 10-second text2video generation task. For video understanding, we verified the effectiveness of ShareGPT4Video on several current LVLM architectures and presented our superb new LVLM ShareGPT4Video-8B. All the models, strategies, and annotations will be open-sourced and we hope this project can serve as a pivotal resource for advancing both the LVLMs and T2VMs community.

summary.tldr: ShareGPT4Video combines detailed temporal captioning, large-scale annotations, and video models to improve video understanding and text-to-video generation.

title: ShareGPT4Video: Improving Video Understanding and Generation with Better Captions

abstract: Recommender systems aim to predict personalized rankings based on user preference data. With the rise of Language Models (LMs), LM-based recommenders have been widely explored due to their extensive world knowledge and powerful reasoning abilities. Most of the LM-based recommenders convert historical interactions into language prompts, pairing with a positive item as the target response and fine-tuning LM with a language modeling loss. However, the current objective fails to fully leverage preference data and is not optimized for personalized ranking tasks, which hinders the performance of LM-based recommenders. Inspired by the current advancement of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in human preference alignment and the success of softmax loss in recommendations, we propose Softmax-DPO (\textbf{S-DPO}) to instill ranking information into the LM to help LM-based recommenders distinguish preferred items from negatives, rather than solely focusing on positives. Specifically, we incorporate multiple negatives in user preference data and devise an alternative version of DPO loss tailored for LM-based recommenders, which is extended from the traditional full-ranking Plackett-Luce (PL) model to partial rankings and connected to softmax sampling strategies. Theoretically, we bridge S-DPO with the softmax loss over negative sampling and find that it has an inherent benefit of mining hard negatives, which assures its exceptional capabilities in recommendation tasks. Empirically, extensive experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of S-DPO to effectively model user preference and further boost recommendation performance while providing better rewards for preferred items. Our codes are available at https://github.com/chenyuxin1999/S-DPO.

paragraphs: Language-model recommenders often learn by turning a user's interaction history into a prompt and training the model to produce a positive item. The paper argues that this objective underuses preference information because personalized recommendation also requires distinguishing preferred items from alternatives. Predicting positives alone does not directly express that ranking task.

Softmax-DPO introduces multiple negative items into preference optimization. Its objective adapts direct preference optimization to recommendation by extending a full-ranking Plackett-Luce formulation to partial rankings and connecting it to softmax sampling. This allows training to encode comparisons between preferred items and several alternatives within the recommendation objective.

The theoretical analysis connects the proposed loss to softmax loss with negative sampling and identifies an inherent hard-negative mining benefit: difficult alternatives receive useful attention during learning. Experiments on three real-world datasets show improved preference modeling and recommendation performance, along with better rewards for preferred items. The contribution is an objective that more directly connects language-model training to personalized ranking.
summary.tldr: Softmax-DPO trains language-model recommenders with multiple negative items to incorporate ranking information and improve recommendation performance.

title: On Softmax Direct Preference Optimization for Recommendation

abstract: Uniformity testing is arguably one of the most fundamental distribution testing problems. Given sample access to an unknown distribution $\mathbf{p}$ on $[n]$, one must decide if $\mathbf{p}$ is uniform or $\varepsilon$-far from uniform (in total variation distance). A long line of work established that uniformity testing has sample complexity $\Theta(\sqrt{n}\varepsilon^{-2})$. However, when the input distribution is neither uniform nor far from uniform, known algorithms may have highly non-replicable behavior. Consequently, if these algorithms are applied in scientific studies, they may lead to contradictory results that erode public trust in science.In this work, we revisit uniformity testing under the framework of algorithmic replicability [STOC '22], requiring the algorithm to be replicable under arbitrary distributions. While replicability typically incurs a $\rho^{-2}$ factor overhead in sample complexity, we obtain a replicable uniformity tester using only $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n} \varepsilon^{-2} \rho^{-1})$ samples. To our knowledge, this is the first replicable learning algorithm with (nearly) linear dependence on $\rho$.Lastly, we consider a class of ``symmetric" algorithms [FOCS '00] whose outputs are invariant under relabeling of the domain $[n]$, which includes all existing uniformity testers (including ours). For this natural class of algorithms, we prove a nearly matching sample complexity lower bound for replicable uniformity testing.

paragraphs: Uniformity testing asks whether an unknown distribution assigns equal probability to n possible outcomes or is at least epsilon away from doing so in total variation distance. Standard methods need on the order of sqrt(n)/epsilon² samples. However, distributions between those two cases can produce inconsistent conclusions across repeated applications.

This paper requires replicability for arbitrary input distributions, including those intermediate cases. The authors construct a tester with sample complexity approximately sqrt(n)/(epsilon² rho), up to logarithmic factors, where rho controls the replicability requirement. The dependence on inverse rho is nearly linear, improving on the inverse-square overhead that replicability typically introduces.

The authors also prove a nearly matching lower bound for symmetric algorithms, whose outputs do not change when domain elements are relabeled. This class includes their method and all existing uniformity testers described in the abstract. The result therefore pairs a more sample-efficient replicable procedure with evidence that its sample requirements are close to unavoidable within this natural class of algorithms.
summary.tldr: A replicable uniformity tester achieves nearly linear inverse dependence on the replicability parameter, with a nearly matching lower bound for symmetric algorithms.

title: Replicable Uniformity Testing

abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) models maximize the mutual information between text and visual modalities to learn representations. This makes the nature of the training data a significant factor in the efficacy of CLIP for downstream tasks. However, the lack of compositional diversity in contemporary image-text datasets limits the compositional reasoning ability of CLIP. We show that generating ``hard'' negative captions via in-context learning and synthesizing corresponding negative images with text-to-image generators offers a solution. We introduce a novel contrastive pre-training strategy that leverages these hard negative captions and images in an alternating fashion to train CLIP. We demonstrate that our method, named TripletCLIP, when applied to existing datasets such as CC3M and CC12M, enhances the compositional capabilities of CLIP, resulting in an absolute improvement of over 9% on the SugarCrepe benchmark on an equal computational budget, as well as improvements in zero-shot image classification and image retrieval. Our code, models, and data are available at: tripletclip.github.io.

paragraphs: TripletCLIP addresses compositional reasoning in models that learn to connect images and text. The paper argues that limited compositional diversity in training datasets restricts how well CLIP understands combinations of visual and linguistic content. It therefore changes the examples used during contrastive pretraining to make these distinctions more explicit.

The method generates challenging negative captions through in-context learning, then uses text-to-image generators to produce corresponding negative images. A new contrastive training strategy alternates the use of these negative captions and images. Providing challenging alternatives in both modalities gives the model training signals about distinctions that ordinary paired data may not adequately emphasize.

Applied to existing datasets including CC3M and CC12M, TripletCLIP improves compositional capability. The paper reports an absolute improvement exceeding 9% on SugarCrepe under an equal computational budget, as well as gains in zero-shot image classification and image retrieval. These results support synthetic negative examples as a useful way to improve the content of contrastive supervision, with benefits extending beyond the targeted compositional benchmark.
summary.tldr: TripletCLIP improves compositional reasoning by alternating synthetic hard negative captions and images during contrastive pretraining.

title: TripletCLIP: Improving Compositional Reasoning of CLIP via Synthetic Vision-Language Negatives

abstract: Deep learning on tabular data, and particularly tabular representation learning, has recently gained growing interest. However, representation learning for relational databases with multiple tables is still an underexplored area, which may be attributed to the lack of openly available resources. To support the development of foundation models for tabular data and relational databases, we introduce WikiDBs, a novel open-source corpus of 100,000 relational databases. Each database consists of multiple tables connected by foreign keys. The corpus is based on Wikidata and aims to follow certain characteristics of real-world databases. In this paper, we describe the dataset and our method for creating it. By making our code publicly available, we enable others to create tailored versions of the dataset, for example, by creating databases in different languages. Finally, we conduct a set of initial experiments to showcase how WikiDBs can be used to train for data engineering tasks, such as missing value imputation and column type annotation.

paragraphs: Learning useful representations for tables has attracted attention, but databases containing several related tables remain less explored. One obstacle is the shortage of open resources for training and studying such systems. WikiDBs addresses this need with an open-source collection of 100,000 relational databases derived from Wikidata.

Each database contains multiple tables connected through foreign keys, which express relationships between records in different tables. The collection is designed to reflect selected characteristics of real-world databases. The paper describes both the resource and its construction method, making the generation process part of the contribution alongside the resulting data.

Publicly available code allows researchers to create tailored variants, including databases in different languages. Initial experiments illustrate training for missing-value imputation and column-type annotation. These demonstrations show concrete uses for the corpus rather than establishing a universal advantage for a particular model. The broader purpose is to provide material for developing foundation models that can learn from tables together with the relationships connecting them.
summary.tldr: WikiDBs supplies 100,000 connected, multitable databases and generation code to support learning for relational data and data-engineering tasks.

title: WikiDBs: A Large-Scale Corpus Of Relational Databases From Wikidata

abstract: Numerous studies have demonstrated that the cognitive processes of the human brain can be modeled using the Bayesian theorem for probabilistic inference of the external world. Spiking neural networks (SNNs), capable of performing Bayesian computation with greater physiological interpretability, offer a novel approach to distributed information processing in the cortex. However, applying these models to real-world scenarios to harness the advantages of brain-like computation remains a challenge. Recently, bio-inspired sensors with high dynamic range and ultra-high temporal resolution have been widely used in extreme vision scenarios. Event streams, generated by various types of motion, represent spatiotemporal data. Inferring motion targets from these streams without prior knowledge remains a difficult task. The Bayesian inference-based Expectation-Maximization (EM) framework has proven effective for motion segmentation in event streams, allowing for decoupling without prior information about the motion or its source. This work demonstrates that Bayesian computation based on spiking neural networks can decouple event streams of different motions. The Winner-Take-All (WTA) circuits in the constructed network implement an equivalent E-step, while STDP achieves an equivalent optimization in M-step. Through theoretical analysis and experiments, we show that STDP-based learning can maximize the contrast of warped events under mixed motion models. Experimental results show that the constructed spiking network can effectively segment the motion contained in event streams.

paragraphs: Event streams from bio-inspired vision sensors contain spatial and temporal signals generated by motion. Separating overlapping motions is difficult when their sources and movement patterns are not known beforehand. This paper connects that task to Bayesian computation in spiking neural networks, seeking a practical application for neural processing mechanisms with physiological interpretability.

The network implements counterparts of the two stages in expectation-maximization, a framework already used for separating motion in event streams. Winner-take-all circuits perform an equivalent of the expectation step, while spike-timing-dependent plasticity, or STDP, supplies an equivalent optimization for the maximization step. This creates a link between the network's activity and learning rules and the underlying probabilistic inference procedure.

Theoretical analysis and experiments show that STDP-based learning can maximize the contrast of warped events under mixed motion models. The experiments also demonstrate that the constructed network effectively segments motion in event streams. The contribution is a concrete connection between spike-based learning, Bayesian motion separation, and the processing of continuous sensor events.
summary.tldr: A spiking neural network separates motions in event streams by implementing Bayesian expectation-maximization through neural competition and STDP.

title: Continuous Spatiotemporal Events Decoupling through Spike-based Bayesian Computation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant advancements across numerous domains, but their capabilities in Chinese Classical Literature and Language Arts (CCLLA) remain largely unexplored due to the limited scope and tasks of existing benchmarks. To fill this gap, we propose WenMind, a comprehensive benchmark dedicated for evaluating LLMs in CCLLA. WenMind covers the sub-domains of Ancient Prose, Ancient Poetry, and Ancient Literary Culture, comprising 4,875 question-answer pairs, spanning 42 fine-grained tasks, 3 question formats, and 2 evaluation scenarios: domain-oriented and capability-oriented. Based on WenMind, we conduct a thorough evaluation of 31 representative LLMs, including general-purpose models and ancient Chinese LLMs. The results reveal that even the best-performing model, ERNIE-4.0, only achieves a total score of 64.3, indicating significant room for improvement of LLMs in the CCLLA domain. We also provide insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different LLMs and highlight the importance of pre-training data in achieving better results.Overall, WenMind serves as a standardized and comprehensive baseline, providing valuable insights for future CCLLA research. Our benchmark and related code are available at \url{https://github.com/SCUT-DLVCLab/WenMind}.

paragraphs: Strong performance on general language tasks does not fully describe a model's command of Chinese classical literature and language arts. WenMind provides a dedicated benchmark for this domain, covering ancient prose, ancient poetry, and ancient literary culture. It is intended to broaden evaluation beyond the limited task coverage of earlier benchmarks.

The benchmark contains 4,875 question-answer pairs across 42 detailed tasks and three question formats. It supports two evaluation scenarios, organized around domains and capabilities. The authors use it to assess 31 representative language models, including general-purpose systems and models specifically focused on ancient Chinese, enabling comparisons within a shared evaluation framework.

The best-performing evaluated model, ERNIE-4.0, receives a total score of 64.3, which the authors interpret as leaving substantial room for improvement. Their analysis also identifies model strengths and weaknesses and emphasizes the importance of pretraining data. WenMind contributes a standardized way to study those differences and to assess progress across the distinct areas of classical Chinese knowledge and language ability.
summary.tldr: WenMind evaluates 31 language models across Chinese classical literature tasks and finds substantial room for improvement.

title: WenMind: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Chinese Classical Literature and Language Arts

abstract: In this article, we study the behaviour of continuous-time gradient methods on a two-layer linear network with square loss. A dichotomy between SGD and GD is revealed: GD preserves the rank at initialization while (label noise) SGD diminishes the rank regardless of the initialization. We demonstrate this rank deficiency by studying the time evolution of the *determinant* of a matrix of parameters. To further understand this phenomenon, we derive the stochastic differential equation (SDE) governing the eigenvalues of the parameter matrix. This SDE unveils a *replusive force* between the eigenvalues: a key regularization mechanism which induces rank deficiency. Our results are well supported by experiments illustrating the phenomenon beyond linear networks and regression tasks.

paragraphs: This paper compares continuous-time gradient methods in a two-layer linear network trained with square loss. Its focus is the rank of a parameter matrix, which describes how many independent directions that matrix retains. The analysis reveals different behavior for ordinary gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent with label noise.

Under the studied formulation, gradient descent preserves the rank present at initialization, whereas label-noise stochastic gradient descent reduces rank regardless of initialization. The authors establish the rank deficiency by examining how the determinant of a parameter matrix changes over time. This gives a concrete mathematical route for tracking the loss of independent parameter directions.

To explain the mechanism further, they derive a stochastic differential equation for the matrix's eigenvalues. It reveals a repulsive interaction between eigenvalues that the authors identify as a key regularizing mechanism inducing rank deficiency. Experiments also illustrate the phenomenon beyond linear networks and regression. Those experiments broaden the supporting evidence, while the stated theoretical analysis remains centered on continuous-time methods for the two-layer linear setting.
summary.tldr: For continuous-time training of two-layer linear networks, the paper shows that label-noise SGD reduces parameter rank while GD preserves its initial rank.

title: SGD vs GD: Rank Deficiency in Linear Networks

abstract: We tackle the efficiency problem of learning local feature matching.Recent advancements have given rise to purely CNN-based and transformer-based approaches, each augmented with deep learning techniques. While CNN-based methods often excel in matching speed, transformer-based methods tend to provide more accurate matches. We propose an efficient transformer-based network architecture for local feature matching.This technique is built on constructing multiple homography hypotheses to approximate the continuous correspondence in the real world and uni-directional cross-attention to accelerate the refinement. On the YFCC100M dataset, our matching accuracy is competitive with LoFTR, a state-of-the-art transformer-based architecture, while the inference speed is boosted to 4 times, even outperforming the CNN-based methods.Comprehensive evaluations on other open datasets such as Megadepth, ScanNet, and HPatches demonstrate our method's efficacy, highlighting its potential to significantly enhance a wide array of downstream applications.

paragraphs: Local feature matching identifies corresponding locations across images. The paper targets a recurring trade-off: convolutional approaches often match quickly, while transformer approaches tend to deliver greater accuracy. ETO introduces a transformer architecture intended to retain competitive matching quality while reducing the time required to produce those correspondences.

Its main design organizes matching around multiple homography hypotheses, using several candidate geometric mappings to approximate real-world correspondence. It then employs cross-attention in one direction to accelerate refinement. These two choices address the structure of the matching problem and the cost of refining matches, respectively, rather than treating efficiency as a separate step after prediction.

On YFCC100M, the authors report accuracy competitive with LoFTR and inference four times as fast, with speed also exceeding the CNN-based methods considered. Additional evaluations on Megadepth, ScanNet, and HPatches support the method's effectiveness. The result matters because it shows an evaluated transformer matcher can substantially improve speed without giving up competitive accuracy, creating potential benefits for applications that depend on image correspondences.
summary.tldr: ETO uses multiple geometric mapping hypotheses and one-way cross-attention to achieve competitive feature matching with substantially faster inference.

title: ETO:Efficient Transformer-based Local Feature Matching by Organizing Multiple Homography Hypotheses

abstract: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) represents a critical frontier in time series analysis, characterized by extensive input sequences, as opposed to the shorter spans typical of traditional approaches. While longer sequences inherently offer richer information for enhanced predictive precision, prevailing studies often respond by escalating model complexity. These intricate models can inflate into millions of parameters, resulting in prohibitive parameter scales. Our study demonstrates, through both theoretical and empirical evidence, that decomposition is key to containing excessive model inflation while achieving uniformly superior and robust results across various datasets. Remarkably, by tailoring decomposition to the intrinsic dynamics of time series data, our proposed model outperforms existing benchmarks, using over 99\% fewer parameters than the majority of competing methods. Through this work, we aim to unleash the power of a restricted set of parameters by capitalizing on domain characteristics—a timely reminder that in the realm of LTSF, bigger is not invariably better. The code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SSCNN-321D/}.

paragraphs: Long-term time-series forecasting can use extensive histories to improve predictions, but many approaches respond to that larger input by building increasingly large models. This paper examines whether the information in long sequences can instead be handled with a much smaller parameter set. Its proposed route is decomposition tailored to the underlying dynamics of time-series data.

The work provides both theoretical and empirical evidence that decomposition can control model growth while supporting strong forecasting. The central design principle is to exploit characteristics of the data when organizing the model, so that useful structure does not have to be captured solely through additional parameters. The proposed model uses this principle to pursue accuracy and compactness together.

Across the datasets studied, the authors report consistently superior and robust results, with over 99% fewer parameters than the majority of competing methods. The comparison concerns parameter counts and forecasting performance in those evaluations. It supports the paper's broader argument that greater model size is not invariably needed for better long-term forecasting when decomposition reflects the dynamics being modeled.
summary.tldr: Dynamics-aware decomposition improves long-term forecasting while using over 99% fewer parameters than most competing methods in the reported comparisons.

title: Parsimony or Capability? Decomposition Delivers Both in Long-term Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Standard federated learning (FL) approaches are vulnerable to the free-rider dilemma: participating agents can contribute little to nothing yet receive a well-trained aggregated model. While prior mechanisms attempt to solve the free-rider dilemma, none have addressed the issue of truthfulness. In practice, adversarial agents can provide false information to the server in order to cheat its way out of contributing to federated training. In an effort to make free-riding-averse federated mechanisms truthful, and consequently less prone to breaking down in practice, we propose FACT. FACT is the first federated mechanism that: (1) eliminates federated free riding by using a penalty system, (2) ensures agents provide truthful information by creating a competitive environment, and (3) encourages agent participation by offering better performance than training alone. Empirically, FACT avoids free-riding when agents are untruthful, and reduces agent loss by over 4x.

paragraphs: Federated learning allows participants to benefit from a jointly trained model, but it can also reward agents that contribute little or nothing. Mechanisms designed to discourage this free riding face another problem: participants can give the coordinating server false information to escape their obligations. This paper makes truthful reporting a central part of the incentive design.

The proposed mechanism, FACT, combines three elements. A penalty system eliminates free riding, a competitive environment creates incentives to report truthfully, and the benefit of a better model encourages participation. The last element matters because discouraging misconduct alone does not explain why an agent would join; FACT also offers better performance than training independently.

The authors position FACT as the first federated mechanism to combine these three properties. Their experiments show that it avoids free riding when agents provide untruthful information and reduces agent loss by more than a factor of four. The findings support addressing contribution and honesty together: a participation mechanism must account for what agents actually do and what they tell the server about it.
summary.tldr: FACT combines penalties, competition, and participation benefits to prevent federated free riding and encourage truthful reporting.

title: FACT or Fiction: Can Truthful Mechanisms Eliminate Federated Free Riding?

abstract: Solving parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) presents significant challenges for data-driven methods due to the sensitivity of spatio-temporal dynamics to variations in PDE parameters. Machine learning approaches often struggle to capture this variability. To address this, data-driven approaches learn parametric PDEs by sampling a very large variety of trajectories with varying PDE parameters. We first show that incorporating conditioning mechanisms for learning parametric PDEs is essential and that among them, \textit{adaptive conditioning}, allows stronger generalization. As existing adaptive conditioning methods do not scale well with respect to the number of parameters to adapt in the neural solver, we propose GEPS, a simple adaptation mechanism to boost GEneralization in Pde Solvers via a first-order optimization and low-rank rapid adaptation of a small set of context parameters. We demonstrate the versatility of our approach for both fully data-driven and for physics-aware neural solvers. Validation performed on a whole range of spatio-temporal forecasting problems demonstrates excellent performance for generalizing to unseen conditions including initial conditions, PDE coefficients, forcing terms and solution domain. *Project page*: https://geps-project.github.io

paragraphs: Parametric partial differential equations describe systems whose behavior changes with parameters and conditions. This creates a challenge for neural solvers: trajectories learned under one configuration may not capture the dynamics of another. The paper studies conditioning mechanisms that let a solver account for these variations, finding adaptive conditioning particularly effective for generalization.

Existing adaptive methods can become difficult to scale as the number of parameters requiring adjustment increases. GEPS addresses this with first-order optimization and a low-rank adaptation mechanism operating on a small set of context parameters. The approach makes rapid adaptation central to handling changing conditions while reducing the scope of what must be adjusted.

The authors demonstrate GEPS with both fully data-driven solvers and solvers that incorporate physical knowledge. Across spatiotemporal forecasting problems, they report strong generalization to unseen initial conditions, equation coefficients, forcing terms, and solution domains. These findings indicate that the adaptation mechanism can support several distinct kinds of variation, with its reported effectiveness spanning both types of neural solver.
summary.tldr: GEPS improves neural PDE solvers' generalization through rapid, low-rank adaptation of a small set of context parameters.

title: Boosting Generalization in Parametric PDE Neural Solvers through Adaptive Conditioning

abstract: Computation graphs are Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) where the nodes correspond to mathematical operations and are used widely as abstractions in optimizations of neural networks. The device placement problem aims to identify optimal allocations of those nodes to a set of (potentially heterogeneous) devices. Existing approaches rely on two types of architectures known as grouper-placer and encoder-placer, respectively. In this work, we bridge the gap between encoder-placer and grouper-placer techniques and propose a novel framework for the task of device placement, relying on smaller computation graphs extracted from the OpenVINO toolkit. The framework consists of five steps, including graph coarsening, node representation learning and policy optimization. It facilitates end-to-end training and takes into account the DAG nature of the computation graphs. We also propose a model variant, inspired by graph parsing networks and complex network analysis, enabling graph representation learning and jointed, personalized graph partitioning, using an unspecified number of groups. To train the entire framework, we use reinforcement learning using the execution time of the placement as a reward. We demonstrate the flexibility and effectiveness of our approach through multiple experiments with three benchmark models, namely Inception-V3, ResNet, and BERT. The robustness of the proposed framework is also highlighted through an ablation study. The suggested placements improve the inference speed for the benchmark models by up to $58.2\%$ over CPU execution and by up to $60.24\%$ compared to other commonly used baselines.

paragraphs: Running a neural network across several devices requires deciding where each mathematical operation should execute. The paper treats this as a problem on a computation graph, whose directed connections describe dependencies between operations. Its framework combines ideas from methods that group operations before assigning devices and methods that learn graph representations before making assignments.

The framework uses smaller computation graphs extracted from OpenVINO and includes graph coarsening, learning node representations, and policy optimization among its five steps. It supports training the whole system together while accounting for the graph's directed, acyclic structure. A further model variant learns representations and customized graph partitions jointly, without requiring a fixed number of groups. Reinforcement learning uses placement execution time to guide training.

Experiments cover Inception-V3, ResNet, and BERT, with an ablation study examining robustness. The proposed placements improve inference speed by up to 58.2% over CPU execution and up to 60.24% over commonly used baselines. These are reported best-case improvements across the evaluated settings, showing the practical value of incorporating graph structure into placement decisions.
summary.tldr: A graph-aware learning framework assigns neural-network operations to devices and reports substantial inference-speed improvements on three benchmark models.

title: A Structure-Aware Framework for Learning Device Placements on Computation Graphs

abstract: Fine-tuned vision-language models (VLMs) often capture spurious correlations between image features and textual attributes, resulting in degraded zero-shot performance at test time. Existing approaches for addressing spurious correlations (i) primarily operate at the global image-level rather than intervening directly on fine-grained image features and (ii) are predominantly designed for unimodal settings. In this work, we present RaVL, which takes a fine-grained perspective on VLM robustness by discovering and mitigating spurious correlations using local image features rather than operating at the global image level. Given a fine-tuned VLM, RaVL first discovers spurious correlations by leveraging a region-level clustering approach to identify precise image features contributing to zero-shot classification errors. Then, RaVL mitigates the identified spurious correlation with a novel region-aware loss function that enables the VLM to focus on relevant regions and ignore spurious relationships during fine-tuning. We evaluate RaVL on 654 VLMs with various model architectures, data domains, and learned spurious correlations. Our results show that RaVL accurately discovers (191% improvement over the closest baseline) and mitigates (8.2% improvement on worst-group image classification accuracy) spurious correlations. Qualitative evaluations on general-domain and medical-domain VLMs confirm our findings.

paragraphs: Fine-tuned vision-language models can learn misleading associations between visual features and textual attributes. Such associations may hurt zero-shot classification at test time. RaVL addresses this problem at the level of local image regions, aiming to identify the particular visual features involved in errors and then change how the model uses them.

The discovery stage clusters image regions to locate features contributing to zero-shot classification mistakes. The mitigation stage introduces a region-aware loss for fine-tuning, encouraging attention to relevant regions and discouraging the identified spurious relationships. Connecting these stages makes the discovered local features directly relevant to the corrective training procedure, rather than diagnosing the problem only at whole-image level.

The evaluation spans 654 vision-language models with different architectures, data domains, and learned spurious correlations. The authors report a 191% improvement over the closest baseline in discovering these correlations and an 8.2% improvement in worst-group classification accuracy after mitigation. Qualitative evaluations in general and medical domains further support the findings, providing evidence for the usefulness of region-level diagnosis and correction.
summary.tldr: RaVL identifies misleading image-region associations and uses a region-aware training loss to improve vision-language model robustness.

title: RaVL: Discovering and Mitigating Spurious Correlations in Fine-Tuned Vision-Language Models

abstract: We present Visual AutoRegressive modeling (VAR), a new generation paradigm that redefines the autoregressive learning on images as coarse-to-fine "next-scale prediction" or "next-resolution prediction", diverging from the standard raster-scan "next-token prediction". This simple, intuitive methodology allows autoregressive (AR) transformers to learn visual distributions fast and generalize well: VAR, for the first time, makes GPT-style AR models surpass diffusion transformers in image generation. On ImageNet 256x256 benchmark, VAR significantly improve AR baseline by improving Frechet inception distance (FID) from 18.65 to 1.73, inception score (IS) from 80.4 to 350.2, with around 20x faster inference speed. It is also empirically verified that VAR outperforms the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) in multiple dimensions including image quality, inference speed, data efficiency, and scalability. Scaling up VAR models exhibits clear power-law scaling laws similar to those observed in LLMs, with linear correlation coefficients near -0.998 as solid evidence. VAR further showcases zero-shot generalization ability in downstream tasks including image in-painting, out-painting, and editing. These results suggest VAR has initially emulated the two important properties of LLMs: Scaling Laws and zero-shot task generalization. We have released all models and codes to promote the exploration of AR/VAR models for visual generation and unified learning.

paragraphs: Visual AutoRegressive modeling changes the sequence an image generator learns to predict. Instead of advancing through image tokens in raster order, VAR predicts progressively finer resolutions. This coarse-to-fine organization makes each stage a next-scale prediction problem, giving an autoregressive transformer a different way to learn visual structure.

On ImageNet at 256-by-256 resolution, VAR improves the reported autoregressive baseline's FID from 18.65 to 1.73 and inception score from 80.4 to 350.2, with approximately twentyfold faster inference. The authors also empirically find that VAR outperforms the tested Diffusion Transformer in image quality, speed, data efficiency, and scalability.

Larger VAR models exhibit clear power-law scaling relationships, with reported linear correlation coefficients near -0.998. The model additionally demonstrates zero-shot inpainting, outpainting, and editing. These findings suggest that changing the prediction order can give visual autoregressive models both strong generation performance and properties associated with language models: predictable scaling and transfer to tasks without task-specific training. The evidence supports these properties in the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: VAR generates images through next-resolution prediction, achieving strong quality, speed, scaling, and zero-shot task performance in the reported evaluations.

title: Visual Autoregressive Modeling: Scalable Image Generation via Next-Scale Prediction

abstract: Federated Instruction Tuning (FIT) advances collaborative training on decentralized data, crucially enhancing model's capability and safeguarding data privacy. However, existing FIT methods are dedicated to handling data heterogeneity across different clients (i.e., client-aware data heterogeneity), while ignoring the variation between data from different domains (i.e., domain-aware data heterogeneity). When scarce data needs supplementation from related fields, these methods lack the ability to handle domain heterogeneity in cross-domain training. This leads to domain-information catastrophic forgetting in collaborative training and therefore makes model perform sub-optimally on the individual domain. To address this issue, we introduce DoFIT, a new Domain-aware FIT framework that alleviates catastrophic forgetting through two new designs. First, to reduce interference information from the other domain, DoFIT finely aggregates overlapping weights across domains on the inter-domain server side. Second, to retain more domain information, DoFIT initializes intra-domain weights by incorporating inter-domain information into a less-conflicted parameter space. Experimental results on diverse datasets consistently demonstrate that DoFIT excels in cross-domain collaborative training and exhibits significant advantages over conventional FIT methods in alleviating catastrophic forgetting. Code is available at [this link](https://github.com/1xbq1/DoFIT).

paragraphs: Federated instruction tuning lets clients collaborate using decentralized data. Existing approaches account for differences between clients, but the paper argues that differences between subject domains need separate treatment. When a domain has little data and draws support from related fields, cross-domain training can erase useful domain information and weaken performance within that domain.

DoFIT tackles this forgetting through two changes to how model weights are combined and initialized. On the server coordinating domains, it selectively aggregates overlapping weights to reduce interference from other domains. Within a domain, it incorporates shared information into a parameter space with less conflict when initializing weights. The two changes aim to make outside information useful while retaining more domain-specific knowledge.

Experiments across diverse datasets report consistent benefits for cross-domain collaborative training and significant improvements over conventional federated instruction-tuning methods in alleviating forgetting. The results support treating domain differences as a distinct source of training interference. DoFIT’s contribution is a framework for controlling where cross-domain sharing occurs, so that collaboration can better support the individual domains involved.
summary.tldr: DoFIT changes cross-domain weight sharing and initialization to reduce catastrophic forgetting during federated instruction tuning.

title: DoFIT: Domain-aware Federated Instruction Tuning with Alleviated Catastrophic Forgetting

abstract: Multi-Channel Imaging (MCI) contains an array of challenges for encoding useful feature representations not present in traditional images. For example, images from two different satellites may both contain RGB channels, but the remaining channels can be different for each imaging source. Thus, MCI models must support a variety of channel configurations at test time. Recent work has extended traditional visual encoders for MCI, such as Vision Transformers (ViT), by supplementing pixel information with an encoding representing the channel configuration. However, these methods treat each channel equally, i.e., they do not consider the unique properties of each channel type, which can result in needless and potentially harmful redundancies in the learned features. For example, if RGB channels are always present, the other channels can focus on extracting information that cannot be captured by the RGB channels. To this end, we propose DiChaViT, which aims to enhance the diversity in the learned features of MCI-ViT models. This is achieved through a novel channel sampling strategy that encourages the selection of more distinct channel sets for training. Additionally, we employ regularization and initialization techniques to increase the likelihood that new information is learned from each channel. Many of our improvements are architecture agnostic and can be incorporated into new architectures as they are developed. Experiments on both satellite and cell microscopy datasets, CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat, report DiChaViT yields a 1.5 - 5.0% gain over the state-of-the-art. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/chaudatascience/diverse_channel_vit.

paragraphs: Multi-channel images can contain different kinds of measurements depending on their source. Two satellites, for example, may both provide RGB channels while differing in their remaining channels. Models therefore need to handle varying channel configurations. This paper argues that treating all channels equally can encourage redundant features and overlook the distinct information each channel offers.
