Experiments on the satellite and cell microscopy datasets CHAMMI, JUMP-CP, and So2Sat report gains of 1.5–5.0% over the state of the art. Many proposed improvements are independent of a particular architecture, allowing their use in other designs. The findings suggest that supporting variable channel inputs benefits from explicitly encouraging complementary features during training.
summary.tldr: DiChaViT encourages complementary information across image channels, improving reported satellite and microscopy results over leading methods.

title: Enhancing Feature Diversity Boosts Channel-Adaptive Vision Transformers

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) offers a robust framework for harnessing the potential of unannotated data. Traditionally, SSL mandates that all classes possess labeled instances. However, the emergence of open-world SSL (OwSSL) introduces a more practical challenge, wherein unlabeled data may encompass samples from unseen classes. This scenario leads to misclassification of unseen classes as known ones, consequently undermining classification accuracy. To overcome this challenge, this study revisits two methodologies from self-supervised and semi-supervised learning, self-labeling and consistency, tailoring them to address the OwSSL problem. Specifically, we propose an effective framework called _OwMatch_, combining conditional self-labeling and open-world hierarchical thresholding. Theoretically, we analyze the estimation of class distribution on unlabeled data through rigorous statistical analysis, thus demonstrating that OwMatch can ensure the unbiasedness of the label assignment estimator with reliability. Comprehensive empirical analyses demonstrate that our method yields substantial performance enhancements across both known and unknown classes in comparison to previous studies. Code is available at [https://github.com/niusj03/OwMatch](https://github.com/niusj03/OwMatch).

Specifically, we propose an effective framework called _OwMatch_, combining conditional self-labeling and open-world hierarchical thresholding. Comprehensive empirical analyses demonstrate that our method yields substantial performance enhancements across both known and unknown classes in comparison to previous studies. Code is available at [https://github.com/niusj03/OwMatch](https://github.com/niusj03/OwMatch).

paragraphs: Conventional semi-supervised learning assumes that every class has at least some labeled examples. Open-world semi-supervised learning relaxes that assumption: the unlabeled data can contain classes absent from the labeled set. A method that treats every unlabeled example as belonging to a familiar class can consequently misclassify unfamiliar examples and reduce overall accuracy.

OwMatch adapts self-labeling and consistency methods to this setting. Its framework combines conditional self-labeling with open-world hierarchical thresholding. These components address the assignment and use of labels when the unlabeled pool includes both known and unknown classes. The paper also analyzes how class distributions can be estimated from the unlabeled data.

The statistical analysis establishes an unbiasedness result for the label-assignment estimator. This is a claim about the estimator, rather than a claim that every assigned label is correct. Empirical evaluations show substantial improvements over previous methods for both known and unknown classes. The findings support explicitly accommodating unfamiliar classes in the learning procedure instead of relying on the conventional shared-class assumption.
summary.tldr: OwMatch adapts self-labeling and consistency to unlabeled data containing unseen classes, improving results for both known and unknown categories.

title: OwMatch: Conditional Self-Labeling with Consistency for Open-World Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Fairness in clustering has been considered extensively in the past; however, the trade-off between the two objectives --- e.g., can we sacrifice just a little in the quality of the clustering to significantly increase fairness, or vice-versa? --- has rarely been addressed. We introduce novel algorithms for tracing the complete trade-off curve, or Pareto front, between quality and fairness in clustering problems; that is, computing all clusterings that are not dominated in both objectives by other clusterings. Unlike previous work that deals with specific objectives for quality and fairness, we deal with all objectives for fairness and quality in two general classes encompassing most of the special cases addressed in previous work. Our algorithm must take exponential time in the worst case as the Parero front itself can be exponential. Even when the Pareto front is polynomial, our algorithm may take exponential time, and we prove that this is inevitable unless P = NP. However, we also present a new polynomial-time algorithm for computing the entire Pareto front when the cluster centers are fixed, and for perhaps the most natural fairness objective: minimizing the sum, over all clusters, of the imbalance between the two groups in each cluster.

paragraphs: Clustering can involve competing goals: producing high-quality groups and satisfying a fairness objective. Choosing one balance hides the other available compromises. This paper develops algorithms for tracing the Pareto front, the set of solutions for which no other clustering improves one objective without worsening the other.

The algorithms cover two broad classes of quality and fairness objectives, encompassing many previously studied cases. Computing the complete front exposes how much quality must be exchanged for a fairness improvement, or vice versa. However, the front itself can contain exponentially many solutions, so listing it can inherently require exponential time.

The authors also prove a stronger obstacle: even when the front has polynomial size, exponential computation cannot generally be avoided unless P equals NP. They identify a tractable special case with fixed cluster centers and a fairness objective that sums the imbalance between two groups across clusters. For that setting, a polynomial-time algorithm computes the entire front, establishing both general computational limits and a concrete setting where complete tradeoff analysis is efficient.
summary.tldr: The paper computes fairness-quality tradeoff fronts for clustering, proves general complexity barriers, and gives an efficient algorithm for a fixed-center special case.

title: The Fairness-Quality Tradeoff in Clustering

abstract: Exploiting the power of pre-trained models, prompt-based approaches stand out compared to other continual learning solutions in effectively preventing catastrophic forgetting, even with very few learnable parameters and without the need for a memory buffer. While existing prompt-based continual learning methods excel in leveraging prompts for state-of-the-art performance, they often lack a theoretical explanation for the effectiveness of prompting. This paper conducts a theoretical analysis to unravel how prompts bestow such advantages in continual learning, thus offering a new perspective on prompt design. We first show that the attention block of pre-trained models like Vision Transformers inherently encodes a special mixture of experts architecture, characterized by linear experts and quadratic gating score functions. This realization drives us to provide a novel view on prefix tuning, reframing it as the addition of new task-specific experts, thereby inspiring the design of a novel gating mechanism termed Non-linear Residual Gates (NoRGa). Through the incorporation of non-linear activation and residual connection, NoRGa enhances continual learning performance while preserving parameter efficiency. The effectiveness of NoRGa is substantiated both theoretically and empirically across diverse benchmarks and pretraining paradigms. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Minhchuyentoancbn/MoE_PromptCL.

paragraphs: Prompt-based continual learning adapts pretrained models with relatively few learned parameters and can reduce forgetting without a memory buffer. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for why prompting works well in that setting. Its analysis connects attention inside pretrained models, including vision transformers, to a particular mixture-of-experts architecture.

In that interpretation, the attention block contains linear experts and gating scores with a quadratic form. Prefix tuning can then be understood as adding new experts associated with particular tasks. This perspective makes the gating mechanism a concrete design target: it governs how the added experts contribute to the model’s computation.

The authors use this insight to propose Non-linear Residual Gates, or NoRGa. The mechanism combines nonlinear activation with a residual connection to improve continual learning while keeping the method parameter efficient. The paper supports its effectiveness theoretically and through experiments across multiple benchmarks and pretraining approaches. Its contribution is both an explanation of prompt adaptation and a practical architectural change derived from that explanation.
summary.tldr: A mixture-of-experts interpretation of attention motivates NoRGa, a parameter-efficient gating mechanism that improves prompt-based continual learning.

title: Mixture of Experts Meets Prompt-Based Continual Learning

abstract: Softmax attention is the principle backbone of foundation models for various artificial intelligence applications, yet its quadratic complexity in sequence length can limit its inference throughput in long-context settings. To address this challenge, alternative architectures such as linear attention, State Space Models (SSMs), and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been considered as more efficient alternatives. While connections between these approaches exist, such models are commonly developed in isolation and there is a lack of theoretical understanding of the shared principles underpinning these architectures and their subtle differences, greatly influencing performance and scalability. In this paper, we introduce the Dynamical Systems Framework (DSF), which allows a principled investigation of all these architectures in a common representation. Our framework facilitates rigorous comparisons, providing new insights on the distinctive characteristics of each model class. For instance, we compare linear attention and selective SSMs, detailing their differences and conditions under which both are equivalent. We also provide principled comparisons between softmax attention and other model classes, discussing the theoretical conditions under which softmax attention can be approximated. Additionally, we substantiate these new insights with empirical validations and mathematical arguments. This shows the DSF's potential to guide the systematic development of future more efficient and scalable foundation models.

These architectures have connections, but developing them separately can obscure the differences that affect performance and scaling. This paper introduces the Dynamical Systems Framework to place them in a shared mathematical representation.

The framework supports comparisons that distinguish shared structure from conditional equivalence. In particular, the authors compare linear attention with selective state space models and specify conditions under which they are equivalent. They also compare softmax attention with other model classes and discuss theoretical conditions that allow it to be approximated.

Mathematical arguments and empirical validations support the resulting insights. The contribution is a framework for analyzing architectural relationships and the conditions behind them, giving model designers a more systematic basis for assessing alternatives. Its potential value for future foundation models lies in connecting efficiency-oriented architectural choices to an explicit understanding of what those choices preserve or change in the represented computation.
summary.tldr: A shared dynamical-systems framework clarifies differences, conditional equivalences, and approximation relationships among major sequence-model architectures.

title: Understanding the Differences in Foundation Models: Attention, State Space Models, and Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across a wide range of natural language processing tasks. However, their exponentially increasing parameters pose significant challenges for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Vector Quantization (VQ) shows great promise for low-bit quantization (e.g., 2 to 4 bits), but existing work faces two key challenges: unconstrained direction error and suboptimal bit allocation. In this paper, we propose RSAVQ, a novel VQ framework to enhance extremely low-bit quantization for LLMs. RSAVQ introduces two geometry-driven innovations that effectively mitigate above limitations: (1) Error Direction Sensitivity Guidance (EDSG), which leverages the Fisher information matrix (FIM)-induced Riemannian metric to project quantization errors onto low-sensitivity directions in the parameter space. Specifically, this projection is performed along the negative natural gradient direction, which effectively suppresses error expansion. (2) Weight Channel Sensitivity Guidance (WCSG) , which constructs a channel-wise sensitivity metric via FIM curvature analysis to dynamically guide bit resource allocation. The approach facilitates a globally optimal quantization solution within prescribed bit constraints. Experiments demonstrate that RSAVQ outperforms existing methods for LLMs. For example, in 2-bit quantization of LLaMA-3 8B, RSAVQ leads baselines like VPTQ and QuIP\# by 0.4 in perplexity (PPL) and 1.5 in zero-shot accuracy. This work offers a practical solution for constrained environments and a theoretical bridge between information geometry and the quantization of neural networks, advancing efficient deep learning.

RSAVQ addresses both issues within vector quantization. Its central idea is to use the model's sensitivity geometry to guide errors and distribute a limited bit budget.

title: RSAVQ: Riemannian Sensitivity-Aware Vector Quantization for Large Language Models

abstract: The remarkable performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) can be enhanced with test-time computation, which relies on external tools and even other deep learning models. However, existing approaches for integrating non-text modality representations into LLMs typically require additional costly supervised training, restricting on-the-fly adaptation to new domains and modalities. In this work, we explore the feasibility of integrating representations from non-text foundational models (FMs) into text-based LLMs in a training-free manner. We propose In-Context Representation Learning (ICRL) as a proof-of-concept to allow LLMs to adaptively utilize non-text modality representations with few-shot learning. Unlike traditional in-context learning, which incorporates text-label pairs, ICRL replaces text inputs with FM representations, enabling the LLM to perform multi-modal inference without fine-tuning. We evaluate ICRL on a suite of tasks in the molecular domain, investigating three core research questions: (i) how to map FM representations into LLMs in a training-free manner, (ii) what factors influence ICRL performance, and (iii) what mechanisms underlie the effectiveness of ICRL. To the best of our knowledge, ICRL is the first training-free framework for integrating non-text modality representations into text-based LLMs, presenting a promising direction for adaptable, multi-modal generalization.

paragraphs: Connecting a text-based language model to information from another modality usually requires additional supervised training. That requirement makes it harder to adapt immediately to a new domain or representation. This paper investigates whether a language model can instead use representations from other foundation models through examples supplied at inference time.

The proposed proof of concept is In-Context Representation Learning, or ICRL. Ordinary in-context learning presents examples pairing text inputs with labels. ICRL substitutes foundation-model representations for those text inputs, allowing the language model to use non-text information without fine-tuning. The central question is whether a few examples can establish a useful relationship between these representations and the requested output.

The authors evaluate the approach on molecular-domain tasks. Their study examines how representations can be mapped into language models without additional training, which factors affect performance, and what mechanisms explain effectiveness. The contribution establishes a promising direction for adaptable multimodal inference, with the evidence framed as a molecular case study and proof of concept.
summary.tldr: ICRL explores using few-shot examples to let text-based language models work with non-text representations without fine-tuning.

title: Can LLMs Reason Over Non-Text Modalities in a Training-Free Manner? A Case Study with In-Context Representation Learning

abstract: Sampling from high dimensional distributions is a computational bottleneck in many scientific applications. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), and in particular the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), are widely used, yet they struggle on problems with a very large number of parameters or a complicated geometry. Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo (MCLMC) has been recently proposed as an alternative which shows striking gains in efficiency over NUTS, especially for high-dimensional problems. However, it produces biased samples, with a bias that is hard to control in general. We introduce the Metropolis-Adjusted Microcanonical sampler (MAMS), which relies on the same dynamics as MCLMC, but introduces a Metropolis-Hastings step and thus produces asymptotically unbiased samples. We develop an automated tuning scheme for the hyperparameters of the algorithm, making it applicable out of the box. We demonstrate that MAMS outperforms NUTS across the board on benchmark problems of varying complexity and dimensionality, achieving up to a factor of seven speedup.

paragraphs: Sampling from distributions with many parameters or complicated geometry can consume substantial computation. The paper starts from a trade-off between established Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods, particularly NUTS, and Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo. The latter has shown strong efficiency gains, especially in high dimensions, but produces bias that can be difficult to control.

The proposed Metropolis-Adjusted Microcanonical sampler, or MAMS, retains the dynamics used by Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo and adds a Metropolis–Hastings step. This adjustment gives asymptotically unbiased samples. That is a long-run property of the sampler, rather than a statement that any finite collection of samples is free from error.

The authors also develop automatic hyperparameter tuning so the method can be used without manual configuration of those choices. Across benchmark problems of differing dimensionality and complexity, MAMS outperforms NUTS, with a maximum reported speedup of sevenfold. The contribution combines the efficiency benefits of microcanonical dynamics with an asymptotic correctness property, and the experiments show that this combination can deliver practical computational gains.
summary.tldr: MAMS adds a Metropolis–Hastings correction to microcanonical dynamics, yielding asymptotically unbiased sampling and up to sevenfold speedups over NUTS on tested problems.

title: Metropolis Adjusted Microcanonical Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: Autoregressive models have achieved significant success in image generation. However, unlike the inherent hierarchical structure of image information in the spectral domain, standard autoregressive methods typically generate pixels sequentially in a fixed spatial order. To better leverage this spectral hierarchy, we introduce Next-Frequency Image Generation (NFIG). NFIG is a novel framework that decomposes the image generation process into multiple frequency-guided stages. NFIG aligns the generation process with the natural image structure. It does this by first generating low-frequency components, which efficiently capture global structure with significantly fewer tokens, and then progressively adding higher-frequency details. This frequency-aware paradigm offers substantial advantages: it not only improves the quality of generated images but crucially reduces inference cost by efficiently establishing global structure early on. Extensive experiments on the ImageNet-256 benchmark validate NFIG's effectiveness, demonstrating superior performance (FID: 2.81) and a notable 1.25x speedup compared to the strong baseline VAR-d20.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image generators construct images through a sequence of predictions. NFIG changes how that sequence is organized, using image frequency structure to determine what should be generated first. The motivation is that broad visual organization and fine detail occupy different parts of the spectrum, offering a useful hierarchy for generation.

The framework begins with low-frequency components, which establish global structure using substantially fewer tokens. Later stages progressively supply higher-frequency detail. This separates the work of arranging the overall image from the work of refining it, allowing the early generation stages to capture important structure efficiently.

On ImageNet-256, the authors report an FID of 2.81 and a 1.25-times speedup relative to VAR-d20, together with superior image-generation performance. The result matters because it connects a change in generation order to both quality and inference cost. In the reported comparison, frequency-guided stages improve the generated images while reducing the computational burden of establishing their overall structure. The evidence supports this particular coarse-to-fine organization as an effective autoregressive design.
summary.tldr: NFIG generates broad image structure before high-frequency detail, reporting improved quality and a 1.25-times speedup over VAR-d20 on ImageNet-256.

title: NFIG: Multi-Scale Autoregressive Image Generation via Frequency Ordering

abstract: Sperm whales communicate in short sequences of clicks known as codas. We present WhAM (Whale Acoustics Model), the first transformer-based model capable of generating synthetic sperm whale codas from any audio prompt. WhAM is built by finetuning VampNet, a masked acoustic token model pretrained on musical audio, using 10k coda recordings collected over the past two decades. Through iterative masked token prediction, WhAM generates high-fidelity synthetic codas that preserve key acoustic features of the source recordings. We evaluate WhAM's synthetic codas using Fréchet Audio Distance and through perceptual studies with expert marine biologists. On downstream tasks including rhythm, social unit, and vowel classification, WhAM's learned representations achieve strong performance, despite being trained for generation rather than classification. Our code is available at https://github.com/Project-CETI/wham

paragraphs: Sperm whales produce short click sequences called codas. WhAM studies these sounds through a transformer that generates synthetic codas from audio prompts. The model adapts VampNet, originally pretrained on musical audio, using 10,000 coda recordings gathered over two decades. This transfers an existing audio-generation model to a specialized biological sound domain.

WhAM generates audio through repeated prediction of masked acoustic tokens. The authors report that the resulting codas preserve important acoustic characteristics of the source recordings. They evaluate the synthetic sounds using Fréchet Audio Distance and perceptual studies with expert marine biologists, combining a quantitative audio comparison with expert listening judgments.

The learned representations also perform strongly on rhythm, social-unit, and vowel classification, despite the model being trained for generation rather than classification. This suggests that learning to synthesize codas captures information useful for analyzing their structure and associations. The demonstrated contribution is a generative and representational model of whale vocalizations: the reported results concern acoustic fidelity and downstream classification, rather than an established translation of the meanings whales communicate.
summary.tldr: WhAM adapts a music-pretrained transformer to generate sperm whale codas and learns representations useful for several coda-classification tasks.

title: WhAM: Towards A Translative Model of Sperm Whale Vocalization

abstract: When fine-tuning pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) to align with human values and intentions, maximizing the estimated reward can lead to superior performance, but it also introduces potential risks due to deviations from the reference model's intended behavior. Most existing methods typically introduce KL divergence to constrain deviations between the trained model and the reference model; however, this may not be sufficient in certain applications that require tight risk control. In this paper, we introduce Risk-aware Direct Preference Optimization (Ra-DPO), a novel approach that incorporates risk-awareness by employing a class of nested risk measures. This approach formulates a constrained risk-aware advantage function maximization problem and then converts the Bradley-Terry model into a token-level representation. The objective function maximizes the likelihood of the policy while suppressing the deviation between a trained model and the reference model using a sequential risk ratio, thereby enhancing the model's risk-awareness. Experimental results across three open-source datasets: IMDb Dataset, Anthropic HH Dataset, and AlpacaEval, demonstrate the proposed method's superior performance in balancing alignment performance and model drift.

paragraphs: Preference-based fine-tuning seeks to make language models better match human values and intentions, but optimizing estimated reward can also move a model away from its reference behavior. The paper argues that KL-divergence constraints may be insufficient in applications requiring tight risk control. Ra-DPO introduces nested risk measures to address that concern explicitly.

The method formulates alignment as constrained maximization of a risk-aware advantage function. It then expresses the Bradley–Terry preference model at the token level. Its objective combines policy-likelihood maximization with a sequential risk ratio that suppresses deviation from the reference model, bringing risk sensitivity into how the sequence is optimized.

Experiments on IMDb, Anthropic HH, and AlpacaEval report a better balance between alignment performance and model drift. The finding concerns the trade-off between improving preference alignment and retaining reference behavior across those evaluations. The contribution is a risk-aware formulation of direct preference optimization, with control of sequential deviation built into the objective rather than represented only through the usual KL constraint.
summary.tldr: Ra-DPO incorporates nested risk measures and token-level deviation control to better balance preference alignment with reference-model drift.

title: Risk-aware Direct Preference Optimization under Nested Risk Measure

abstract: Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) aims to reconstruct the 3D geometry and semantics of the surrounding environment. With dense voxel labels, prior works typically formulate SSC as a *dense segmentation task*, independently classifying each voxel. However, this paradigm neglects critical instance-centric discriminability, leading to instance-level incompleteness and adjacent ambiguities. To address this, we highlight a "free lunch" of SSC labels: the voxel-level class label has implicitly told the instance-level insight, which is ever-overlooked by the community. Motivated by this observation, we first introduce a training-free **Voxel-to-Instance (VoxNT) trick**: a simple yet effective method that freely converts voxel-level class labels into instance-level offset labels. Building on this, we further propose **VoxDet**, an instance-centric framework that reformulates the voxel-level SSC as *dense object detection* by decoupling it into two sub-tasks: offset regression and semantic prediction. Specifically, based on the lifted 3D volume, VoxDet first uses (a) Spatially-decoupled Voxel Encoder to generate disentangled feature volumes for the two sub-tasks, which learn task-specific spatial deformation in the densely projected tri-perceptive space. Then, we deploy (b) Task-decoupled Dense Predictor to address SSC via dense detection. Here, we first regress a 4D offset field to estimate distances (6 directions) between voxels and the corresponding object boundaries in the voxel space. The regressed offsets are then used to guide the instance-level aggregation in the classification branch, achieving instance-aware scene completion. VoxDet can be deployed on both camera and LiDAR input and jointly achieves state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, which gives 63.0 IoU on the SemanticKITTI test set, **ranking 1$^{st}$** on the online leaderboard.
originalAbstract: Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) aims to reconstruct the 3D geometry and semantics of the surrounding environment. With dense voxel labels, prior works typically formulate SSC as a *dense segmentation task*, independently classifying each voxel. However, this paradigm neglects critical instance-centric discriminability, leading to instance-level incompleteness and adjacent ambiguities. To address this, we highlight a "free lunch" of SSC labels: the voxel-level class label has implicitly told the instance-level insight, which is ever-overlooked by the community. Motivated by this observation, we first introduce a training-free **Voxel-to-Instance (VoxNT) trick**: a simple yet effective method that freely converts voxel-level class labels into instance-level offset labels. Building on this, we further propose **VoxDet**, an instance-centric framework that reformulates the voxel-level SSC as *dense object detection* by decoupling it into two sub-tasks: offset regression and semantic prediction. Specifically, based on the lifted 3D volume, VoxDet first uses (a) Spatially-decoupled Voxel Encoder to generate disentangled feature volumes for the two sub-tasks, which learn task-specific spatial deformation in the densely projected tri-perceptive space. Then, we deploy (b) Task-decoupled Dense Predictor to address SSC via dense detection. Here, we first regress a 4D offset field to estimate distances (6 directions) between voxels and the corresponding object boundaries in the voxel space. The regressed offsets are then used to guide the instance-level aggregation in the classification branch, achieving instance-aware scene completion. VoxDet can be deployed on both camera and LiDAR input and jointly achieves state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks, which gives 63.0 IoU on the SemanticKITTI test set, **ranking 1$^{st}$** on the online leaderboard.

paragraphs: Semantic scene completion reconstructs both the 3D shape and semantic categories of an environment. Treating it as independent classification of small spatial cells, or voxels, can miss object-level structure and blur distinctions between neighboring objects. VoxDet reformulates the task around dense detection, using information about object boundaries to guide semantic predictions.

The first component, VoxNT, converts existing voxel class labels into instance-level offset labels without training. VoxDet then separates feature processing into offset regression and semantic prediction. Its spatially decoupled encoder creates task-specific feature volumes, while a dense predictor estimates distances from voxels to object boundaries in six directions. These offsets guide the classification branch in aggregating information at the object-instance level.

This design makes boundary relationships part of the scene-completion process, helping organize predictions around objects rather than only individual cells. The method supports both camera and LiDAR inputs and reports state-of-the-art results on both benchmarks. On the SemanticKITTI test set, it achieves 63.0 IoU and is reported as ranking first on the online leaderboard.
summary.tldr: VoxDet uses object-boundary offsets derived from voxel labels to make 3D semantic scene completion instance-aware.

title: VoxDet: Rethinking 3D Semantic Scene Completion as Dense Object Detection

abstract: Understanding the behavior of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents—particularly as task and agent sophistication increase—requires more than simple comparison of reward curves, yet standard methods for behavioral analysis remain underdeveloped in DRL. We apply tools from neuroscience and ethology to study DRL agents in a novel, complex, partially observable environment, ForageWorld, designed to capture key aspects of real-world animal foraging—including sparse, depleting resource patches, predator threats, and spatially extended arenas. We use this environment as a platform for applying joint behavioral and neural analysis to agents, revealing detailed, quantitatively grounded insights into agent strategies, memory, and planning. Contrary to common assumptions, we find that model-free RNN-based DRL agents can exhibit structured, planning-like behavior purely through emergent dynamics—without requiring explicit memory modules or world models. Our results show that studying DRL agents like animals—analyzing them with neuroethology-inspired tools that reveal structure in both behavior and neural dynamics—uncovers rich structure in their learning dynamics that would otherwise remain invisible. We distill these tools into a general analysis framework linking core behavioral and representational features to diagnostic methods, which can be reused for a wide range of tasks and agents. As agents grow more complex and autonomous, bridging neuroscience, cognitive science, and AI will be essential—not just for understanding their behavior, but for ensuring safe alignment and maximizing desirable behaviors that are hard to measure via reward. We show how this can be done by drawing on lessons from how biological intelligence is studied.

This paper studies agents using methods inspired by neuroscience and the study of animal behavior. Its environment, ForageWorld, combines partial observability, scattered resource patches that become depleted, predator threats, and large spaces in which agents must forage.

The researchers examine behavior alongside internal neural activity to investigate strategy, memory, and planning. They find that model-free agents built with recurrent neural networks can develop structured behavior resembling planning through their internal dynamics. These agents do so without explicit memory modules or world models. The finding concerns emergent planning-like behavior, rather than establishing that every model-free agent plans.

Joint analysis reveals patterns in learning and representation that reward comparisons alone would miss. The authors organize their tools into a reusable framework connecting behavioral and representational features with diagnostic methods. This makes the contribution broader than a new environment: it offers a way to investigate increasingly complex agents and behaviors that may be difficult to characterize through reward alone.
summary.tldr: Behavioral and neural analysis reveals that recurrent model-free agents can develop planning-like foraging strategies without explicit world models.

title: Deep RL Needs Deep Behavior Analysis: Exploring Implicit Planning by Model-Free Agents in Open-Ended Environments

abstract: We investigate optimal transport (OT) for measures on graph metric spaces with different total masses. To mitigate the limitations of traditional $L^p$ geometry, Orlicz-Wasserstein (OW) and generalized Sobolev transport (GST) employ \emph{Orlicz geometric structure}, leveraging convex functions to capture nuanced geometric relationships and remarkably contribute to advance certain machine learning approaches. However, both OW and GST are restricted to measures with equal total mass, limiting their applicability to real-world scenarios where mass variation is common, and input measures may have noisy supports, or outliers. To address unbalanced measures, OW can either incorporate mass constraints or marginal discrepancy penalization, but this leads to a more complex two-level optimization problem. Additionally, GST provides a scalable yet rigid framework, which poses significant challenges to extend GST to accommodate nonnegative measures. To tackle these challenges, in this work we revisit the entropy partial transport (EPT) problem. By exploiting Caffarelli \& McCann's insights, we develop a novel variant of EPT endowed with Orlicz geometric structure, called \emph{Orlicz-EPT}. We establish theoretical background to solve Orlicz-EPT using a binary search algorithmic approach. Especially, by leveraging the dual EPT and the underlying graph structure, we formulate a novel regularization approach that leads to the proposed \emph{Orlicz-Sobolev transport} (OST). Notably, we demonstrate that OST can be efficiently computed by simply solving a univariate optimization problem, in stark contrast to the intensive computation needed for Orlicz-EPT. Building on this, we derive geometric structures for OST and draw its connections to other transport distances. We empirically illustrate that OST is several-order faster than Orlicz-EPT. Furthermore, we show preliminary evidence on the advantages of OST for measures on a graph in document classification and topological data analysis.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares how mass is distributed across a space by accounting for movement between locations. This paper considers graph-based spaces where the two distributions can have different total masses. That matters when observations contain mass variation, noisy locations, or outliers. Existing transport approaches using flexible Orlicz geometry either require equal mass or become computationally complicated when extended.

The authors first develop Orlicz-EPT, an entropy partial transport formulation that incorporates Orlicz geometry, and establish a binary-search approach for solving it. They then use its dual formulation and the graph's structure to construct a regularized alternative called Orlicz-Sobolev transport, or OST. Its central computational advantage is that evaluation reduces to optimizing a function of one variable.

The paper derives geometric properties of OST and connections to other transport distances. Experiments find it several orders of magnitude faster than Orlicz-EPT. Applications to document classification and topological data analysis provide preliminary evidence of practical benefits. Those application results are exploratory support, while the computational simplification is the main methodological contribution.
summary.tldr: Orlicz-Sobolev transport compares unequal-mass measures on graphs through a one-variable optimization, with substantial reported speed advantages.

title: An Efficient Orlicz-Sobolev Approach for Transporting Unbalanced Measures on a Graph

abstract: Distributed training often suffers from high communication overhead due to large-scale gradient synchronization. Although gradient compression—particularly at 4-bit or even lower precision—significantly reduces transfer volume, it typically results in sacrifice in precision and degradation of the final model accuracy. In this work, we introduce DUO, a distributed training framework designed to mitigate accuracy degradation incurred by gradient compression without involving additional overhead. DUO achieves this by inserting an additional high-precision gradient synchronization step into a previously computation-only phase, so that its communication is fully hidden by computation. We provide a comprehensive theoretical proof of convergence for DUO and validate its effectiveness through extensive pre-training experiments on GPT models. Our results indicate that DUO effectively restores accuracy when using 4-bit gradient compression, achieving performance comparable to uncompressed training. Remarkably, DUO maintains minimal accuracy degradation even under extreme compression scenarios, including 1-bit gradients or complete omission of the low-precision gradient communication step (0-bit transmission).

paragraphs: Distributed training requires machines to exchange gradients so that their model updates remain coordinated. Compressing those gradients reduces communication volume, but very low precision can harm final accuracy. DUO addresses this tradeoff by changing when additional high-precision communication occurs, aiming to recover accuracy without adding execution overhead.

The framework inserts a high-precision gradient synchronization into a phase previously devoted only to computation. Its scheduling allows that communication to be fully overlapped with computation. The design therefore retains a more accurate synchronization signal while avoiding an exposed communication delay. The authors also provide a theoretical convergence proof and evaluate the approach through GPT pre-training experiments.

With four-bit gradient compression, the experiments report accuracy comparable to uncompressed training. They also find minimal degradation with one-bit gradients and when the low-precision communication step is omitted entirely. That zero-bit case still includes DUO’s high-precision synchronization; it does not mean training without communication. The results show how scheduling and precision can work together to reduce the accuracy penalty of compression.
summary.tldr: DUO overlaps high-precision gradient synchronization with computation to recover accuracy lost through aggressive gradient compression.

title: DUO: No Compromise to Accuracy Degradation

abstract: "Machine unlearning" is a popular proposed solution for mitigating the existence of content in an AI model that is problematic for legal or moral reasons, including privacy, copyright, safety, and more. For example, unlearning is often invoked as a solution for removing the effects of specific information from a generative-AI model's parameters, e.g., a particular individual's personal data or the inclusion of copyrighted content in the model's training data. Unlearning is also proposed as a way to prevent a model from generating targeted types of information in its outputs, e.g., generations that closely resemble a particular individual's data or reflect the concept of "Spiderman." Both of these goals--the targeted removal of information from a model and the targeted suppression of information from a model's outputs--present various technical and substantive challenges. We provide a framework for ML researchers and policymakers to think rigorously about these challenges, identifying several mismatches between the goals of unlearning and feasible implementations. These mismatches explain why unlearning is not a general-purpose solution for circumscribing generative-AI model behavior in service of broader positive impact.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning is often proposed as a response to problematic information in generative models, including concerns involving privacy, copyright, and safety. This paper examines what such proposals are actually asking a system to do and whether available implementations match those goals.

It distinguishes two objectives. One is removing the effects of particular information from a model's parameters, such as a person's data or copyrighted training material. The other is preventing outputs that contain targeted information, resemble particular data, or express a specified concept. These objectives concern different aspects of a model: what training has left inside it and what it produces when used.

The authors provide a framework for researchers and policymakers to reason about technical and substantive difficulties in both objectives. They identify mismatches between desired outcomes and feasible implementations, arguing that these explain why unlearning is not a general-purpose way to constrain generative-model behavior. The practical contribution is a clearer basis for evaluating an unlearning proposal against the particular change it is meant to achieve.
summary.tldr: The paper distinguishes removing learned information from suppressing outputs and explains why unlearning cannot generally fulfill every proposed policy goal.

title: Machine Unlearning Doesn't Do What You Think: Lessons for Generative AI Policy and Research

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models often exhibit degraded performance when generating images beyond their training resolution. Recent training-free methods can mitigate this limitation, but they often require substantial computation or are incompatible with recent Diffusion Transformer models. In this paper, we propose ScaleDiff, a model-agnostic and highly efficient framework for extending the resolution of pretrained diffusion models without any additional training. A core component of our framework is Neighborhood Patch Attention (NPA), an efficient mechanism that reduces computational redundancy in the self-attention layer with non-overlapping patches. We integrate NPA into an SDEdit pipeline and introduce Latent Frequency Mixing (LFM) to better generate fine details. Furthermore, we apply Structure Guidance to enhance global structure during the denoising process. Experimental results demonstrate that ScaleDiff achieves state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods in terms of both image quality and inference speed on both U-Net and Diffusion Transformer architectures.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can lose image quality when asked to generate beyond the resolution used during training. ScaleDiff addresses this without additional training, while targeting the computational cost and architectural compatibility problems of earlier approaches. It is designed to work with pretrained models built around either U-Nets or Diffusion Transformers.

Its central attention mechanism, Neighborhood Patch Attention, uses non-overlapping patches to reduce redundant self-attention computation. The framework incorporates this mechanism into an SDEdit pipeline. Latent Frequency Mixing helps generate fine detail, while Structure Guidance supports the overall arrangement of the image during denoising. These components address local detail and global structure alongside inference efficiency.

The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art image quality and inference speed among training-free methods on both architecture families. This matters because extending resolution requires more than simply producing a larger image: the method also has to preserve coherent structure and useful detail. ScaleDiff's results support combining attention efficiency with separate mechanisms for fine-scale content and global organization.
summary.tldr: ScaleDiff extends pretrained diffusion models to higher resolutions without training, combining efficient attention with detail and structure guidance.

title: ScaleDiff: Higher-Resolution Image Synthesis via Efficient and Model-Agnostic Diffusion

abstract: In settings where ML models are used to inform the allocation of resources, agents affected by the allocation decisions might have an incentive to strategically change their features to secure better outcomes. While prior work has studied strategic responses broadly, disentangling misreporting from genuine adaptation remains a fundamental challenge. In this paper, we propose a causally-motivated approach to identify and quantify how much an agent misreports on average by distinguishing deceptive changes in their features from genuine adaptation. Our key insight is that, unlike genuine adaptation, misreported features do not causally affect downstream variables (i.e., causal descendants). We exploit this asymmetry by comparing the causal effect of misreported features on their causal descendants as derived from manipulated datasets against those from unmanipulated datasets. We formally prove identifiability of the misreporting rate and characterize the variance of our estimator. We empirically validate our theoretical results using a semi-synthetic and real Medicare dataset with misreported data, demonstrating that our approach can be employed to identify misreporting in real-world scenarios.

paragraphs: When a machine-learning model influences resource allocation, affected people or organizations may change their recorded features to obtain better outcomes. Such changes can reflect real adaptation or deceptive reporting, and observing changed features alone does not separate the two. This paper develops a causal method for estimating how much misreporting occurs on average.

The method relies on a specific asymmetry: a genuine change can affect downstream variables, whereas merely misreporting a feature does not causally change those descendants. The authors compare causal effects derived from manipulated data with those derived from unmanipulated data. That comparison provides a basis for distinguishing reported changes from changes that propagate through the underlying causal system.

The paper proves that the misreporting rate is identifiable in its formulation and characterizes the estimator's variance. Empirical checks use semi-synthetic data and a real Medicare dataset containing misreported data. These results support using downstream causal relationships to quantify misreporting in strategic settings, with the target being an average rate rather than a claim to classify every individual report.
summary.tldr: The paper estimates average misreporting by comparing how reported features relate causally to downstream variables in manipulated and unmanipulated data.

title: Disentangling misreporting from genuine adaptation in strategic settings: a causal approach

abstract: The increasing reliance on large-scale datasets in machine learning poses significant privacy and ethical challenges, particularly in sensitive domains such as face recognition. Synthetic data generation offers a promising alternative; however, most existing methods depend heavily on external datasets or pre-trained models, increasing complexity and resource demands. In this paper, we introduce **AugGen**, a self-contained synthetic augmentation technique. AugGen strategically samples from a class-conditional generative model trained exclusively on the target FR dataset, eliminating the need for external resources. Evaluated across 8 FR benchmarks, including IJB-C and IJB-B, our method achieves **1–12% performance improvements**, outperforming models trained solely on real data and surpassing state-of-the-art synthetic data generation approaches, while using less real data. Notably, these gains often exceed those from architectural modifications, underscoring the value of synthetic augmentation in data-limited scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that carefully integrated synthetic data can both mitigate privacy constraints and substantially enhance discriminative performance in face recognition. Code and datasets will be made publicly available upon publication.

paragraphs: AugGen investigates whether carefully generated training examples can improve face recognition while reducing dependence on large collections of real images. The paper motivates this direction through privacy and ethical concerns surrounding such datasets. Its central design choice is to build the augmentation process entirely around the target face recognition dataset.

The method trains a class-conditional generative model exclusively on that dataset, then strategically samples synthetic examples from it. This makes the augmentation self-contained: it does not require external datasets or pretrained models. The approach emphasizes how generated data are selected and integrated into recognition training, rather than relying on additional outside resources.

Across eight face recognition benchmarks, including IJB-C and IJB-B, the authors report improvements of 1–12%. AugGen outperforms training on real data alone and the compared leading synthetic generation approaches while using less real data. The gains often exceed those from architectural changes, supporting synthetic augmentation as a useful option in data-limited settings. The stated privacy benefit is mitigation of constraints, rather than a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: AugGen generates augmentation data using only the target face dataset, improving recognition across eight benchmarks while using less real data.

title: AugGen: Synthetic Augmentation using Diffusion Models Can Improve Recognition

abstract: Recent advancements in static feed-forward scene reconstruction have demonstrated significant progress in high-quality novel view synthesis. However, these models often struggle with generalizability across diverse environments and fail to effectively handle dynamic content. We present BTimer (short for Bullet Timer), the first motion-aware feed-forward model for real-time reconstruction and novel view synthesis of dynamic scenes. Our approach reconstructs the full scene in a 3D Gaussian Splatting representation at a given target (‘bullet’) timestamp by aggregating information from all the context frames. Such a formulation allows BTimer to gain scalability and generalization by leveraging both static and dynamic scene datasets. Given a casual monocular dynamic video, BTimer reconstructs a bullet-time scene within 150ms while reaching state-of-the-art performance on both static and dynamic scene datasets, even compared with optimization-based approaches.

paragraphs: BTimer reconstructs a dynamic scene at a chosen instant from a monocular video, meaning a video captured through one camera view at a time. The resulting bullet-time representation supports viewing that frozen moment from new viewpoints. This addresses a difficulty for feed-forward reconstruction systems developed around static scenes: moving content changes across the available frames.

The model aggregates information from all context frames to reconstruct the complete scene at the requested timestamp. It represents that scene using 3D Gaussian Splatting. By making a target moment the focus of reconstruction, the formulation can draw on both static and dynamic scene datasets, which the authors identify as a source of scalability and generalization.

The reported system reconstructs a bullet-time scene from a casual monocular dynamic video within 150 milliseconds. It also achieves state-of-the-art performance on the evaluated static and dynamic datasets, including comparisons with optimization-based methods. The findings show that the reported fast reconstruction approach can handle scene motion while producing competitive novel views, connecting dynamic reconstruction quality with real-time operation.
summary.tldr: BTimer reconstructs a dynamic scene at a chosen moment from monocular video in 150 milliseconds, enabling high-quality novel views.

title: Feed-Forward Bullet-Time Reconstruction of Dynamic Scenes from Monocular Videos

abstract: Image-based 3D texture transfer from a single 2D reference image enables practical customization of 3D object appearances with minimal manual effort. Adapted 2D editing and text-driven 3D editing approaches can serve this purpose. However, 2D editing typically involves frame-by-frame manipulation, often resulting in inconsistencies across views, while text-driven 3D editing struggles to preserve texture characteristics from reference images. To tackle these challenges, we introduce \textbf{3DOT}, a \textbf{3D} Gaussian Splatting \textbf{O}bject \textbf{T}exture Transfer method based on a single reference image, integrating: 1) progressive generation, 2) view-consistency gradient guidance, and 3) prompt-tuned gradient guidance. To ensure view consistency, progressive generation starts by transferring texture from the reference image and gradually propagates it to adjacent views. View-consistency gradient guidance further reinforces coherence by conditioning the generation model on feature differences between consistent and inconsistent outputs. To preserve texture characteristics, prompt-tuning-based gradient guidance learns a token that describes differences between original and reference textures, guiding the transfer for faithful texture preservation across views. Overall, 3DOT combines these strategies to achieve effective texture transfer while maintaining structural coherence across viewpoints. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations confirm that our three components enable convincing and effective 2D-to-3D texture transfer. Our project page is available here: https://massyzs.github.io/3DOT_web/.

paragraphs: 3DOT changes the appearance of a 3D Gaussian Splatting object using a single reference image. The challenge is to preserve the reference texture while making the edited object look coherent from different viewpoints. Editing individual views can produce inconsistencies, while describing the desired change through text can lose distinctive texture characteristics.

The method combines three ways of guiding generation. First, it transfers the reference texture into an initial view and progressively spreads that change to neighboring views. Second, it uses feature differences between consistent and inconsistent outputs to reinforce agreement across viewpoints. Third, it learns a text token describing how the original texture differs from the reference, then uses that token to guide texture preservation.

These components address related but distinct requirements: transferring the intended appearance and keeping that appearance coherent around the object. The reported qualitative and quantitative evaluations support the effectiveness of their combination. The contribution is a coordinated procedure for image-driven texture transfer that preserves texture characteristics while maintaining structural coherence across views.
summary.tldr: 3DOT transfers texture from one image onto a 3D Gaussian Splatting object through progressive generation and guidance for texture fidelity and view consistency.

title: 3DOT: Texture Transfer for 3DGS Objects from a Single Reference Image

abstract: Data attribution methods, which quantify the influence of individual training data points on a machine learning model, have gained increasing popularity in data-centric applications in modern AI. Despite a recent surge of new methods developed in this space, the impact of hyperparameter tuning in these methods remains under-explored. In this work, we present the first large-scale empirical study to understand the hyperparameter sensitivity of common data attribution methods. Our results show that most methods are indeed sensitive to certain key hyperparameters. However, unlike typical machine learning algorithms---whose hyperparameters can be tuned using computationally-cheap validation metrics---evaluating data attribution performance often requires retraining models on subsets of training data, making such metrics prohibitively costly for hyperparameter tuning. This poses a critical open challenge for the practical application of data attribution methods. To address this challenge, we advocate for better theoretical understandings of hyperparameter behavior to inform efficient tuning strategies. As a case study, we provide a theoretical analysis of the regularization term that is critical in many variants of influence function methods. Building on this analysis, we propose a lightweight procedure for selecting the regularization value without model retraining, and validate its effectiveness across a range of standard data attribution benchmarks. Overall, our study identifies a fundamental yet overlooked challenge in the practical application of data attribution, and highlights the importance of careful discussion on hyperparameter selection in future method development.

paragraphs: Data attribution estimates how individual training examples influence a machine-learning model. This paper examines a practical complication: the attribution method’s own settings can substantially affect its results. A large empirical study finds that most common methods are sensitive to particular hyperparameters, making careful selection important for their use.

Ordinary model tuning often relies on inexpensive validation measurements. Evaluating attribution quality, by contrast, can require retraining models on different subsets of the training data. Repeating that procedure across candidate settings makes conventional hyperparameter search costly, so the paper argues for using theoretical understanding to guide more efficient selection.

As a concrete case study, the authors analyze the regularization term used in many influence-function methods. That analysis leads to a lightweight procedure for choosing the regularization value without retraining the model, which they validate on standard attribution benchmarks. The contribution combines evidence of a broad sensitivity problem with a targeted solution for one important setting, showing why attribution methods should specify how their hyperparameters are selected.
summary.tldr: The paper reveals widespread hyperparameter sensitivity in data attribution and derives a retraining-free way to select regularization for influence-function methods.

title: Taming Hyperparameter Sensitivity in Data Attribution: Practical Selection Without Costly Retraining

abstract: Boosted decision trees are one of the most popular and successful learning techniques used today. While exhibiting fast speeds at test time, relatively slow training makes them impractical for applications with real-time learning requirements. We propose a principled approach to overcome this drawback. We prove a bound on the error of a decision stump given its preliminary error on a subset of the training data; the bound may be used to prune unpromising features early on in the training process. We propose a fast training algorithm that exploits this bound, yielding speedups of an order of magnitude at no cost in the final performance of the classifier. Our method is not a new variant of Boosting; rather, it may be used in conjunction with existing Boosting algorithms and other sampling heuristics to achieve even greater speedups.

paragraphs: Boosted decision trees can make predictions quickly, yet training them can be too slow for applications that need to learn in real time. This paper targets training cost by identifying features that are unlikely to be useful before spending the full effort evaluating them. The approach uses preliminary evidence from a subset of the training data.

The authors prove a bound relating a decision stump's error to its preliminary error on that subset. A decision stump is a simple tree with one split. The bound can be used to prune unpromising features early, and the proposed training algorithm turns this theoretical result into a mechanism for reducing work.

The paper reports speedups of roughly an order of magnitude without reducing final classifier performance. The technique can be combined with existing boosting algorithms and other sampling heuristics, potentially producing further speedups. Its contribution is therefore a way to accelerate training within established boosting procedures through principled early elimination of weak feature candidates.
summary.tldr: Error bounds on partial-data evaluations let boosted-tree training prune unpromising features early, yielding reported tenfold speedups without performance loss.

title: Quickly Boosting Decision Trees – Pruning Underachieving Features Early

abstract: Computational topology has recently seen an important development toward data analysis, giving birth to Topological Data Analysis. Persistent homology appears as a fundamental tool in this field. We show that the use of persistent homology can be naturally considered in general statistical frameworks. We establish convergence rates of persistence diagrams associated to data randomly sampled from any compact metric space to a well defined limit diagram encoding the topological features of the support of the measure from which the data have been sampled. Our approach relies on a recent and deep stability result for persistence that allows to relate our problem to support estimation problems (with respect to the Gromov-Hausdorff distance). Some numerical experiments are performed in various contexts to illustrate our results.

paragraphs: The paper places persistent homology within a statistical estimation framework. Its question is how persistence diagrams computed from random data relate to the topology of the underlying source of those data. This shifts attention from computing a diagram for one sample to understanding how that diagram behaves as an estimate.

The authors establish convergence rates for diagrams associated with observations randomly sampled from any compact metric space. The estimates converge toward a well-defined limit diagram encoding topological features of the sampling distribution’s support. The target is therefore a property of the underlying space occupied by the distribution, giving the statistical analysis a precise object to recover.

The argument uses a stability result for persistence to connect diagram estimation with support estimation measured through Gromov–Hausdorff distance. This connection allows geometric estimation results to inform the accuracy of topological summaries. Numerical experiments in several settings illustrate the theory. The contribution provides rates of convergence, going beyond a qualitative claim that more data should improve the diagrams.
summary.tldr: Persistence diagrams receive statistical convergence guarantees by linking topological stability to estimation of a distribution’s support.

title: Convergence rates for persistence diagram estimation in Topological Data Analysis

abstract: Modern classification problems frequently present mild to severe label imbalance as well as specific requirements on classification characteristics, and require optimizing performance measures that are non-decomposable over the dataset, such as F-measure. Such measures have spurred much interest and pose specific challenges to learning algorithms since their non-additive nature precludes a direct application of well-studied large scale optimization methods such as stochastic gradient descent. In this paper we reveal that for two large families of performance measures that can be expressed as functions of true positive/negative rates, it is indeed possible to implement point stochastic updates. The families we consider are concave and pseudo-linear functions of TPR, TNR which cover several popularly used performance measures such as F-measure, G-mean and H-mean. Our core contribution is an adaptive linearization scheme for these families, using which we develop optimization techniques that enable truly point-based stochastic updates. For concave performance measures we propose SPADE, a stochastic primal dual solver; for pseudo-linear measures we propose STAMP, a stochastic alternate maximization procedure. Both methods have crisp convergence guarantees, demonstrate significant speedups over existing methods - often by an order of magnitude or more, and give similar or more accurate predictions on test data.

paragraphs: Classification measures such as F-measure evaluate predictions collectively across a dataset. They cannot generally be written as a sum of independent losses for individual examples, which makes direct use of ordinary stochastic gradient methods difficult. This matters particularly when labels are imbalanced or the application requires a specific balance of classification outcomes.

The paper identifies two broad families of measures, concave and pseudo-linear functions of true-positive and true-negative rates, for which individual-example stochastic updates are possible. These families include F-measure, G-mean, and H-mean. The key device is adaptive linearization, which creates an optimization form that supports point-based updates despite the original measure's aggregate dependence.

The authors develop SPADE, a stochastic primal-dual solver for concave measures, and STAMP, a stochastic alternating-maximization procedure for pseudo-linear measures. Both have convergence guarantees. Experiments report substantial speedups over existing methods, often at least an order of magnitude, while producing similar or better test accuracy. The results show that nonadditive evaluation measures in these families can still support scalable stochastic training.
summary.tldr: Adaptive linearization enables efficient individual-example stochastic updates for two broad families of non-decomposable classification measures.

title: Optimizing Non-decomposable Performance Measures: A Tale of Two Classes

abstract: Significant progress has been made recently on theoretical analysis of estimators for the stochastic block model (SBM). In this paper, we consider the multi-graph SBM, which serves as a foundation for many application settings including dynamic and multi-layer networks. We explore the asymptotic properties of two estimators for the multi-graph SBM, namely spectral clustering and the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE), as the number of layers of the multi-graph increases. We derive sufficient conditions for consistency of both estimators and propose a variational approximation to the MLE that is computationally feasible for large networks. We verify the sufficient conditions via simulation and demonstrate that they are practical. In addition, we apply the model to two real data sets: a dynamic social network and a multi-layer social network with several types of relations.

paragraphs: Networks can provide multiple views of relationships, either through observations over time or through different types of connections. This paper studies the multi-graph stochastic block model as a framework for these settings. Its central question is how reliably network structure can be estimated as the number of observed graph layers grows.

The authors analyze two estimation approaches: spectral clustering and maximum likelihood. They derive sufficient conditions under which each estimator is consistent as additional layers become available. These results identify circumstances where accumulating graph observations supports reliable estimation; they do not claim that adding layers guarantees consistency in every setting.

To make maximum-likelihood estimation usable on large networks, the paper also proposes a computationally feasible variational approximation. Simulations examine the sufficient conditions and support their practical relevance. Applications to a changing social network and a social network with multiple relationship types demonstrate the model in both motivating settings. Together, the contributions connect asymptotic guarantees with a practical estimation approach.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for consistent estimation from multiple network layers and develops a scalable approximation to maximum likelihood.

title: Consistent estimation of dynamic and multi-layer block models

abstract: Recently, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been used as a powerful tool to solve many problems of machine learning and computer vision. In this paper, we aim to provide insight on the property of convolutional neural networks, as well as a generic method to improve the performance of many CNN architectures. Specifically, we first examine existing CNN models and observe an intriguing property that the filters in the lower layers form pairs (i.e., filters with opposite phase). Inspired by our observation, we propose a novel, simple yet effective activation scheme called concatenated ReLU (CReLU) and theoretically analyze its reconstruction property in CNNs. We integrate CReLU into several state-of-the-art CNN architectures and demonstrate improvement in their recognition performance on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet datasets with fewer trainable parameters. Our results suggest that better understanding of the properties of CNNs can lead to significant performance improvement with a simple modification.

paragraphs: The paper begins with an observation about existing convolutional networks: filters in lower layers tend to form pairs with opposite phases. The authors use this recurring structure as a clue for architecture design. Their aim is both to understand a property of these networks and to turn that understanding into a useful modification.

They propose an activation scheme called concatenated ReLU, or CReLU, motivated by the observed filter pairing. They also analyze its reconstruction property theoretically. This gives the proposed change an analytical component alongside its origin in observed network behavior, connecting activation design with the information represented inside a convolutional network.

The authors incorporate CReLU into several established architectures and report improved recognition performance on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with fewer trainable parameters. These results suggest that a simple modification informed by network structure can improve performance without increasing the learned parameter count. The empirical claim concerns the architectures and datasets evaluated, while the broader lesson is the value of examining existing representations to guide design.
summary.tldr: Inspired by opposite-phase filter pairs, CReLU improves recognition across evaluated convolutional architectures while using fewer trainable parameters.

title: Understanding and Improving Convolutional Neural Networks via Concatenated Rectified Linear Units

abstract: To date, the tightest upper and lower-bounds for the active learning of general concept classes have been in terms of a parameter of the learning problem called the splitting index. We provide, for the first time, an efficient algorithm that is able to realize this upper bound, and we empirically demonstrate its good performance.

We provide, for the first time, an efficient algorithm that is able to realize this upper bound, and we empirically demonstrate its good performance.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a gap between theoretical guarantees and efficient algorithms in active learning. For general concept classes, the tightest upper and lower bounds described in the abstract depend on a quantity called the splitting index. That parameter provides a way to express the difficulty of a learning problem and the performance that theory allows.

The main contribution is an efficient algorithm that attains the upper bound expressed through the splitting index. This matters because an upper bound and an efficient procedure realizing it are distinct achievements. The result connects the existing theoretical description of achievable performance to an algorithm that can deliver that guarantee.

The authors also report good empirical performance, adding experimental support to the theoretical contribution. The central finding is therefore an alignment between an established bound and efficient algorithm design for general concept classes. The splitting index remains the organizing parameter: the result realizes the associated upper bound, giving that theoretical characterization a concrete algorithmic counterpart.
summary.tldr: The paper provides an efficient active-learning algorithm that realizes the established upper bound expressed through the splitting index.

title: Diameter-Based Active Learning

abstract: In recent years, the multiclass and mutlilabel classification problems we encounter in many applications have very large ($10^3$–$10^6$) number of classes. However, each instance belongs to only one or few classes, i.e., the label vectors are sparse. In this work, we propose a novel approach based on group testing to solve such large multilabel classification problems with sparse label vectors. We describe various group testing constructions, and advocate the use of concatenated Reed Solomon codes and unbalanced bipartite expander graphs for extreme classification problems. The proposed approach has several advantages theoretically and practically over existing popular methods. Our method operates on the binary alphabet and can utilize the well-established binary classifiers for learning. The error correction capabilities of the codes are leveraged for the first time in the learning problem to correct prediction errors. Even if a linearly growing number of classifiers mis-classify, these errors are fully corrected. We establish Hamming loss error bounds for the approach. More importantly, our method utilizes a simple prediction algorithm and does not require matrix inversion or solving optimization problems making the algorithm very inexpensive. Numerical experiments with various datasets illustrate the superior performance of our method.

paragraphs: Extreme multilabel classification may involve thousands to millions of possible labels, even though each example has only a few relevant ones. This paper uses that sparsity to formulate prediction through group testing. The approach operates with binary outputs, allowing it to use established binary classifiers as its learning components.

The authors describe several constructions and advocate concatenated Reed Solomon codes and unbalanced bipartite expander graphs. Error-correcting structure plays a central role: errors in individual classifier predictions can be repaired when decoding the labels. The stated correction capability includes a linearly growing number of classifier errors, and the paper establishes Hamming loss bounds for the approach.

The contribution combines sparse label structure, binary classification, and coding-based correction so that a large output space can be handled with efficient prediction and explicit protection against classifier mistakes.
summary.tldr: Group testing and error-correcting codes enable inexpensive multilabel prediction with provable error control for sparse label vectors.

title: Multilabel Classification with Group Testing and Codes

abstract: We introduce and study two algorithms to accelerate greedy coordinate descent in theory and in practice: Accelerated Semi-Greedy Coordinate Descent (ASCD) and Accelerated Greedy Coordinate Descent (AGCD). On the theory side, our main results are for ASCD: we show that ASCD achieves $O(1/k^2)$ convergence, and it also achieves accelerated linear convergence for strongly convex functions. On the empirical side, while both AGCD and ASCD outperform Accelerated Randomized Coordinate Descent on most instances in our numerical experiments, we note that AGCD significantly outperforms the other two methods in our experiments, in spite of a lack of theoretical guarantees for this method. To complement this empirical finding for AGCD, we present an explanation why standard proof techniques for acceleration cannot work for AGCD, and we further introduce a technical condition under which AGCD is guaranteed to have accelerated convergence. Finally, we confirm that this technical condition holds in our numerical experiments.
