paragraphs: Coordinate descent improves an objective by updating individual coordinates. Greedy versions choose coordinates according to their immediate promise, but combining that choice with acceleration raises theoretical challenges. This paper introduces two methods, Accelerated Semi-Greedy Coordinate Descent (ASCD) and Accelerated Greedy Coordinate Descent (AGCD), to investigate both provable convergence and practical performance.

The strongest general theoretical results concern ASCD. The authors establish an O(1/k²) convergence rate and accelerated linear convergence for strongly convex functions. In numerical experiments, both proposed methods outperform Accelerated Randomized Coordinate Descent on most instances. AGCD performs substantially better than the other two methods in those experiments, despite lacking the same general theoretical guarantees.

The paper examines this gap between observed behavior and available proofs. It explains why standard acceleration proof techniques cannot establish the desired result for AGCD, then identifies a technical condition that does guarantee accelerated convergence. That condition holds in the reported experiments. The contribution therefore combines a theoretically supported method with a stronger empirical performer whose acceleration receives a conditional justification.
summary.tldr: Two accelerated greedy coordinate methods offer complementary theoretical and empirical strengths, with AGCD’s acceleration guaranteed under a stated technical condition.

title: Accelerating Greedy Coordinate Descent Methods

abstract: We show that training a deep network using batch normalization is equivalent to approximate inference in Bayesian models. We further demonstrate that this finding allows us to make meaningful estimates of the model uncertainty using conventional architectures, without modifications to the network or the training procedure. Our approach is thoroughly validated by measuring the quality of uncertainty in a series of empirical experiments on different tasks. It outperforms baselines with strong statistical significance, and displays competitive performance with recent Bayesian approaches.

It outperforms baselines with strong statistical significance, and displays competitive performance with recent Bayesian approaches.

paragraphs: This paper connects training with batch normalization to approximate inference in Bayesian models. The connection provides a way to interpret an existing neural-network training practice in terms of uncertainty about the model. That perspective matters because making a prediction and estimating how uncertain the model is about that prediction are distinct tasks.

The authors use this equivalence to obtain meaningful model-uncertainty estimates from conventional network architectures. Their approach requires no changes to the network or its training procedure. The practical contribution is therefore a route to uncertainty estimation that builds on batch-normalized networks, allowing the Bayesian interpretation to inform how those models are used.

The evaluation measures uncertainty quality across experiments on different tasks. The approach outperforms the tested baselines with strong statistical significance and performs competitively with recent Bayesian methods. These findings support the usefulness of the derived uncertainty estimates in the evaluated settings, alongside the theoretical connection that makes the approach possible.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian interpretation of batch normalization enables useful uncertainty estimates without changing the network or its training procedure.

title: Bayesian Uncertainty Estimation for Batch Normalized Deep Networks

abstract: Vanishing and exploding gradients are two of the main obstacles in training deep neural networks, especially in capturing long range dependencies in recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In this paper, we present an efficient parametrization of the transition matrix of an RNN that allows us to stabilize the gradients that arise in its training. Specifically, we parameterize the transition matrix by its singular value decomposition (SVD), which allows us to explicitly track and control its singular values. We attain efficiency by using tools that are common in numerical linear algebra, namely Householder reflectors for representing the orthogonal matrices that arise in the SVD. By explicitly controlling the singular values, our proposed Spectral-RNN method allows us to easily solve the exploding gradient problem and we observe that it empirically solves the vanishing gradient issue to a large extent. We note that the SVD parameterization can be used for any rectangular weight matrix, hence it can be easily extended to any deep neural network, such as a multi-layer perceptron. Theoretically, we demonstrate that our parameterization does not lose any expressive power, and show how it potentially makes the optimization process easier. Our extensive experimental results also demonstrate that the proposed framework converges faster, and has good generalization, especially in capturing long range dependencies, as shown on the synthetic addition and copy tasks, as well as on MNIST and Penn Tree Bank data sets.

paragraphs: Training recurrent networks on long-range dependencies is difficult when gradients vanish or explode. Spectral-RNN addresses this by representing the recurrent transition matrix through its singular value decomposition. This exposes the singular values directly so that the method can track and control them during training.

The orthogonal matrices in the decomposition are represented efficiently using Householder reflectors. Explicit singular-value control addresses exploding gradients, while the authors observe that vanishing gradients are also reduced substantially in experiments. They prove that the parameterization preserves expressive power and explain how it could make optimization easier. Because it applies to rectangular weight matrices, it can also extend to other deep networks.

Experiments report faster convergence and good generalization, especially for learning long-range dependencies. Evaluations include addition and copy tasks, MNIST, and Penn Tree Bank. The paper thus combines an efficient matrix representation with direct control over properties relevant to gradient propagation, while distinguishing its theoretical expressivity result from its empirical findings about vanishing gradients.
summary.tldr: Spectral-RNN efficiently controls singular values to stabilize training gradients while preserving expressive power.

title: Stabilizing Gradients for Deep Neural Networks via Efficient SVD Parameterization

abstract: Differentially private learning algorithms protect individual participants in the training dataset by guaranteeing that their presence does not significantly change the resulting model. In order to make this promise, such algorithms need to know the maximum contribution that can be made by a single user: the more data an individual can contribute, the more noise will need to be added to protect them. While most existing analyses assume that the maximum contribution is known and fixed in advance{—}indeed, it is often assumed that each user contributes only a single example{—}we argue that in practice there is a meaningful choice to be made. On the one hand, if we allow users to contribute large amounts of data, we may end up adding excessive noise to protect a few outliers, even when the majority contribute only modestly. On the other hand, limiting users to small contributions keeps noise levels low at the cost of potentially discarding significant amounts of excess data, thus introducing bias. Here, we characterize this trade-off for an empirical risk minimization setting, showing that in general there is a “sweet spot” that depends on measurable properties of the dataset, but that there is also a concrete cost to privacy that cannot be avoided simply by collecting more data.

paragraphs: Differentially private learning limits how much an individual participant can influence a trained model. Providing that protection requires accounting for the largest contribution any user can make. If one person supplies many examples, protecting that person can require substantially more noise, even when most users contribute relatively little.

This paper treats the contribution limit as a meaningful design choice. A generous limit retains more data but can force the algorithm to add excessive noise because of a few unusually large contributors. A restrictive limit reduces the required noise, but discards excess examples and can introduce bias. The authors characterize this tension in empirical risk minimization, where training seeks to reduce loss on the available data.

The analysis identifies a generally useful balance between these competing effects, with the appropriate contribution level depending on measurable dataset properties. Thus, a fixed assumption that every user contributes one example can miss an important practical decision. The paper also establishes a privacy cost that cannot simply be eliminated by collecting more data, making contribution control part of the learning problem itself.
summary.tldr: Choosing how much data each user may contribute balances discarded-data bias against privacy noise, with a useful balance determined by dataset properties.

title: Bounding User Contributions: A Bias-Variance Trade-off in Differential Privacy

abstract: In high dimensions, most machine learning methods are brittle to even a small fraction of structured outliers. To address this, we introduce a new meta-algorithm that can take in a base learner such as least squares or stochastic gradient descent, and harden the learner to be resistant to outliers. Our method, Sever, possesses strong theoretical guarantees yet is also highly scalable – beyond running the base learner itself, it only requires computing the top singular vector of a certain n{\texttimes}d matrix. We apply Sever on a drug design dataset and a spam classification dataset, and find that in both cases it has substantially greater robustness than several baselines. On the spam dataset, with 1% corruptions, we achieved 7.4% test error, compared to 13.4%-20.5% for the baselines, and 3% error on the uncorrupted dataset. Similarly, on the drug design dataset, with 10% corruptions, we achieved 1.42 mean-squared error test error, compared to 1.51-2.33 for the baselines, and 1.23 error on the uncorrupted dataset.

paragraphs: Structured outliers can make high-dimensional learning methods unreliable even when only a small fraction of the data is corrupted. Sever is a meta-algorithm designed to strengthen an existing learner, such as least squares or stochastic gradient descent, against these outliers. The approach allows robustness to be added around a base learning procedure.

The method combines theoretical guarantees with a scalable computational requirement. Beyond running the underlying learner, it requires computing the top singular vector of a particular n-by-d matrix. This identifies the additional linear-algebra operation involved, making computational cost part of the proposed method's appeal.

Experiments on spam classification and drug design report substantially greater robustness than several baselines. With 1% corruption on spam data, Sever obtains 7.4% test error versus 13.4–20.5% for baselines, with 3% on uncorrupted data. With 10% corruption on drug data, its mean-squared error is 1.42 versus 1.51–2.33, with 1.23 on uncorrupted data. These results show reduced damage from corruption, while performance remains below the uncorrupted reference.
summary.tldr: Sever strengthens existing learners against structured outliers, with theoretical guarantees and substantial robustness gains on two evaluated datasets.

title: Sever: A Robust Meta-Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Existing attention mechanisms are trained to attend to individual items in a collection (the memory) with a predefined, fixed granularity, e.g., a word token or an image grid. We propose area attention: a way to attend to areas in the memory, where each area contains a group of items that are structurally adjacent, e.g., spatially for a 2D memory such as images, or temporally for a 1D memory such as natural language sentences. Importantly, the shape and the size of an area are dynamically determined via learning, which enables a model to attend to information with varying granularity. Area attention can easily work with existing model architectures such as multi-head attention for simultaneously attending to multiple areas in the memory. We evaluate area attention on two tasks: neural machine translation (both character and token-level) and image captioning, and improve upon strong (state-of-the-art) baselines in all the cases. These improvements are obtainable with a basic form of area attention that is parameter free.

paragraphs: Attention lets a model select information from a collection, such as words in a sentence or locations in an image. Conventional mechanisms operate on individual items at a fixed granularity. Area attention instead allows the model to select groups of adjacent items, making the unit of attention more flexible.

An area follows the structure of the underlying information: its items can be neighboring positions in an image or consecutive positions in a sequence. Learning determines the area’s size and shape dynamically. The mechanism can also work with existing architectures, including multi-head attention, so a model can attend to several areas at once.

The authors evaluate the approach on machine translation at both character and token levels, and on image captioning. They report improvements over strong, state-of-the-art baselines in every evaluated case. These gains are available with a basic parameter-free form of area attention, indicating that changing how information is grouped can help without requiring extra learned parameters in that form of the mechanism.
summary.tldr: Area attention learns to focus on adjacent groups of varying sizes, improving translation and image captioning even in a parameter-free form.

title: Area Attention

abstract: We clarify what fairness guarantees we can and cannot expect to follow from unconstrained machine learning. Specifically, we show that in many settings, unconstrained learning on its own implies group calibration, that is, the outcome variable is conditionally independent of group membership given the score. A lower bound confirms the optimality of our upper bound. Moreover, we prove that as the excess risk of the learned score decreases, the more strongly it violates separation and independence, two other standard fairness criteria. Our results challenge the view that group calibration necessitates an active intervention, suggesting that often we ought to think of it as a byproduct of unconstrained machine learning.

paragraphs: This paper asks which fairness properties can emerge from ordinary machine learning without explicit fairness constraints. Its central result concerns group calibration: once a prediction score is known, group membership provides no further information about the outcome. The authors show that unconstrained learning implies this property in many settings.

The analysis supplies an upper bound and a matching lower bound that establishes its optimality. This gives a quantitative foundation for viewing calibration as a possible consequence of learning itself. It challenges the assumption that achieving group calibration always requires a separate intervention, while retaining the qualification that the result applies in the settings studied.

The same analysis reveals tension with two other fairness criteria, separation and independence. As the learned score’s excess risk decreases, the authors prove that violations of those criteria become stronger. Better predictive optimization therefore does not imply simultaneous progress on all fairness definitions. The paper clarifies which fairness behavior unconstrained learning can produce and why calibration alone cannot stand in for every fairness objective.
summary.tldr: In many settings, unconstrained learning produces group calibration while lower excess risk strengthens violations of separation and independence.

title: The Implicit Fairness Criterion of Unconstrained Learning

abstract: By enabling correct differentiation in Stochastic Computation Graphs (SCGs), the infinitely differentiable Monte-Carlo estimator (DiCE) can generate correct estimates for the higher order gradients that arise in, e.g., multi-agent reinforcement learning and meta-learning. However, the baseline term in DiCE that serves as a control variate for reducing variance applies only to first order gradient estimation, limiting the utility of higher-order gradient estimates. To improve the sample efficiency of DiCE, we propose a new baseline term for higher order gradient estimation. This term may be easily included in the objective, and produces unbiased variance-reduced estimators under (automatic) differentiation, without affecting the estimate of the objective itself or of the first order gradient estimate. It reuses the same baseline function (e.g., the state-value function in reinforcement learning) already used for the first order baseline. We provide theoretical analysis and numerical evaluations of this new baseline, which demonstrate that it can dramatically reduce the variance of DiCE’s second order gradient estimators and also show empirically that it reduces the variance of third and fourth order gradients. This computational tool can be easily used to estimate higher order gradients with unprecedented efficiency and simplicity wherever automatic differentiation is utilised, and it has the potential to unlock applications of higher order gradients in reinforcement learning and meta-learning.

paragraphs: Stochastic computation graphs combine calculations with random sampling, making differentiation more complicated than in a fully deterministic computation. DiCE provides correct Monte Carlo estimates of higher-order derivatives, which arise in settings such as meta-learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning. However, its existing variance-reduction baseline helps only with first-order derivatives, leaving higher-order estimates potentially noisy.

The paper introduces an additional baseline term that works through automatic differentiation to reduce variance in higher-order estimates without introducing bias. It can be added to the objective without changing the objective estimate or the first-order gradient estimate. It also reuses the baseline function already available for first-order estimation, such as a reinforcement learning state-value function.

Theoretical analysis and numerical evaluations show that the term can substantially reduce variance in second-order estimates. Experiments also show variance reductions for third- and fourth-order derivatives. The contribution is a simpler route to more sample-efficient higher-order differentiation; its potential to enable further reinforcement learning and meta-learning applications remains a prospective benefit.
summary.tldr: A new DiCE baseline reduces higher-order gradient variance while preserving unbiasedness and leaving objective and first-order estimates unchanged.

title: A Baseline for Any Order Gradient Estimation in Stochastic Computation Graphs

abstract: Building upon recent advances in entropy-regularized optimal transport, and upon Fenchel duality between measures and continuous functions, we propose a generalization of the logistic loss that incorporates a metric or cost between classes. Unlike previous attempts to use optimal transport distances for learning, our loss results in unconstrained convex objective functions, supports infinite (or very large) class spaces, and naturally defines a geometric generalization of the softmax operator. The geometric properties of this loss make it suitable for predicting sparse and singular distributions, for instance supported on curves or hyper-surfaces. We study the theoretical properties of our loss and showcase its effectiveness on two applications: ordinal regression and drawing generation.

paragraphs: When predictions are distributions over classes, the classes may have meaningful distances or costs between them. This paper generalizes logistic loss so that those relationships become part of the learning objective. Its construction combines entropy-regularized optimal transport with a duality between measures and continuous functions.

The resulting loss gives unconstrained convex objective functions and supports class spaces that are extremely large or infinite. It also produces a geometric counterpart of the softmax operator. These properties connect the representation of predictions to the geometry of the possible outcomes, while retaining the stated convex structure of the proposed objectives.

The loss is suitable for predicting sparse or singular distributions, including distributions concentrated on curves or hypersurfaces. That matters when the desired output occupies a structured subset of the available space. The authors analyze the loss theoretically and demonstrate its effectiveness in ordinal regression and drawing generation, illustrating its use for both ordered outcomes and geometrically structured outputs.
summary.tldr: A geometric generalization of logistic loss incorporates distances between classes and supports structured distributions over very large or infinite output spaces.

title: Geometric Losses for Distributional Learning

abstract: Representation learning is typically applied to only one mode of a data matrix, either its rows or columns. Yet in many applications, there is an underlying geometry to both the rows and the columns. We propose utilizing this coupled structure to perform co-manifold learning: uncovering the underlying geometry of both the rows and the columns of a given matrix, where we focus on a missing data setting. Our unsupervised approach consists of three components. We first solve a family of optimization problems to estimate a complete matrix at multiple scales of smoothness. We then use this collection of smooth matrix estimates to compute pairwise distances on the rows and columns based on a new multi-scale metric that implicitly introduces a coupling between the rows and the columns. Finally, we construct row and column representations from these multi-scale metrics. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms competing methods in both data visualization and clustering.

paragraphs: A data matrix can contain meaningful relationships among both its rows and its columns. Representation learning often concentrates on only one of these two directions. This paper develops co-manifold learning for incomplete matrices, seeking representations that reveal the geometry of both directions while using the connection between them.

The method has three stages. First, it solves a family of optimization problems to produce completed versions of the matrix at different levels of smoothness. It then combines information from those versions into a new multiscale measure of distance between rows and between columns. These distances implicitly couple the two directions, so their representations are informed by a shared collection of matrix estimates.

Finally, the method constructs row and column representations from the resulting distances. The authors report better visualization and clustering performance than competing approaches. The contribution is therefore more than filling empty entries: the completion process supplies information at several scales that helps uncover structure on both sides of the matrix.
summary.tldr: Co-manifold learning uses multiscale matrix completion to jointly reveal row and column structure, improving visualization and clustering in the reported evaluations.

title: Co-manifold learning with missing data

abstract: Recently, there has been a great deal of research attention on understanding the convergence behavior of first-order methods. One line of this research focuses on analyzing the convergence behavior of first-order methods using tools from continuous dynamical systems such as ordinary differential equations and differential inclusions. These research results shed lights on better understanding first-order methods from a non-optimization point of view. The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) is a widely used first-order method for solving optimization problems arising from machine learning and statistics, and it is important to investigate its behavior using these new techniques from dynamical systems. Existing works along this line have been mainly focusing on problems with smooth objective functions, which exclude many important applications that are traditionally solved by ADMM variants. In this paper, we analyze some well-known and widely used ADMM variants for nonsmooth optimization problems using tools of differential inclusions. In particular, we analyze the convergence behavior of linearized ADMM, gradient-based ADMM, generalized ADMM and accelerated generalized ADMM for nonsmooth problems and show their connections with dynamical systems. We anticipate that these results will provide new insights on understanding ADMM for solving nonsmooth problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization algorithms by connecting their iterative behavior to continuous dynamical systems. The focus is the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, which is widely used in machine learning and statistics. Much previous work on this connection considered smooth objectives, leaving out nonsmooth problems that are important applications of ADMM.

The authors use differential inclusions to analyze nonsmooth versions of several established algorithms: linearized ADMM, gradient-based ADMM, generalized ADMM, and accelerated generalized ADMM. Differential inclusions provide the continuous-system language for this analysis. The contribution is to investigate convergence behavior and establish connections between these discrete optimization methods and corresponding dynamical descriptions.

This perspective matters because it extends the continuous-limit study of ADMM beyond objectives covered by smooth analyses. It brings multiple widely used variants into a framework suited to nonsmooth problems. The authors anticipate that these connections will offer new understanding of ADMM; the stated contribution centers on analysis and interpretation of existing methods rather than an empirical performance improvement.
summary.tldr: Differential inclusions connect several nonsmooth ADMM variants to continuous dynamical systems and support analysis of their convergence behavior.

title: Differential Inclusions for Modeling Nonsmooth ADMM Variants: A Continuous Limit Theory

abstract: Normalizing flows are a powerful class of generative models for continuous random variables, showing both strong model flexibility and the potential for non-autoregressive generation. These benefits are also desired when modeling discrete random variables such as text, but directly applying normalizing flows to discrete sequences poses significant additional challenges. We propose a VAE-based generative model which jointly learns a normalizing flow-based distribution in the latent space and a stochastic mapping to an observed discrete space. In this setting, we find that it is crucial for the flow-based distribution to be highly multimodal. To capture this property, we propose several normalizing flow architectures to maximize model flexibility. Experiments consider common discrete sequence tasks of character-level language modeling and polyphonic music generation. Our results indicate that an autoregressive flow-based model can match the performance of a comparable autoregressive baseline, and a non-autoregressive flow-based model can improve generation speed with a penalty to performance.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows offer flexible probability models for continuous variables and the possibility of generating outputs without a sequential autoregressive process. Applying those advantages to discrete sequences, such as text, is more difficult. This paper places the flow inside a latent-variable model, allowing continuous modeling machinery to support discrete observations.

The proposed model uses a variational autoencoder framework to learn two components together: a flow-based distribution in latent space and a probabilistic mapping from that space to discrete sequences. The authors find that the latent distribution needs to accommodate many distinct modes. They therefore introduce several flow architectures intended to increase flexibility and capture this multimodal structure.

Experiments examine character-level language modeling and polyphonic music generation. An autoregressive flow model can match a comparable autoregressive baseline, while a non-autoregressive version generates faster at a cost in modeling performance. The findings establish a practical tradeoff: latent flows can support discrete sequence generation, but the speed advantage reported for non-autoregressive generation comes with reduced performance.
summary.tldr: Latent normalizing flows model discrete sequences through a probabilistic decoder, with faster non-autoregressive generation trading off against performance.

title: Latent Normalizing Flows for Discrete Sequences

abstract: Graph embeddings are a ubiquitous tool for machine learning tasks, such as node classification and link prediction, on graph-structured data. However, computing the embeddings for large-scale graphs is prohibitively inefficient even if we are interested only in a small subset of relevant vertices. To address this, we present an efficient graph coarsening approach, based on Schur complements, for computing the embedding of the relevant vertices. We prove that these embeddings are preserved exactly by the Schur complement graph that is obtained via Gaussian elimination on the non-relevant vertices. As computing Schur complements is expensive, we give a nearly-linear time algorithm that generates a coarsened graph on the relevant vertices that provably matches the Schur complement in expectation in each iteration. Our experiments involving prediction tasks on graphs demonstrate that computing embeddings on the coarsened graph, rather than the entire graph, leads to significant time savings without sacrificing accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings represent vertices in a form useful for tasks such as node classification and link prediction. Computing them on a large graph can be expensive even when only a small subset of vertices matters. This paper asks how to reduce the graph around those relevant vertices while preserving the information needed for their embeddings.

The authors use Schur complements, obtained by applying Gaussian elimination to the non-relevant vertices. They prove that the embeddings under consideration are preserved exactly in the resulting Schur complement graph. This supplies a mathematical basis for eliminating unwanted vertices without losing the target embeddings, but computing the exact Schur complement is itself expensive.

To address that cost, the paper introduces a nearly-linear-time coarsening algorithm whose output matches the Schur complement in expectation at each iteration. This expectation guarantee is distinct from the exact preservation result for the Schur complement itself. In graph prediction experiments, computing embeddings on the coarsened graph delivers significant time savings without sacrificing accuracy.
summary.tldr: Schur-complement-based graph coarsening accelerates embeddings for selected vertices, with theoretical preservation results and empirical time savings without accuracy loss.

title: Faster Graph Embeddings via Coarsening

abstract: Discrete choice models with unobserved heterogeneity are commonly used Econometric models for dynamic Economic behavior which have been adopted in practice to predict behavior of individuals and firms from schooling and job choices to strategic decisions in market competition. These models feature optimizing agents who choose among a finite set of options in a sequence of periods and receive choice-specific payoffs that depend on both variables that are observed by the agent and recorded in the data and variables that are only observed by the agent but not recorded in the data. Existing work in Econometrics assumes that optimizing agents are fully rational and requires finding a functional fixed point to find the optimal policy. We show that in an important class of discrete choice models the value function is globally concave in the policy. That means that simple algorithms that do not require fixed point computation, such as the policy gradient algorithm, globally converge to the optimal policy. This finding can both be used to relax behavioral assumption regarding the optimizing agents and to facilitate Econometric analysis of dynamic behavior. In particular, we demonstrate significant computational advantages in using a simple implementation policy gradient algorithm over existing “nested fixed point” algorithms used in Econometrics.

paragraphs: Dynamic discrete choice models describe agents who repeatedly choose among a finite set of options. Their payoffs can depend both on recorded variables and on information known to the agents but absent from the data. These models are used to study decisions such as schooling, employment, and market competition, where choices unfold over time.

Existing econometric approaches assume fully rational agents and compute optimal policies by solving a functional fixed-point problem. The paper proves that, for an important class of these models, the value function is globally concave in the policy. Within this class, simple methods such as policy gradient can therefore converge globally to an optimal policy without requiring fixed-point computation.

The result matters for both computation and behavioral modeling. It offers a way to relax assumptions about how agents reach optimal behavior while simplifying the analysis of their decisions. The authors also demonstrate significant computational advantages for a simple policy-gradient implementation over existing nested fixed-point algorithms. The concavity and convergence conclusions apply to the identified model class.
summary.tldr: Global concavity in a class of dynamic discrete choice models enables globally convergent policy-gradient optimization without fixed-point computation.

title: Global Concavity and Optimization in a Class of Dynamic Discrete Choice Models

abstract: In this paper, we consider matrix completion with absolute deviation loss and obtain an estimator of the median matrix. Despite several appealing properties of median, the non-smooth absolute deviation loss leads to computational challenge for large-scale data sets which are increasingly common among matrix completion problems. A simple solution to large-scale problems is parallel computing. However, embarrassingly parallel fashion often leads to inefficient estimators. Based on the idea of pseudo data, we propose a novel refinement step, which turns such inefficient estimators into a rate (near-)optimal matrix completion procedure. The refined estimator is an approximation of a regularized least median estimator, and therefore not an ordinary regularized empirical risk estimator. This leads to a non-standard analysis of asymptotic behaviors. Empirical results are also provided to confirm the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries from partially observed data. This paper targets a median matrix using absolute deviation loss. Although the median has appealing properties, the loss is nonsmooth, making large-scale optimization challenging. Dividing the work into independent parallel computations is straightforward, but the resulting estimators can be statistically inefficient.

The authors introduce a refinement step based on pseudo data to improve those initial estimators. The refinement turns an inefficient parallel estimate into a matrix completion procedure with an optimal or near-optimal statistical rate. Its role is to recover estimation quality while starting from the computationally convenient parallel approach.

The refined result approximates a regularized least median estimator, rather than being an ordinary regularized empirical-risk estimator itself. That distinction requires a nonstandard analysis of its asymptotic behavior. Empirical results also support the method's effectiveness. The paper therefore addresses both sides of the large-data problem: obtaining an initial estimate through parallel computation and refining it enough to achieve strong statistical accuracy.
summary.tldr: A pseudo-data refinement makes parallel median matrix completion statistically optimal or near-optimal.

title: Median Matrix Completion: from Embarrassment to Optimality

abstract: In this work, we explore the unique challenges—and opportunities—of unsupervised federated learning (FL). We develop and analyze a one-shot federated clustering scheme, kfed, based on the widely-used Lloyd’s method for $k$-means clustering. In contrast to many supervised problems, we show that the issue of statistical heterogeneity in federated networks can in fact benefit our analysis. We analyse kfed under a center separation assumption and compare it to the best known requirements of its centralized counterpart. Our analysis shows that in heterogeneous regimes where the number of clusters per device $(k’)$ is smaller than the total number of clusters over the network $k$, $(k’\le \sqrt{k})$, we can use heterogeneity to our advantage—significantly weakening the cluster separation requirements for kfed. From a practical viewpoint, kfed also has many desirable properties: it requires only round of communication, can run asynchronously, and can handle partial participation or node/network failures. We motivate our analysis with experiments on common FL benchmarks, and highlight the practical utility of one-shot clustering through use-cases in personalized FL and device sampling.

paragraphs: Federated devices often hold different kinds of data, a property that can complicate supervised learning. This paper shows how such heterogeneity can help the analysis of unsupervised clustering. It introduces kfed, a federated clustering scheme based on Lloyd’s method for k-means that requires only one round of communication.

The theoretical analysis assumes separation between cluster centers and compares the required separation with known centralized requirements. A favorable regime occurs when each device contains relatively few clusters: the number per device is at most the square root of the total number across the network. In this regime, heterogeneity significantly weakens the separation requirements for kfed.

The scheme can operate asynchronously and accommodate partial participation or node and network failures. Experiments on common federated-learning benchmarks motivate the analysis, while applications to personalized federated learning and device sampling illustrate practical uses. The central finding is conditional but useful: differences across devices can become an analytical advantage when their local cluster structure satisfies the stated regime.
summary.tldr: One-shot federated clustering can benefit from heterogeneous data when each device contains sufficiently few of the network’s clusters.

title: Heterogeneity for the Win: One-Shot Federated Clustering

abstract: Deep learning models often raise privacy concerns as they leak information about their training data. This leakage enables membership inference attacks (MIA) that can identify whether a data point was in a model’s training set. Research shows that some ’data augmentation’ mechanisms may reduce the risk by combatting a key factor increasing the leakage, overfitting. While many mechanisms exist, their effectiveness against MIAs and privacy properties have not been studied systematically. Employing two recent MIAs, we explore the lower bound on the risk in the absence of formal upper bounds. First, we evaluate 7 mechanisms and differential privacy, on three image classification tasks. We find that applying augmentation to increase the model’s utility does not mitigate the risk and protection comes with a utility penalty. Further, we also investigate why popular label smoothing mechanism consistently amplifies the risk. Finally, we propose ’loss-rank-correlation’ (LRC) metric to assess how similar the effects of different mechanisms are. This, for example, reveals the similarity of applying high-intensity augmentation against MIAs to simply reducing the training time. Our findings emphasize the utility-privacy trade-off and provide practical guidelines on using augmentation to manage the trade-off.

paragraphs: Membership inference attacks try to determine whether a particular example was used to train a model. Data augmentation might reduce this leakage by limiting overfitting, but different augmentation mechanisms need not provide the same protection. This paper systematically examines that question using two recent attacks, seven mechanisms, differential privacy, and three image classification tasks.

In the evaluated settings, augmentation chosen to improve model utility does not mitigate membership-inference risk, while protection carries a utility penalty. The authors also investigate why label smoothing consistently increases risk in their study. Because the assessment uses attacks without formal upper bounds, it explores a lower bound on privacy risk: successful attacks establish leakage that is demonstrably possible.

The paper introduces loss-rank-correlation to compare the effects of different mechanisms. This reveals, for example, a similarity between high-intensity augmentation against membership inference and simply shortening training. The findings support practical guidance centered on the observed privacy-utility trade-off, showing why improved predictive performance alone is insufficient evidence that an augmentation strategy protects training-set membership.
summary.tldr: The study finds that augmentation-driven utility gains do not necessarily reduce membership leakage, and observed protection comes with a utility penalty.

title: When Does Data Augmentation Help With Membership Inference Attacks?

abstract: Having the ability to acquire inherent skills from environments without any external rewards or supervision like humans is an important problem. We propose a novel unsupervised skill discovery method named Information Bottleneck Option Learning (IBOL). On top of the linearization of environments that promotes more various and distant state transitions, IBOL enables the discovery of diverse skills. It provides the abstraction of the skills learned with the information bottleneck framework for the options with improved stability and encouraged disentanglement. We empirically demonstrate that IBOL outperforms multiple state-of-the-art unsupervised skill discovery methods on the information-theoretic evaluations and downstream tasks in MuJoCo environments, including Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper and D’Kitty. Our code is available at https://vision.snu.ac.kr/projects/ibol.

paragraphs: Unsupervised skill discovery asks an agent to acquire useful behaviors without external rewards or supervision. The challenge is to discover a varied set of behaviors and organize them into meaningful skills. This paper introduces Information Bottleneck Option Learning, or IBOL, which combines a mechanism for encouraging varied transitions with an abstraction method for the skills that emerge.

The approach builds on environment linearization that promotes transitions to more varied and more distant states. It then uses the information-bottleneck framework to abstract learned skills into options. The authors describe this abstraction as improving stability and encouraging disentanglement, so the method addresses both the diversity of discovered behavior and how that behavior is represented.

The evaluation compares IBOL with multiple leading unsupervised skill-discovery methods in MuJoCo environments, including Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, and D’Kitty. IBOL performs better on the reported information-theoretic evaluations and downstream tasks. These results support the combination of broader transition discovery and bottleneck-based skill abstraction in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: IBOL combines diverse state transitions with information-bottleneck skill abstraction, outperforming compared skill-discovery methods on reported MuJoCo evaluations.

title: Unsupervised Skill Discovery with Bottleneck Option Learning

abstract: Despite the vast literature on sparse Gaussian graphical models, current methods either are asymptotically tuning-free (which still require fine-tuning in practice) or hinge on computationally expensive methods (e.g., cross-validation) to determine the proper level of regularization. We propose a completely tuning-free approach for estimating sparse Gaussian graphical models. Our method uses model-agnostic regularization parameters to estimate each column of the target precision matrix and enjoys several desirable properties. Computationally, our estimator can be computed efficiently by linear programming. Theoretically, the proposed estimator achieves minimax optimal convergence rates under various norms. We further propose a second-stage enhancement with non-convex penalties which possesses the strong oracle property. Through comprehensive numerical studies, our methods demonstrate favorable statistical performance. Remarkably, our methods exhibit strong robustness to the violation of the Gaussian assumption and significantly outperform competing methods in the heavy-tailed settings.

paragraphs: Estimating a sparse Gaussian graphical model usually requires choosing how strongly to regularize the model. That choice can involve expensive cross-validation, even for methods described as tuning-free in an asymptotic sense. This paper proposes an estimator that removes this practical tuning step by using regularization parameters that do not depend on the particular model being estimated.

The method estimates the target precision matrix one column at a time, and its optimization problems can be solved through linear programming. The authors establish minimax optimal convergence rates under several norms: the estimator meets theoretical benchmarks for estimation accuracy measured in different ways. They also introduce a second stage using nonconvex penalties and prove that it has the strong oracle property.

Numerical studies report favorable statistical performance, including robustness when the Gaussian assumption is violated. In the evaluated heavy-tailed settings, the methods substantially outperform competing approaches. The contribution therefore combines a reduction in tuning effort with theoretical accuracy guarantees and empirical evidence that the approach remains useful beyond Gaussian data.
summary.tldr: A tuning-free estimator for sparse precision matrices combines optimal convergence guarantees with strong empirical performance on heavy-tailed data.

title: A Completely Tuning-Free and Robust Approach to Sparse Precision Matrix Estimation

abstract: Despite the widespread use of graph neural networks (GNNs) we lack methods to reliably quantify their uncertainty. We propose a conformal procedure to equip GNNs with prediction sets that come with distribution-free guarantees – the output set contains the true label with arbitrarily high probability. Our post-processing procedure can wrap around any (pretrained) GNN, and unlike existing methods, results in meaningful sets even when the model provides only the top class. The key idea is to diffuse the node-wise conformity scores to incorporate neighborhood information. By leveraging the network homophily we construct sets with comparable or better efficiency (average size) and significantly improved singleton hit ratio (correct sets of size one). In addition to an extensive empirical evaluation, we investigate the theoretical conditions under which smoothing provably improves efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper equips graph neural networks with prediction sets that express uncertainty about a node’s label. Instead of returning only one answer, the procedure returns a collection of possible labels with a distribution-free guarantee of containing the true label at an arbitrarily high probability level. It operates as post-processing around an existing, potentially pretrained GNN.

The main idea is to spread node-level conformity scores through the graph so that uncertainty estimates incorporate neighboring information. The method uses network homophily, the tendency for connected nodes to be similar. It can also produce meaningful sets when the underlying model supplies only its top predicted class, broadening the kinds of GNN outputs it can use.

The empirical evaluation finds comparable or smaller average prediction sets and a substantially improved rate of correct singleton sets. Smaller sets make uncertainty statements more specific, while correct singleton sets give an unambiguous answer. The authors also study theoretical conditions under which smoothing improves set efficiency, so that particular improvement is conditional rather than universal.
summary.tldr: Diffusing conformity scores across a graph gives GNNs prediction sets with coverage guarantees and improved empirical usefulness.

title: Conformal Prediction Sets for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Federated bilevel learning has received increasing attention in various emerging machine learning and communication applications. Recently, several Hessian-vector-based algorithms have been proposed to solve the federated bilevel optimization problem. However, several important properties in federated learning such as the partial client participation and the linear speedup for convergence (i.e., the convergence rate and complexity are improved linearly with respect to the number of sampled clients) in the presence of non-i.i.d. datasets, still remain open. In this paper, we fill these gaps by proposing a new federated bilevel algorithm named FedMBO with a novel client sampling scheme in the federated hypergradient estimation. We show that FedMBO achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{nK}}+\frac{1}{K}+\frac{\sqrt{n}}{K^{3/2}}\big)$ on non-i.i.d. datasets, where $n$ is the number of participating clients in each round, and $K$ is the total number of iteration. This is the first theoretical linear speedup result for non-i.i.d. federated bilevel optimization. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical results and demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Federated bilevel learning involves two connected optimization problems distributed across clients. The paper addresses a difficult combination: clients have differently distributed data, and only some clients participate in each round. Previous approaches left open whether increasing participation could provide a provable linear improvement in convergence under this data heterogeneity.

The proposed algorithm, FedMBO, introduces a client sampling scheme for estimating the hypergradient, the quantity used to update the outer optimization problem. This makes sampling part of the optimization design itself. The analysis explicitly accounts for both the number of participating clients and the total number of iterations.

The stated convergence rate is O(1/√(nK) + 1/K + √n/K^(3/2)), where n denotes participating clients and K denotes iterations. The authors establish the first theoretical linear speedup result for non-identically distributed federated bilevel optimization. The full expression also shows that convergence has several contributing terms, rather than depending on participation alone. Experiments support the theoretical results and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness.
summary.tldr: FedMBO establishes theoretical linear speedup for federated bilevel optimization with heterogeneous data and partial client participation.

title: Achieving Linear Speedup in Non-IID Federated Bilevel Learning

abstract: As Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) platforms become prevalent, deep neural network (DNN) watermarking techniques are gaining increasing attention, which enables one to verify the ownership of a target DNN model in a black-box scenario. Unfortunately, previous watermarking methods are vulnerable to functionality stealing attacks, thus allowing an adversary to falsely claim the ownership of a DNN model stolen from its original owner. In this work, we propose a novel margin-based DNN watermarking approach that is robust to the functionality stealing attacks based on model extraction and distillation. Specifically, during training, our method maximizes the margins of watermarked samples by using projected gradient ascent on them so that their predicted labels cannot change without compromising the accuracy of the model that the attacker tries to steal. We validate our method on multiple benchmarks and show that our watermarking method successfully defends against model extraction attacks, outperforming recent baselines.

paragraphs: Neural network watermarks help an owner verify a model through its outputs, without requiring access to its internal parameters. The paper addresses a weakness in earlier watermarking methods: attacks that copy a model’s functionality through extraction or distillation can undermine ownership verification and allow false ownership claims.

The proposed method strengthens watermarked samples during training by maximizing their margins using projected gradient ascent on those samples. The margin expresses how firmly the model assigns the intended label. The aim is to make the watermark’s predictions sufficiently robust that changing them would compromise the accuracy of the functionality an attacker is trying to copy.

Evaluations on multiple benchmarks show that the method withstands model extraction attacks and outperforms recent watermarking baselines. The approach links watermark persistence to the copied model’s useful predictive behavior. Its stated robustness targets functionality stealing through extraction and distillation, and the reported benchmark results support the use of larger watermark margins for preserving evidence of ownership.
summary.tldr: Margin-based watermarking strengthens watermark predictions so removing them compromises the accuracy sought by functionality-stealing attacks.

title: Margin-based Neural Network Watermarking

abstract: In this paper, we use Prior-data Fitted Networks (PFNs) as a flexible surrogate for Bayesian Optimization (BO). PFNs are neural processes that are trained to approximate the posterior predictive distribution (PPD) through in-context learning on any prior distribution that can be efficiently sampled from. We describe how this flexibility can be exploited for surrogate modeling in BO. We use PFNs to mimic a naive Gaussian process (GP), an advanced GP, and a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN). In addition, we show how to incorporate further information into the prior, such as allowing hints about the position of optima (user priors), ignoring irrelevant dimensions, and performing non-myopic BO by learning the acquisition function. The flexibility underlying these extensions opens up vast possibilities for using PFNs for BO. We demonstrate the usefulness of PFNs for BO in a large-scale evaluation on artificial GP samples and three different hyperparameter optimization testbeds: HPO-B, Bayesmark, and PD1. We publish code alongside trained models at https://github.com/automl/PFNs4BO.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a surrogate model to guide the search for good inputs to an objective. This paper explores Prior-data Fitted Networks, or PFNs, as flexible surrogates. PFNs are trained to approximate posterior predictive distributions through in-context learning, using prior distributions from which training examples can be sampled efficiently.

The authors use this approach to mimic both simpler and more advanced Gaussian processes, as well as a Bayesian neural network. They also show how the prior can include hints about where an optimum lies or account for irrelevant dimensions. Another extension learns an acquisition function for non-myopic optimization, allowing the search strategy to consider more than immediate benefit.

A large evaluation uses artificial Gaussian-process samples and the HPO-B, Bayesmark, and PD1 hyperparameter-optimization testbeds to demonstrate usefulness. The contribution is the flexibility of the surrogate framework: changing what the model learns from its prior can support several forms of optimization knowledge. The authors also release code and trained models to accompany the method.
summary.tldr: PFNs provide flexible Bayesian-optimization surrogates that can incorporate user hints, irrelevant dimensions, and learned non-myopic acquisition strategies.

title: PFNs4BO: In-Context Learning for Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Stochastic restoration algorithms allow to explore the space of solutions that correspond to the degraded input. In this paper we reveal additional fundamental advantages of stochastic methods over deterministic ones, which further motivate their use. First, we prove that any restoration algorithm that attains perfect perceptual quality and whose outputs are consistent with the input must be a posterior sampler, and is thus required to be stochastic. Second, we illustrate that while deterministic restoration algorithms may attain high perceptual quality, this can be achieved only by filling up the space of all possible source images using an extremely sensitive mapping, which makes them highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Indeed, we show that enforcing deterministic models to be robust to such attacks profoundly hinders their perceptual quality, while robustifying stochastic models hardly influences their perceptual quality, and improves their output variability. These findings provide a motivation to foster progress in stochastic restoration methods, paving the way to better recovery algorithms.

paragraphs: Image restoration reconstructs an image from degraded observations, which can correspond to multiple possible originals. Stochastic methods can explore these alternatives. This paper investigates additional advantages of randomness, focusing on whether restored outputs look perceptually correct, remain consistent with the observations, and withstand adversarial changes to the input.

The central theorem states that a restoration algorithm achieving both perfect perceptual quality and input consistency must sample from the posterior distribution. Under these requirements, stochastic behavior is necessary. The authors also illustrate how deterministic restoration can achieve high perceptual quality through an extremely sensitive mapping, leaving it vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

Their robustness results reveal a practical contrast: enforcing robustness strongly harms the perceptual quality of deterministic models, whereas robustifying stochastic models barely affects perceptual quality and improves output variability. The findings give a reason to pursue stochastic restoration beyond its ability to produce multiple answers. Randomness can help reconcile the competing demands of believable outputs, agreement with the degraded input, and resistance to perturbations.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes conditional necessity for stochastic restoration and shows advantages in balancing perceptual quality, consistency, and robustness.

title: Reasons for the Superiority of Stochastic Estimators over Deterministic Ones: Robustness, Consistency and Perceptual Quality

abstract: This paper investigates the dynamics-inspired neuromorphic architecture for visual representation learning following Hamilton’s principle. Our method converts weight-based neural structure to its dynamics-based form that consists of finite sub-models, whose mutual relations measured by computing path integrals amongst their dynamical states are equivalent to the typical neural weights. Based on the entropy reduction process derived from the Euler-Lagrange equations, the feedback signals interpreted as stress forces amongst sub-models push them to move. We first train a dynamics-based neural model from scratch and observe that this model outperforms traditional neural models on MNIST. We then convert several pre-trained neural structures into dynamics-based forms, followed by fine-tuning via entropy reduction to obtain the stabilized dynamical states. We observe consistent improvements in these transformed models over their weight-based counterparts on ImageNet and WebVision in terms of computational complexity, parameter size, testing accuracy, and robustness. Besides, we show the correlation between model performance and structural entropy, providing deeper insight into weight-free neuromorphic learning.

paragraphs: This paper recasts visual neural networks as dynamical systems following Hamilton's principle. Instead of expressing the network through conventional weights, it uses a finite collection of sub-models with dynamical states. Relations between these states, measured through path integrals, play a role equivalent to ordinary neural weights.

Learning is described through an entropy-reduction process derived from the Euler-Lagrange equations. Feedback acts like stress forces between sub-models, causing their states to move. The authors explore both training a dynamics-based model from scratch and converting pretrained neural structures into this form, then fine-tuning them until their dynamical states stabilize.

The model trained from scratch outperforms traditional neural models on MNIST in the reported experiment. Converted models show consistent improvements over their weight-based counterparts on ImageNet and WebVision in computational complexity, parameter size, test accuracy, and robustness. The authors also report a correlation between structural entropy and model performance. Together, these observations support the proposed dynamical representation as a practical learning approach while connecting its behavior to a structural quantity.
summary.tldr: A dynamics-based representation replaces conventional neural weights with relations between moving sub-models and shows improvements in visual-learning experiments.

title: Dynamics-inspired Neuromorphic Visual Representation Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the optimal transport map between two probability distributions, $P$ and $Q$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, on the basis of i.i.d. samples. All existing statistical analyses of this problem require the assumption that the transport map is Lipschitz, a strong requirement that, in particular, excludes any examples where the transport map is discontinuous. As a first step towards developing estimation procedures for discontinuous maps, we consider the important special case where the data distribution $Q$ is a discrete measure supported on a finite number of points in $\mathbb{R}^d$. We study a computationally efficient estimator initially proposed by (Pooladian & Niles-Weed, 2021), based on entropic optimal transport, and show in the semi-discrete setting that it converges at the minimax-optimal rate $n^{-1/2}$, independent of dimension. Other standard map estimation techniques both lack finite-sample guarantees in this setting and provably suffer from the curse of dimensionality. We confirm these results in numerical experiments, and provide experiments for other settings, not covered by our theory, which indicate that the entropic estimator is a promising methodology for other discontinuous transport map estimation problems.

paragraphs: An optimal transport map describes how to move one probability distribution to another. Estimating that map from independent samples becomes difficult when it has abrupt changes. Previous statistical analyses required a Lipschitz condition, which excludes discontinuous maps. This paper studies an important special case: the destination distribution is supported on a finite set of points.

The authors analyze an existing computationally efficient estimator based on entropic optimal transport. In this semi-discrete setting, they prove that it converges at the minimax-optimal rate n^(-1/2), independently of dimension. Minimax optimality means that the rate matches the best achievable worst-case rate in the setting being analyzed. The dimension-independent rate avoids the deterioration established for other standard map estimators.

Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical findings. The authors also test other discontinuous transport problems beyond the scope of their proof, where the results are promising. The distinction matters: the optimal rate is established for the semi-discrete case, while the broader experiments suggest that entropic estimation may be useful more widely.
summary.tldr: An entropic estimator achieves a dimension-independent minimax-optimal rate for transport maps with a finitely supported destination distribution.

title: Minimax estimation of discontinuous optimal transport maps: The semi-discrete case

abstract: We study the problem of (learning) algorithm comparison, where the goal is to find differences between models trained with two different learning algorithms. We begin by formalizing this goal as one of finding distinguishing feature transformations, i.e., input transformations that change the predictions of models trained with one learning algorithm but not the other. We then present ModelDiff, a method that leverages the datamodels framework (Ilyas et al., 2022) to compare learning algorithms based on how they use their training data. We demonstrate ModelDiff through three case studies, comparing models trained with/without data augmentation, with/without pre-training, and with different SGD hyperparameters.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of (learning) algorithm comparison, where the goal is to find differences between models trained with two different learning algorithms. We begin by formalizing this goal as one of finding distinguishing feature transformations, i.e., input transformations that change the predictions of models trained with one learning algorithm but not the other. We then present ModelDiff, a method that leverages the datamodels framework (Ilyas et al., 2022) to compare learning algorithms based on how they use their training data. We demonstrate ModelDiff through three case studies, comparing models trained with/without data augmentation, with/without pre-training, and with different SGD hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Different learning algorithms can produce models that use information differently. This paper makes that comparison concrete by asking which input transformations distinguish their behavior. A distinguishing transformation changes the predictions of models trained with one algorithm while leaving those trained with another unaffected. This turns a broad comparison into a specific behavioral question.

ModelDiff approaches the problem through the datamodels framework, comparing learning algorithms according to how their resulting models use training data. The connection to training data gives the comparison an organizing principle: differences in learned behavior are examined through the examples used to produce that behavior. The goal is to identify meaningful differences between training procedures.

The authors demonstrate the framework in three case studies: training with or without data augmentation, with or without pretraining, and with different stochastic gradient descent hyperparameters. These examples span changes to the data, the starting model, and the optimization process. They illustrate ModelDiff as a tool for investigating how training choices alter model behavior, rather than establishing one training choice as universally preferable.
summary.tldr: ModelDiff compares learning algorithms through their use of training data and input transformations that distinguish their models’ predictions.

title: ModelDiff: A Framework for Comparing Learning Algorithms

abstract: We study the problem of convergence to a stationary point in zero-sum games. We propose competitive gradient optimization (CGO), a gradient-based method that incorporates the interactions between two players in zero-sum games for its iterative updates. We provide a continuous-time analysis of CGO and its convergence properties while showing that in the continuous limit, previous methods degenerate to their gradient descent ascent (GDA) variants. We further provide a rate of convergence to stationary points in the discrete-time setting. We propose a generalized class of $\alpha$-coherent functions and show that for strictly $\alpha$-coherent functions, CGO ensures convergence to a saddle point. Moreover, we propose optimistic CGO (oCGO), an optimistic variant, for which we show a convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{n})$ to saddle points for $\alpha$-coherent functions.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of convergence to a stationary point in zero-sum games. We propose competitive gradient optimization (CGO), a gradient-based method that incorporates the interactions between two players in zero-sum games for its iterative updates. We provide a continuous-time analysis of CGO and its convergence properties while showing that in the continuous limit, previous methods degenerate to their gradient descent ascent (GDA) variants. We further provide a rate of convergence to stationary points in the discrete-time setting. We propose a generalized class of $\alpha$-coherent functions and show that for strictly $\alpha$-coherent functions, CGO ensures convergence to a saddle point. Moreover, we propose optimistic CGO (oCGO), an optimistic variant, for which we show a convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{n})$ to saddle points for $\alpha$-coherent functions.

paragraphs: In a zero-sum game, one player’s improvement comes at the other player’s expense, so optimization must account for their interaction. This paper introduces competitive gradient optimization, or CGO, whose iterative updates explicitly incorporate interactions between the two players. The initial objective is convergence to stationary points, where the relevant gradients vanish.

The authors analyze CGO in both continuous and discrete time. Their continuous-time analysis examines its convergence behavior and shows that previous methods reduce to variants of gradient descent ascent in the continuous limit. For discrete updates, they also establish a convergence rate to stationary points, giving a guarantee directly relevant to an iterative algorithm.

Stronger conclusions require additional structure. The paper defines a generalized class of alpha-coherent functions and proves that CGO converges to a saddle point for strictly alpha-coherent functions. An optimistic variant, oCGO, achieves an O(1/n) rate to saddle points for alpha-coherent functions. These results distinguish reaching a stationary point from reaching a saddle point and make the structural conditions behind the latter guarantees explicit.
summary.tldr: CGO incorporates player interactions into zero-sum optimization and provides stationary-point and conditional saddle-point convergence guarantees.

title: Competitive Gradient Optimization

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) with biologically inspired spatio-temporal dynamics demonstrate superior energy efficiency on neuromorphic architectures. Error backpropagation in SNNs is prohibited by the all-or-none nature of spikes. The existing solution circumvents this problem by a relaxation on the gradient calculation using a continuous function with a constant relaxation de- gree, so-called surrogate gradient learning. Nevertheless, such a solution introduces additional smoothing error on spike firing which leads to the gradients being estimated inaccurately. Thus, how to adaptively adjust the relaxation degree and eliminate smoothing error progressively is crucial. Here, we propose a methodology such that training a prototype neural network will evolve into training an SNN gradually by fusing the learnable relaxation degree into the network with random spike noise. In this way, the network learns adaptively the accurate gradients of loss landscape in SNNs. The theoretical analysis further shows optimization on such a noisy network could be evolved into optimization on the embedded SNN with shared weights progressively. Moreover, The experiments on static images, dynamic event streams, speech, and instrumental sounds show the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance across all the datasets with remarkable robustness on different relaxation degrees.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks communicate through discrete firing events and can be energy efficient on neuromorphic hardware. Their all-or-none spikes, however, prevent ordinary backpropagation through the firing operation. Existing surrogate-gradient methods use smooth substitutes, but a fixed amount of smoothing introduces error into the estimated gradients.

The proposed approach makes the amount of relaxation learnable and combines it with random spike noise. Training begins with a prototype network and gradually evolves toward training a spiking network. This gives the optimization process a way to adjust its approximation instead of using the same smoothing throughout. The theoretical analysis shows how optimization of the noisy network can progressively become optimization of an embedded spiking network sharing its weights.

Experiments cover static images, dynamic event streams, speech, and instrumental sounds. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated datasets and strong robustness to different relaxation degrees. These findings support adapting the smoothing during training as a practical way to address the mismatch between continuous gradient calculations and discrete spike behavior.
summary.tldr: Learning the amount of gradient smoothing lets training progressively approach a spiking network, with strong reported results across several data types.

title: Adaptive Smoothing Gradient Learning for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: In conventional supervised classification, true labels are required for individual instances. However, it could be prohibitive to collect the true labels for individual instances, due to privacy concerns or unaffordable annotation costs. This motivates the study on classification from aggregate observations (CFAO), where the supervision is provided to groups of instances, instead of individual instances. CFAO is a generalized learning framework that contains various learning problems, such as multiple-instance learning and learning from label proportions. The goal of this paper is to present a novel universal method of CFAO, which holds an unbiased estimator of the classification risk for arbitrary losses—previous research failed to achieve this goal. Practically, our method works by weighing the importance of each instance and each label in the group, which provides purified supervision for the classifier to learn. Theoretically, our proposed method not only guarantees the risk consistency due to the unbiased risk estimator but also can be compatible with arbitrary losses. Extensive experiments on various problems of CFAO demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Classification usually relies on a label for each training example, but obtaining those labels can be expensive or raise privacy concerns. Classification from aggregate observations uses information attached to groups instead. This setting includes multiple-instance learning and learning from label proportions, which provide different forms of group supervision.

The paper proposes a shared approach that weights the importance of each example and each possible label within its group. These weights turn aggregate information into supervision that a classifier can use. The central theoretical result is an unbiased estimate of classification risk that works with arbitrary loss functions, rather than requiring a particular loss to make the method valid.

An unbiased risk estimate targets the intended classification objective on average, and the authors establish risk consistency for their method. Experiments across several aggregate-supervision problems report advantages over compared approaches. Together, the results suggest that group labels can support a broadly applicable training strategy, with flexibility in the loss function and a theoretical connection to the classification risk being optimized.
summary.tldr: The paper turns group-level supervision into weighted training signals with an unbiased classification-risk estimator compatible with arbitrary losses.

title: A Universal Unbiased Method for Classification from Aggregate Observations

abstract: Effective brain representation learning is a key step toward the understanding of cognitive processes and diagnosis of neurological diseases/disorders. Existing studies have focused on either (1) voxel-level activity, where only a single weight relating the voxel activity to the task (i.e., aggregation of voxel activity over a time window) is considered, missing their temporal dynamics, or (2) functional connectivity of the brain in the level of region of interests, missing voxel-level activities. We bridge this gap and design BrainMixer, an unsupervised learning framework that effectively utilizes both functional connectivity and associated time series of voxels to learn voxel-level representation in an unsupervised manner. BrainMixer employs two simple yet effective MLP-based encoders to simultaneously learn the dynamics of voxel-level signals and their functional correlations. To encode voxel activity, BrainMixer fuses information across both time and voxel dimensions via a dynamic attention mechanism. To learn the structure of the functional connectivity, BrainMixer presents a temporal graph patching and encodes each patch by combining its nodes’ features via a new adaptive temporal pooling. Our experiments show that BrainMixer attains outstanding performance and outperforms 14 baselines in different downstream tasks and setups.
