paragraphs: Brain-activity representations can lose useful information when they focus only on summarized voxel activity or only on connections between larger brain regions. The first approach can miss temporal dynamics, while the second can omit voxel-level signals. BrainMixer brings voxel time series and functional connectivity into one unsupervised framework for learning voxel-level representations.

The architecture uses two encoders built from multilayer perceptrons to learn signal dynamics and functional correlations together. For voxel activity, a dynamic attention mechanism combines information across time and voxels. For connectivity, the method forms temporal graph patches and encodes each patch by combining node features through adaptive temporal pooling. These components address the two information sources within the same learning framework.

Experiments report that BrainMixer outperforms 14 baselines across different downstream tasks and setups. The findings support combining fine-grained temporal activity with connectivity structure when learning brain representations without supervision. The paper positions this representation learning as a step toward understanding cognition and neurological disorders, while the stated experimental result concerns performance on the evaluated downstream tasks.
summary.tldr: BrainMixer jointly learns voxel dynamics and functional connectivity, outperforming 14 baselines across evaluated downstream tasks and setups.

title: Unsupervised Representation Learning of Brain Activity via Bridging Voxel Activity and Functional Connectivity

abstract: For partial differential equations on domains of arbitrary shapes, existing works of neural operators attempt to learn a mapping from geometries to solutions. It often requires a large dataset of geometry-solution pairs in order to obtain a sufficiently accurate neural operator. However, for many industrial applications, e.g., engineering design optimization, it can be prohibitive to satisfy the requirement since even a single simulation may take hours or days of computation. To address this issue, we propose reference neural operators (RNO), a novel way of implementing neural operators, i.e., to learn the smooth dependence of solutions on geometric deformations. Specifically, given a reference solution, RNO can predict solutions corresponding to arbitrary deformations of the referred geometry. This approach turns out to be much more data efficient. Through extensive experiments, we show that RNO can learn the dependence across various types and different numbers of geometry objects with relatively small datasets. RNO outperforms baseline models in accuracy by a large lead and achieves up to 80% error reduction.

paragraphs: Learning PDE solutions across different geometries can require many geometry-solution training pairs. Producing those pairs is expensive when each simulation takes hours or days, as can happen in engineering design optimization. Reference Neural Operators address this data burden by organizing predictions around a known reference solution.

Given that solution, an RNO learns how the solution changes as the reference geometry is deformed. The learning target is the smooth dependence on geometric deformation. This gives the model a reference point from which to predict solutions for altered geometries, and the authors describe the approach as substantially more data efficient.

Experiments show that RNO can learn across different types and numbers of geometric objects using relatively small datasets. It outperforms the evaluated baselines in accuracy, with error reductions reaching 80%. These results support using reference solutions as a useful basis for geometry-dependent PDE prediction. The practical significance is greater accuracy with less training data in a setting where obtaining each additional solution can be costly.
summary.tldr: Reference Neural Operators improve data efficiency by predicting how PDE solutions change when a geometry is deformed from a known reference.

title: Reference Neural Operators: Learning the Smooth Dependence of Solutions of PDEs on Geometric Deformations

abstract: While stochastic bilevel optimization methods have been extensively studied for addressing large-scale nested optimization problems in machine learning, it remains an open question whether the optimal complexity bounds for solving bilevel optimization are the same as those in single-level optimization. Our main result resolves this question: SPABA, an adaptation of the PAGE method for nonconvex optimization in (Li et al., 2021) to the bilevel setting, can achieve optimal sample complexity in both the finite-sum and expectation settings. We show the optimality of SPABA by proving that there is no gap in complexity analysis between stochastic bilevel and single-level optimization when implementing PAGE. Notably, as indicated by the results of (Dagréou et al., 2022), there might exist a gap in complexity analysis when implementing other stochastic gradient estimators, like SGD and SAGA. In addition to SPABA, we propose several other single-loop stochastic bilevel algorithms, that either match or improve the state-of-the-art sample complexity results, leveraging our convergence rate and complexity analysis. Numerical experiments demonstrate the superior practical performance of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves nested optimization problems, raising the question of whether nesting necessarily worsens sample complexity relative to a single optimization level. This paper addresses that question through SPABA, a single-loop stochastic algorithm adapted from the PAGE method for nonconvex optimization.

The authors prove that SPABA achieves optimal sample complexity in both finite-sum and expectation settings. Their analysis shows no complexity gap between stochastic bilevel and single-level optimization when PAGE is used. The scope of that statement matters: the paper notes that a gap may exist in analyses using other gradient estimators, including SGD and SAGA.

The authors also derive additional single-loop bilevel algorithms whose sample-complexity guarantees match or improve the state of the art. Numerical experiments show superior practical performance for the proposed methods. The combined contribution links an optimal theoretical result to algorithm design, demonstrating that the choice of stochastic estimator can be central to whether nested optimization incurs an additional complexity burden.
summary.tldr: SPABA achieves optimal stochastic bilevel sample complexity, matching single-level complexity when using the PAGE estimator.

title: SPABA: A Single-Loop and Probabilistic Stochastic Bilevel Algorithm Achieving Optimal Sample Complexity

abstract: We warn against a common but incomplete understanding of empirical research in machine learning that leads to non-replicable results, makes findings unreliable, and threatens to undermine progress in the field. To overcome this alarming situation, we call for more awareness of the plurality of ways of gaining knowledge experimentally but also of some epistemic limitations. In particular, we argue most current empirical machine learning research is fashioned as confirmatory research while it should rather be considered exploratory.
originalAbstract: We warn against a common but incomplete understanding of empirical research in machine learning that leads to non-replicable results, makes findings unreliable, and threatens to undermine progress in the field. To overcome this alarming situation, we call for more awareness of the plurality of ways of gaining knowledge experimentally but also of some epistemic limitations. In particular, we argue most current empirical machine learning research is fashioned as confirmatory research while it should rather be considered exploratory.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges how empirical machine learning research understands its own results. The authors argue that a common but incomplete view of experimentation contributes to findings that cannot be replicated and conclusions that are unreliable. They present this as a threat to progress because later research depends on what earlier experiments appear to establish.

The central distinction is between exploratory and confirmatory research. Exploration helps develop possible explanations and directions for investigation; confirmation presents evidence as testing a claim. The authors argue that much current empirical ML work is presented in the second category even though it should be understood in the first. Their concern is therefore about the interpretation and status of experimental knowledge.

The proposed response is greater awareness of the different ways experiments can contribute knowledge, together with their epistemic limits. Recognizing research as exploratory changes the strength of the conclusions it can support. The paper's contribution is a methodological argument for aligning claims with the kind of evidence the research actually provides.
summary.tldr: The authors argue that much empirical ML research should be treated as exploratory and that miscasting it as confirmatory undermines reliability.

title: Position: Why We Must Rethink Empirical Research in Machine Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where adversaries can maliciously trigger model misclassifications by implanting a hidden backdoor during model training. This paper proposes a simple yet effective input-level backdoor detection (dubbed IBD-PSC) as a ‘firewall’ to filter out malicious testing images. Our method is motivated by an intriguing phenomenon, i.e., parameter-oriented scaling consistency (PSC), where the prediction confidences of poisoned samples are significantly more consistent than those of benign ones when amplifying model parameters. In particular, we provide theoretical analysis to safeguard the foundations of the PSC phenomenon. We also design an adaptive method to select BN layers to scale up for effective detection. Extensive experiments are conducted on benchmark datasets, verifying the effectiveness and efficiency of our IBD-PSC method and its resistance to adaptive attacks. Codes are available at https://github.com/THUYimingLi/BackdoorBox.

paragraphs: A backdoor attack implants hidden behavior during training so that particular inputs can later trigger incorrect predictions. This paper introduces IBD-PSC, a detector intended to filter malicious images at test time. Its focus is identifying suspicious incoming inputs through how the trained model responds to controlled changes in its parameters.

The method builds on an observed difference called parameter-oriented scaling consistency. When model parameters are amplified, prediction confidence for poisoned samples remains substantially more consistent than confidence for benign samples. The authors provide theoretical analysis supporting this phenomenon and design an adaptive procedure for selecting which batch normalization layers to scale for detection.

Benchmark experiments report that IBD-PSC is effective and efficient, and that it resists the adaptive attacks evaluated in the study. The approach matters because it uses the response to parameter scaling as a detection signal, going beyond the confidence of a single unchanged prediction. The reported resistance supports the detector under the tested attacks without establishing universal protection against every possible adaptation.
summary.tldr: IBD-PSC detects backdoor inputs using their unusually consistent prediction confidence when selected model parameters are scaled up.

title: IBD-PSC: Input-level Backdoor Detection via Parameter-oriented Scaling Consistency

abstract: We consider sequential maximization of performance metrics that are general functions of a confusion matrix of a classifier (such as precision, F-measure, or G-mean). Such metrics are, in general, non-decomposable over individual instances, making their optimization very challenging. While they have been extensively studied under different frameworks in the batch setting, their analysis in the online learning regime is very limited, with only a few distinguished exceptions. In this paper, we introduce and analyze a general online algorithm that can be used in a straightforward way with a variety of complex performance metrics in binary, multi-class, and multi-label classification problems. The algorithm’s update and prediction rules are appealingly simple and computationally efficient without the need to store any past data. We show the algorithm attains $\mathcal{O}(\frac{\ln n}{n})$ regret for concave and smooth metrics and verify the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in empirical studies.

paragraphs: Classification measures such as precision, F-measure, and G-mean summarize patterns of correct and incorrect predictions across examples. Improving them is difficult because their values generally cannot be split into separate contributions that can each be optimized independently. This paper studies how to maximize such measures when examples arrive sequentially, extending a problem studied extensively in batch learning into the online setting.

The authors introduce a general algorithm whose prediction and update rules support binary, multiclass, and multilabel classification. Its rules are computationally efficient and do not require retaining earlier examples. This makes the contribution relevant to sequential learning, where repeatedly revisiting an accumulated dataset would undermine the appeal of an online procedure.

For metrics that are both concave and smooth, the authors prove a regret rate of O(ln n / n). Those conditions matter: the stated guarantee does not cover every possible confusion-matrix metric. Empirical studies also support the algorithm’s efficiency, complementing the theoretical analysis with evidence about its practical behavior.
summary.tldr: A simple online classification algorithm optimizes complex performance metrics without storing past data, with regret guarantees for smooth, concave metrics.

title: A General Online Algorithm for Optimizing Complex Performance Metrics

abstract: The prevalent employment of narrow neural networks, characterized by their minimal parameter count per layer, has led to a surge in research exploring their potential as universal function approximators. A notable result in this field states that networks with just a width of $d+1$ can approximate any continuous function for input dimension $d$ arbitrarily well. However, the optimal approximation rate for these narrowest networks, i.e., the optimal relation between the count of tunable parameters and the approximation error, remained unclear. In this paper, we address this gap by proving that ReLU networks with width $d+1$ can achieve the optimal approximation rate for continuous functions over the domain $[0,1]^d$ under $L^p$ norm for $p\in[1,\infty)$. We further show that for the uniform norm, a width of $d+11$ is sufficient. We also extend the results to narrow feed-forward networks with various activations, confirming their capability to approximate at the optimal rate. This work adds to the understanding of universal approximation of narrow networks.

paragraphs: A narrow neural network can use very few units in each layer while still approximating a broad class of functions. Earlier work established that width d+1 suffices to approximate any continuous function arbitrarily well for input dimension d. This paper asks a sharper question: how efficiently can such a network reduce approximation error as its number of tunable parameters grows?

The authors prove that ReLU networks of width d+1 achieve the optimal approximation rate for continuous functions on the unit cube under Lp norms for finite p at least one. These norms assess approximation error differently from the uniform norm, which controls the largest error across the domain. For the uniform norm, the paper proves that width d+11 is sufficient.

The results also extend to narrow feed-forward networks with several other activation functions. They strengthen universal approximation statements by addressing the relationship between parameter count and error. The width d+11 result is a sufficiency claim; it does not establish that every network achieving the uniform-norm rate must have that width.
summary.tldr: Narrow ReLU networks achieve optimal approximation rates at width d+1 for finite Lp norms, while width d+11 suffices for the uniform norm.

title: ReLU Network with Width $d+\mathcalO(1)$ Can Achieve Optimal Approximation Rate

abstract: A topic of great current interest is Causal Representation Learning (CRL), whose goal is to learn a causal model for hidden features in a data-driven manner. Unfortunately, CRL is severely ill-posed since it is a combination of the two notoriously ill-posed problems of representation learning and causal discovery. Yet, finding practical identifiability conditions that guarantee a unique solution is crucial for its practical applicability. Most approaches so far have been based on assumptions on the latent causal mechanisms, such as temporal causality, or existence of supervision or interventions; these can be too restrictive in actual applications. Here, we show identifiability based on novel, weak constraints, which requires no temporal structure, intervention, nor weak supervision. The approach is based on assuming the observational mixing exhibits a suitable grouping of the observational variables. We also propose a novel self-supervised estimation framework consistent with the model, prove its statistical consistency, and experimentally show its superior CRL performances compared to the state-of-the-art baselines. We further demonstrate its robustness against latent confounders and causal cycles.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning aims to uncover hidden features and the causal relationships among them from observed data. This is difficult because both the representation and its causal structure can admit multiple explanations. Identifiability conditions address this ambiguity by specifying when the observations determine a unique solution within the model.

The paper establishes identifiability through constraints on how hidden features are mixed into groups of observed variables. Its assumptions concern suitable grouping in the observational mixing, without requiring temporal structure, interventions, or weak supervision. This shifts the source of identifying information toward the organization of the observations themselves.

The authors also introduce a self-supervised estimation framework compatible with this model and prove statistical consistency. Their experiments report better causal representation learning performance than state-of-the-art baselines, along with robustness to hidden confounders and causal cycles. The theoretical contribution remains conditional on the proposed grouping constraints; the practical results show how an estimator built around those constraints performs in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Suitable grouping of observed variables enables identifiable causal representation learning under the paper’s constraints, without temporal data, interventions, or weak supervision.

title: Causal Representation Learning Made Identifiable by Grouping of Observational Variables

abstract: The robust $\phi$-regularized Markov Decision Process (RRMDP) framework focuses on designing control policies that are robust against parameter uncertainties due to mismatches between the simulator (nominal) model and real-world settings. This work makes two important contributions. First, we propose a model-free algorithm called Robust $\phi$-regularized fitted Q-iteration for learning an $\epsilon$-optimal robust policy that uses only the historical data collected by rolling out a behavior policy (with robust exploratory requirement) on the nominal model. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first unified analysis for a class of $\phi$-divergences achieving robust optimal policies in high-dimensional systems of arbitrary large state space with general function approximation. Second, we introduce the hybrid robust $\phi$-regularized reinforcement learning framework to learn an optimal robust policy using both historical data and online sampling. Towards this framework, we propose a model-free algorithm called Hybrid robust Total-variation-regularized Q-iteration. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first improved out-of-data-distribution assumption in large-scale problems of arbitrary large state space with general function approximation under the hybrid robust $\phi$-regularized reinforcement learning framework.

Towards this framework, we propose a model-free algorithm called Hybrid robust Total-variation-regularized Q-iteration. paragraphs: A policy learned in a simulator may encounter different dynamics in the real world. The robust phi-regularized Markov decision process framework addresses this mismatch by seeking policies resistant to parameter uncertainty. This paper develops model-free learning algorithms within that framework, covering both historical data alone and historical data supplemented with online sampling.

The first algorithm is robust phi-regularized fitted Q-iteration. It learns an approximately optimal robust policy from data collected by a behavior policy in the nominal model, subject to a robust exploration requirement. The authors provide a unified analysis across a class of phi-divergences, accommodating arbitrarily large state spaces and general function approximation.

The second contribution introduces a hybrid framework and a total-variation-regularized Q-iteration algorithm that combines offline and online data. For this setting, the authors report an improved out-of-data-distribution assumption for large-scale problems. The results broaden the analyzed routes to robust policy learning, while retaining explicit conditions on the data: the offline guarantee requires robust exploration, and the hybrid contribution improves an assumption rather than eliminating distribution-related requirements.
summary.tldr: The paper develops model-free robust reinforcement learning algorithms and guarantees for offline data and for a hybrid of offline and online data.

title: Model-Free Robust $φ$-Divergence Reinforcement Learning Using Both Offline and Online Data

abstract: Training a modern machine learning architecture on a new task requires extensive learning-rate tuning, which comes at a high computational cost. Here we develop new Polyak-type adaptive learning rates that can be used on top of any momentum method, and require less tuning to perform well. We first develop MoMo, a Momentum Model based adaptive learning rate for SGD-M (stochastic gradient descent with momentum). MoMo uses momentum estimates of the batch losses and gradients sampled at each iteration to build a model of the loss function. Our model also makes use of any known lower bound of the loss function by using truncation, e.g. most losses are lower-bounded by zero. The models is then approximately minimized at each iteration to compute the next step. We show how MoMo can be used in combination with any momentum-based method, and showcase this by developing MoMo-Adam - which is Adam with our new model-based adaptive learning rate. We show that MoMo attains a $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ convergence rate for convex problems with interpolation, needing knowledge of no problem-specific quantities other than the optimal value. Additionally, for losses with unknown lower bounds, we develop on-the-fly estimates of a lower bound, that are incorporated in our model. We demonstrate that MoMo and MoMo-Adam improve over SGD-M and Adam in terms of robustness to hyperparameter tuning for training image classifiers on MNIST, CIFAR, and Imagenet, for recommender systems on the Criteo dataset, for a transformer model on the translation task IWSLT14, and for a diffusion model.

summary.tldr: MoMo uses momentum-based loss models to adapt learning rates and reduce sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning.

title: MoMo: Momentum Models for Adaptive Learning Rates

abstract: Graph augmentation has received great attention in recent years for graph contrastive learning (GCL) to learn well-generalized node/graph representations. However, mainstream GCL methods often favor randomly disrupting graphs for augmentation, which shows limited generalization and inevitably leads to the corruption of high-level graph information, i.e., the graph community. Moreover, current knowledge-based graph augmentation methods can only focus on either topology or node features, causing the model to lack robustness against various types of noise. To address these limitations, this research investigated the role of the graph community in graph augmentation and figured out its crucial advantage for learnable graph augmentation. Based on our observations, we propose a community-invariant GCL framework to maintain graph community structure during learnable graph augmentation. By maximizing the spectral changes, this framework unifies the constraints of both topology and feature augmentation, enhancing the model’s robustness. Empirical evidence on 21 benchmark datasets demonstrates the exclusive merits of our framework. Code is released on Github (https://github.com/ShiyinTan/CI-GCL.git).

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning uses augmented versions of a graph to learn useful node or graph representations. The paper identifies a problem with randomly disrupting graphs: changes can damage community structure, a form of higher-level information. It also argues that augmentation methods focused only on connections or only on node features can leave models vulnerable to different kinds of noise.

The proposed framework learns augmentations while maintaining graph communities. It uses an objective that maximizes spectral changes to bring constraints on graph connections and node features into one framework. Community preservation supplies the structural requirement, while the spectral objective guides the changes made during augmentation.

Experiments across 21 benchmark datasets provide evidence for the framework's advantages and robustness. The findings support community structure as a useful organizing principle when deciding how to alter a graph for learning. The broader contribution is a method for coordinating changes to both topology and features while retaining the group structure that the paper identifies as important for generalization.
summary.tldr: Community-invariant graph contrastive learning coordinates topology and feature augmentations while preserving communities, with benefits demonstrated across 21 datasets.

title: Community-Invariant Graph Contrastive Learning

abstract: Probabilistic time series modeling based on generative models has attracted lots of attention because of its wide applications and excellent performance. However, existing state-of-the-art models, based on stochastic differential equation, not only struggle to determine the drift and diffusion coefficients during the design process but also have slow generation speed. To tackle this challenge, we firstly propose decomposable denoising diffusion model ($\text{D}^3\text{M}$) and prove it is a general framework unifying denoising diffusion models and continuous flow models. Based on the new framework, we propose some simple but efficient probability paths with high generation speed. Furthermore, we design a module that combines a special state space model with linear gated attention modules for sequence modeling. It preserves inductive bias and simultaneously models both local and global dependencies. Experimental results on 8 real-world datasets show that $\text{D}^3\text{M}$ reduces RMSE and CRPS by up to 4.6% and 4.3% compared with state-of-the-arts on imputation tasks, and achieves comparable results with state-of-the-arts on forecasting tasks with only 10 steps.

paragraphs: Probabilistic time-series models must represent uncertainty while capturing how observations relate over time. This paper addresses generative approaches whose stochastic differential equations are difficult to design and slow to sample. It introduces the decomposable denoising diffusion model, D³M, and proves that the framework unifies denoising diffusion models with continuous flow models.

Within that framework, the authors construct simple probability paths intended to speed generation. They also design a sequence-modeling module that combines a specialized state-space model with linear gated attention. This combination preserves inductive bias while representing both nearby and long-range dependencies, connecting the generation framework to the structure of time-series data.

Experiments cover eight real-world datasets. For imputation, D³M reduces RMSE by up to 4.6% and CRPS by up to 4.3% relative to state-of-the-art methods. For forecasting, it achieves comparable results with only ten steps. The findings show improved imputation performance and competitive forecasting with a short generation process, rather than uniform superiority across both tasks.
summary.tldr: D³M unifies diffusion and continuous flow modeling, improving time-series imputation and achieving competitive forecasting with ten generation steps.

title: Probabilistic Time Series Modeling with Decomposable Denoising Diffusion Model

abstract: Auto-regressive generation models achieve competitive performance across many different NLP tasks such as summarization, question answering, and classifications. However, they are also known for being slow in inference, which makes them challenging to deploy in real-time applications. We propose a switchable decision to accelerate inference by dynamically assigning computation resources for each data instance. Automatically making decisions on where to skip and how to balance quality and computation cost with constrained optimization, our dynamic neural generation networks enforce the efficient inference path and determine the optimized trade-off. Experiments across question answering, summarization, and classification benchmarks show that our method benefits from less computation cost during inference while keeping the same accuracy. Extensive experiments and ablation studies demonstrate that our method can be general, effective, and beneficial for many NLP tasks.

paragraphs: Autoregressive generation models perform well on tasks including question answering, summarization, and classification, but inference can be slow. This paper addresses that cost by allowing the amount of computation to vary with each input. The aim is to choose an efficient computation path while preserving the quality of the task output.

The proposed dynamic neural generation networks use a switchable decision mechanism to determine where computation can be skipped. A constrained optimization formulation balances output quality against computational cost. This turns the allocation of inference resources into a decision made for each data instance, with the optimization defining the tradeoff the network should pursue.

Experiments across question answering, summarization, and classification benchmarks report lower inference computation while maintaining the same accuracy. Additional experiments and ablations support the method's effectiveness across multiple NLP tasks. The findings suggest that adaptive computation can reduce the cost of these generation models in the tested settings, with the quality-cost balance built into the mechanism that selects the inference path.
summary.tldr: Dynamic neural generation networks select computation paths per input, reducing inference computation while maintaining accuracy on tested NLP benchmarks.

title: Switchable Decision: Dynamic Neural Generation Networks

abstract: Protein language models have demonstrated significant potential in the field of protein engineering. However, current protein language models primarily operate at the residue scale, which limits their ability to provide information at the atom level. This limitation prevents us from fully exploiting the capabilities of protein language models for applications involving both proteins and small molecules. In this paper, we propose ESM-AA (ESM All-Atom), a novel approach that enables atom-scale and residue-scale unified molecular modeling. ESM-AA achieves this by pre-training on multi-scale code-switch protein sequences and utilizing a multi-scale position encoding to capture relationships among residues and atoms. Experimental results indicate that ESM-AA surpasses previous methods in protein-molecule tasks, demonstrating the full utilization of protein language models. Further investigations reveal that through unified molecular modeling, ESM-AA not only gains molecular knowledge but also retains its understanding of proteins.

paragraphs: Protein language models usually describe proteins at the residue level. That level of representation limits the atom-level information they can provide, which matters for applications involving proteins together with small molecules. ESM All-Atom, or ESM-AA, addresses this gap by bringing residue-scale and atom-scale molecular information into a unified modeling approach.

The model is pretrained on protein sequences that switch between the two scales. It also uses a position encoding designed to capture relationships among residues and atoms. These components give the pretraining process access to both levels of description and a way to relate them, making the relationship between molecular scales part of the learned representation.

Experiments report better performance than previous methods on protein–molecule tasks. Further investigations indicate that ESM-AA acquires molecular knowledge while retaining its understanding of proteins. That combination is central to the contribution: the model extends the scope of protein language modeling to finer molecular detail while preserving knowledge useful at the protein scale.
summary.tldr: ESM-AA unifies residue- and atom-scale pretraining, improving protein–molecule tasks while retaining protein knowledge.

title: ESM All-Atom: Multi-Scale Protein Language Model for Unified Molecular Modeling

abstract: Suppose a self-driving car is crashing into pedestrians, or a chatbot is instructing its users to conduct criminal wrongdoing; the stakeholders of such products will undoubtedly want to patch these catastrophic errors as soon as possible. To address such concerns, Model Editing: the study of efficiently patching model behaviors without significantly altering their general performance, has seen considerable activity, with hundreds of editing techniques developed in various domains such as CV and NLP. However, the graph learning community has objectively fallen behind with only a few Graph Neural Network-compatible — and just one GNN-specific — model editing methods available, where all of which are limited in their practical scope. We argue that the impracticality of these methods lies in their lack of Sequential Editing Robustness: the ability to edit multiple errors sequentially, and therefore fall short in effectiveness, as this approach mirrors how errors are discovered and addressed in the real world. In this paper, we delve into the specific reasons behind the difficulty of editing GNNs in succession and observe the root cause to be model overfitting. We subsequently propose a simple yet effective solution — SEED-GNN — by leveraging overfit-prevention techniques in a GNN-specific context to derive the first and only GNN model editing method that scales practically. Additionally, we formally frame the task paradigm of GNN editing and hope to inspire future research in this crucial but currently overlooked field. Please refer to our GitHub repository for code and checkpoints.

paragraphs: This paper studies model editing for graph neural networks: efficiently correcting unwanted behavior while largely preserving general performance. Its central concern is what happens when a model needs several corrections in succession. Errors are often discovered over time, so a useful editing method must remain effective after earlier edits have already changed the model.

The authors call this capability sequential editing robustness and argue that existing GNN-compatible editing approaches lack it. Their investigation attributes the difficulty of repeated editing to model overfitting. This diagnosis connects the failure of later edits to how the model adapts during the correction process.

They propose SEED-GNN, which applies techniques for preventing overfitting in a GNN-specific editing setting. The authors present it as a method that makes sequential GNN editing practically scalable. They also formally define the GNN editing task to support further research. The main contribution is to make repeated correction an explicit requirement and to address the identified overfitting problem, rather than judging editing solely through an isolated successful patch.
summary.tldr: SEED-GNN addresses overfitting to make graph neural networks more robust to repeated model edits.

title: GNNs Also Deserve Editing, and They Need It More Than Once

abstract: Memory layers use a trainable key-value lookup mechanism to add extra parameters to a model without increasing FLOPs. Conceptually, sparsely activated memory layers complement compute-heavy dense feed-forward layers, providing dedicated capacity to store and retrieve information cheaply. This work takes memory layers beyond proof-of-concept, proving their utility at contemporary scale. On downstream tasks, language models augmented with our improved memory layer outperform dense models with more than twice the computation budget, as well as mixture-of-expert models when matched for both compute and parameters. We find gains are especially pronounced for factual tasks. We provide a fully parallelizable memory layer implementation, demonstrating scaling laws with up to 128B memory parameters, pretrained to 1 trillion tokens, comparing to base models with up to 8B parameters.

paragraphs: A model can gain storage capacity without increasing its floating-point computation by using a trainable key-value lookup mechanism. Memory layers follow this approach: they activate sparsely and retrieve information from additional parameters. This paper develops improved memory layers and evaluates whether their benefits extend to contemporary language-model scales.

The authors position memory as a complement to dense feed-forward layers, which perform substantial computation. They provide a fully parallelizable implementation and study scaling with as many as 128 billion memory parameters, pretraining up to one trillion tokens, and base models containing up to eight billion parameters. These experiments move the idea beyond a small proof of concept.

On downstream tasks, the memory-augmented models outperform dense models using more than twice the computation budget. They also outperform mixture-of-experts models matched for both computation and parameter count. Gains are particularly strong on factual tasks, supporting the value of dedicated capacity for storing and retrieving information. The findings show that how parameters are accessed can matter alongside how many parameters a model contains.
summary.tldr: Sparse trainable memory layers improve language-model performance at scale, with especially strong gains on factual tasks.

title: Memory Layers at Scale

abstract: We study the task of online learning in the presence of Massart noise. Specifically, instead of assuming that the online adversary chooses an arbitrary sequence of labels, we assume that the context $\boldsymbol{x}$ is selected adversarially but the label $y$ presented to the learner disagrees with the ground-truth label of $\boldsymbol{x}$ with unknown probability at most $\eta$. We focus on the fundamental class of $\gamma$-margin linear classifiers and present the first computationally efficient algorithm that achieves mistake bound $\eta T + o(T)$. We point out that the mistake bound achieved by our algorithm is qualitatively tight for computationally efficient algorithms; this follows from the fact that, even in the offline setting, achieving 0-1 error better than $\eta$ requires super-polynomial time under standard complexity assumptions. We extend our online learning model to a $k$-arm contextual bandit setting where the rewards—instead of satisfying commonly used realizability assumptions—are consistent, in expectation, with some linear ranking function with weight vector $\boldsymbol{w}^\ast$. Given a list of contexts $\boldsymbol{x}_1,\ldots \boldsymbol{x}_k$, if $\boldsymbol{w}^*\cdot \boldsymbol{x}_i > \boldsymbol{w}^* \cdot \boldsymbol{x}_j$, the expected reward of action $i$ must be larger than that of $j$ by at least $\Delta$. We use our Massart online learner to design an efficient bandit algorithm that obtains expected reward at least $(1-1/k) \Delta T - o(T)$ bigger than choosing a random action at every round.

paragraphs: In this online classification problem, an adversary chooses the inputs, but labels are constrained by Massart noise: each observed label differs from its ground truth with an unknown probability at most eta. The paper focuses on linear classifiers with a gamma margin, combining difficult input selection with bounded label corruption.

The authors give the first computationally efficient algorithm with a mistake bound of eta times T plus a term that grows more slowly than T. Over many rounds, the extra mistakes per round therefore vanish. The result is qualitatively tight for efficient algorithms under standard complexity assumptions, because even offline learning cannot efficiently guarantee classification error below eta.

The paper extends the approach to contextual bandits with k actions. Expected rewards need only respect a linear ranking, with a gap of at least Delta whenever one action ranks above another. Using the online learner, the bandit algorithm exceeds random action selection in expected total reward by at least (1 minus one over k) times Delta times T, minus a sublinear term.
summary.tldr: An efficient online classifier reaches a qualitatively tight Massart-noise mistake bound and supports a bandit algorithm under linear reward-ranking assumptions.

title: Online Linear Classification with Massart Noise

abstract: Mental disorders are among the most widespread diseases globally. Analyzing functional brain networks through functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) is crucial for understanding mental disorder behaviors. Although existing fMRI-based graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant potential in brain network feature extraction, they often fail to characterize complex relationships between brain regions and demographic information in mental disorders. To overcome these limitations, we propose a learnable NeuroTree framework that integrates a $k$-hop AGE-GCN with neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and contrastive masked functional connectivity (CMFC) to enhance similarities and dissimilarities of brain region distance. Furthermore, NeuroTree effectively decodes fMRI network features into tree structures, which improves the capture of high-order brain regional pathway features and enables the identification of hierarchical neural behavioral patterns essential for understanding disease-related brain subnetworks. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that NeuroTree achieves state-of-the-art performance across two distinct mental disorder datasets. It provides valuable insights into age-related deterioration patterns, elucidating their underlying neural mechanisms. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Ding1119/NeuroTree.

NeuroTree is designed to capture richer organization in functional networks associated with mental disorders.

The framework combines a k-hop AGE-GCN, neural ordinary differential equations, and contrastive masked functional connectivity. NeuroTree then decodes the network features into trees, providing a hierarchical representation of regional pathways and neural behavioral patterns.

The work’s contribution combines predictive feature learning with a structured representation of brain-network organization. Its reported findings concern the evaluated datasets and the patterns revealed by that representation, tying performance improvements to an effort to understand hierarchical functional pathways.
summary.tldr: NeuroTree converts functional brain-network features into hierarchical trees and reports state-of-the-art results on two mental-disorder datasets.

title: NeuroTree: Hierarchical Functional Brain Pathway Decoding for Mental Health Disorders

abstract: Large agent networks are abundant in applications and nature and pose difficult challenges in the field of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) due to their computational and theoretical complexity. While graphon mean field games and their extensions provide efficient learning algorithms for dense and moderately sparse agent networks, the case of realistic sparser graphs remains largely unsolved. Thus, we propose a novel mean field control model inspired by local weak convergence to include sparse graphs such as power law networks with coefficients above two. Besides a theoretical analysis, we design scalable learning algorithms which apply to the challenging class of graph sequences with finite first moment. We compare our model and algorithms for various examples on synthetic and real world networks with mean field algorithms based on Lp graphons and graphexes. As it turns out, our approach outperforms existing methods in many examples and on various networks due to the special design aiming at an important, but so far hard to solve class of MARL problems.

paragraphs: Learning to coordinate large networks of agents is difficult because both computation and mathematical analysis become demanding. Mean field methods offer efficient approaches for dense and moderately sparse networks, but realistic networks with fewer connections remain challenging. This paper develops a mean field control model specifically aimed at that sparser regime.

The model draws on local weak convergence and includes sparse networks such as power law networks with coefficients above two. Alongside theoretical analysis, the authors design scalable learning algorithms for graph sequences with a finite first moment. This condition identifies the class their algorithms address and is part of the contribution's stated scope.

The authors compare their approach with methods based on Lp graphons and graphexes across examples involving synthetic and real-world networks. Their method performs better in many examples and on various networks. These findings support the value of designing the approximation around sparse network structure, extending efficient learning tools to an important class of multi-agent problems that earlier approaches have struggled to handle.
summary.tldr: A mean field control model tailored to sparse graphs enables scalable learning and improves over existing methods in many evaluated networks.

title: Learning Mean Field Control on Sparse Graphs

abstract: Crystal symmetry plays a fundamental role in determining its physical, chemical, and electronic properties such as electrical and thermal conductivity, optical and polarization behavior, and mechanical strength. Almost all known crystalline materials have internal symmetry. However, this is often inadequately addressed by existing generative models, making the consistent generation of stable and symmetrically valid crystal structures a significant challenge. We introduce WyFormer, a generative model that directly tackles this by formally conditioning on space group symmetry. It achieves this by using Wyckoff positions as the basis for an elegant, compressed, and discrete structure representation. To model the distribution, we develop a permutation-invariant autoregressive model based on the Transformer encoder and an absence of positional encoding. Extensive experimentation demonstrates WyFormer’s compelling combination of attributes: it achieves best-in-class symmetry-conditioned generation, incorporates a physics-motivated inductive bias, produces structures with competitive stability, predicts material properties with competitive accuracy even without atomic coordinates, and exhibits unparalleled inference speed.

paragraphs: Crystal symmetry influences properties including conductivity, optical behavior, and mechanical strength. Generative models that inadequately represent symmetry can struggle to produce structures that are both stable and symmetrically valid. This paper introduces WyFormer, which explicitly conditions generation on space group symmetry and represents crystal structure through Wyckoff positions.

The resulting representation is discrete and compressed, making symmetry part of how structures are described. To learn its distribution, the authors construct an autoregressive model based on a Transformer encoder without positional encoding. The model is permutation invariant, so its treatment of the representation does not depend on an arbitrary ordering of its elements.

Experiments report best-in-class symmetry-conditioned generation alongside competitive structural stability and material-property prediction accuracy, including prediction without atomic coordinates. The authors also report unmatched inference speed in their evaluations. The contribution combines a physics-motivated representation with a suitable generative architecture, showing that explicit symmetry structure can support generation, property prediction, and efficient inference within the same modeling approach.
summary.tldr: WyFormer uses a compact symmetry-based crystal representation to support strong symmetry-conditioned generation, competitive property prediction, and fast inference.

title: Wyckoff Transformer: Generation of Symmetric Crystals

abstract: Extensive research has shown that a wide range of machine learning problems can be formulated as bilevel optimization, where two levels of learning processes intertwine through distinct sets of optimization variables. However, prevailing approaches often impose stringent assumptions, such as strong convexity of the lower-level loss function or uniqueness of the optimal solution, to enable algorithmic development and convergence analysis. However, these assumptions tend to be overly restrictive in real-world scenarios. In this work, we explore a recently popularized Moreau envelope based reformulation of bilevel optimization problems, accommodating nonconvex objective functions at both levels. We propose a stochastic primal-dual method that incorporates smoothing on both sides, capable of finding Karush-Kuhn-Tucker solutions for this general class of nonconvex bilevel optimization problems. A key feature of our algorithm is its ability to dynamically weigh the lower-level problems, enhancing its performance, particularly in stochastic learning scenarios. Numerical experiments underscore the superiority of our proposed algorithm over existing penalty-based methods in terms of both the convergence rate and the test accuracy.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization describes problems where one optimization process depends on another, with separate variables at each level. Many machine learning problems fit this structure. Existing methods often rely on a strongly convex lower-level objective or a unique lower-level optimum, assumptions the paper argues are too restrictive for many practical settings.

The authors work with a Moreau-envelope reformulation that accommodates nonconvex objectives at both levels. They propose TSP, a stochastic primal-dual algorithm with smoothing on both sides. Its target is a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker solution, a form of constrained optimality condition. The method also changes the weights assigned to lower-level problems dynamically, a feature intended to improve behavior particularly in stochastic learning.

Numerical experiments show better convergence rates and test accuracy than existing penalty-based methods. The findings support the proposed combination of smoothing, primal-dual updates, and adaptive weighting for the studied problems. Its theoretical contribution concerns finding KKT solutions in the stated nonconvex bilevel setting; that solution target should be understood as distinct from a guarantee of global optimality.
summary.tldr: TSP combines two-sided smoothing and adaptive primal-dual optimization to find KKT solutions for nonconvex bilevel problems.

title: TSP: A Two-Sided Smoothed Primal-Dual Method for Nonconvex Bilevel Optimization

abstract: We introduce Wasserstein Policy Optimization (WPO), an actor-critic algorithm for reinforcement learning in continuous action spaces. WPO can be derived as an approximation to Wasserstein gradient flow over the space of all policies projected into a finite-dimensional parameter space (e.g., the weights of a neural network), leading to a simple and completely general closed-form update. The resulting algorithm combines many properties of deterministic and classic policy gradient methods. Like deterministic policy gradients, it exploits knowledge of the gradient of the action-value function with respect to the action. Like classic policy gradients, it can be applied to stochastic policies with arbitrary distributions over actions – without using the reparameterization trick. We show results on the DeepMind Control Suite and a magnetic confinement fusion task which compare favorably with state-of-the-art continuous control methods.

paragraphs: Wasserstein Policy Optimization, or WPO, is an actor-critic algorithm for reinforcement learning with continuous actions. This produces a general closed-form update.

It uses the gradient of the action-value function with respect to the action, allowing the update to exploit how value changes as an action changes. It can also train stochastic policies with arbitrary action distributions without requiring the reparameterization trick.

The authors evaluate WPO on the DeepMind Control Suite and a magnetic confinement fusion task, reporting results that compare favorably with state-of-the-art continuous control methods. The contribution is a policy update that connects distribution-level optimization with practical parameterized learning. Its combination of action-value gradients and support for general stochastic policies provides the central methodological motivation for the reported control experiments.
summary.tldr: WPO derives a continuous-control policy update that combines action-value gradients with support for arbitrary stochastic action distributions.

title: Wasserstein Policy Optimization

abstract: Fine-Grained Openset Detection (FGOD) poses a fundamental challenge due to the similarity between the openset classes and those closed-set ones. Since real-world objects/entities tend to form a hierarchical structure, the fine-grained relationship among the closed-set classes as captured by the hierarchy could potentially improve the FGOD performance. Intuitively, the hierarchical dependency among different classes allows the model to recognize their subtle differences, which in turn makes it better at differentiating similar open-set classes even they may share the same parent. However, simply performing openset detection in a top-down fashion by building a local detector for each node may result in a poor detection performance. Our theoretical analysis also reveals that maximizing the probability of the path leading to the ground-truth leaf node also results in a sub-optimal training process. To systematically address this issue, we propose to formulate a novel state-based node representation, which constructs a state space based upon the entire hierarchical structure. We prove that the state-based representation guarantees to maximize the probability on the path leading to the ground-truth leaf node. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world hierarchical datasets clearly demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Fine-grained open-set detection asks a model to recognize unfamiliar classes that closely resemble familiar ones. A class hierarchy can expose subtle relationships among known categories, potentially helping distinguish an unknown category even when it shares a parent with known categories. The challenge is to turn that hierarchy into an effective learning representation.

The paper argues that placing a separate detector at each hierarchy node and proceeding from top to bottom can perform poorly. Its theoretical analysis also finds that directly maximizing the probability of the path to the correct leaf leads to a suboptimal training process. Simply adding hierarchical decisions therefore does not resolve the learning problem.

The proposed alternative represents nodes through a state space constructed from the entire hierarchy. The authors prove that this state-based representation guarantees maximization of the probability along the correct leaf's path. The distinction is between directly optimizing that path objective and obtaining the property through the proposed representation. Experiments on multiple real-world hierarchical datasets report superior detection performance, supporting the value of modeling the hierarchy as a whole.
summary.tldr: State-based representations built from a whole class hierarchy improve detection of unfamiliar classes that closely resemble known ones.

title: Learning State-Based Node Representations from a Class Hierarchy for Fine-Grained Open-Set Detection

abstract: Time-series forecasting finds application across domains such as finance, climate science, and energy systems. We introduce the Conditional Diffusion with Nonlinear Data Transformation Model (CN-Diff), a generative framework that employs novel nonlinear transformations and learnable conditions in the forward process for time series forecasting. A new loss formulation for training is proposed, along with a detailed derivation of both forward and reverse process. The new additions improve the diffusion model’s capacity to capture complex time series patterns, thus simplifying the reverse process. Our novel condition facilitates learning an efficient prior distribution. This also reduces the gap between the true negative log-likelihood and its variational approximation. CN-Diff is shown to perform better than other leading time series models on nine real-world datasets. Ablation studies are conducted to elucidate the role of each component of CN-Diff.

paragraphs: CN-Diff is a generative approach to time-series forecasting that changes how a diffusion model prepares data for generation. The paper focuses on nonlinear transformations and learnable conditioning in the forward process. These additions are intended to help the model represent complex patterns in time series before it learns to reverse that process.

The authors derive both the forward and reverse processes and introduce a corresponding training loss. They report that the richer forward construction simplifies the reverse process. The learned condition also helps establish an efficient prior distribution and reduces the gap between the true negative log-likelihood and the variational approximation used in the framework.

The practical evaluation covers nine real-world datasets, where CN-Diff outperforms other leading time-series models. Ablation studies examine the contribution of its individual components. The combined message is that forecasting improvements can come from redesigning the diffusion process and its training objective together, with the reported gains supported across the evaluated datasets rather than a single forecasting example.
summary.tldr: CN-Diff improves time-series forecasting by adding nonlinear transformations and learned conditions to a diffusion model’s forward process.

title: Conditional Diffusion Model with Nonlinear Data Transformation for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Foundation model-based agents are increasingly used to automate complex tasks, enhancing efficiency and productivity. However, their access to sensitive resources and autonomous decision-making also introduce significant security risks, where successful attacks could lead to severe consequences. To systematically uncover these vulnerabilities, we propose AdvAgent, a black-box red-teaming framework for attacking web agents. Unlike existing approaches, AdvAgent employs a reinforcement learning-based pipeline to train an adversarial prompter model that optimizes adversarial prompts using feedback from the black-box agent. With careful attack design, these prompts effectively exploit agent weaknesses while maintaining stealthiness and controllability. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that AdvAgent achieves high success rates against state-of-the-art GPT-4-based web agents across diverse web tasks. Furthermore, we find that existing prompt-based defenses provide only limited protection, leaving agents vulnerable to our framework. These findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in current web agents and emphasize the urgent need for stronger defense mechanisms. We release code at https://ai-secure.github.io/AdvAgent/.

paragraphs: Web agents combine language models with the ability to act on websites, making security failures potentially consequential when they can access sensitive resources. AdvAgent studies these vulnerabilities through automated red-teaming: deliberately challenging an agent to discover where its behavior can be manipulated. Its black-box setting uses feedback from the target agent to develop attacks.

The framework trains an adversarial prompting model through reinforcement learning. Instead of relying only on fixed attack prompts, it uses the target agent’s responses to improve the prompts it generates. The attack design also aims to preserve stealthiness and controllability, making these properties part of the framework’s objectives alongside attack effectiveness.

Evaluations report high attack success against GPT-4-based web agents across varied web tasks. The authors also find that existing prompt-based defenses offer limited protection against these attacks. Together, these results show that the tested agents remain vulnerable even when such defenses are present, motivating stronger protections for agents whose outputs can trigger actions.
summary.tldr: AdvAgent learns adversarial prompts from black-box feedback and exposes weaknesses in GPT-4-based web agents and their prompt-based defenses.

title: AdvAgent: Controllable Blackbox Red-teaming on Web Agents

abstract: Self-speculative decoding (SSD) accelerates LLM inference by skipping layers to create an efficient draft model, yet existing methods often rely on static heuristics that ignore the dynamic computational overhead of attention in long-context scenarios. We propose KnapSpec, a training-free framework that reformulates draft model selection as a knapsack problem to maximize tokens-per-time throughput. By decoupling Attention and MLP layers and modeling their hardware-specific latencies as functions of context length, KnapSpec adaptively identifies optimal draft configurations on the fly via a parallel dynamic programming algorithm. Furthermore, we provide the first rigorous theoretical analysis establishing cosine similarity between hidden states as a mathematically sound proxy for the token acceptance rate. This foundation allows our method to maintain high drafting faithfulness while navigating the shifting bottlenecks of real-world hardware. Our experiments on Qwen3 and Llama3 demonstrate that KnapSpec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art SSD baselines, achieving up to 1.47$\times$ wall-clock speedup across various benchmarks. Our plug-and-play approach ensures high-speed inference for long sequences without requiring additional training or compromising the target model’s output distribution.

paragraphs: Self-speculative decoding speeds up generation by using a reduced version of a language model to draft tokens. Selecting which layers to skip creates a trade-off between drafting cost and how faithfully the draft matches the full model. KnapSpec addresses the fact that this trade-off changes with context length and hardware, particularly as attention becomes more expensive.

The method treats draft selection as a knapsack optimization problem aimed at maximizing tokens generated per unit time. It considers attention and MLP layers separately, models their hardware-specific latency as context length changes, and uses parallel dynamic programming to adapt the draft configuration. A theoretical analysis supports cosine similarity between hidden states as a proxy for token acceptance.

Experiments on Qwen3 and Llama3 report consistent improvements over leading self-speculative decoding methods, with wall-clock speedups reaching 1.47 times. KnapSpec requires no additional training and preserves the target model's output distribution. Its contribution is an adaptive selection procedure that balances draft faithfulness against changing computation costs during long-sequence inference.
summary.tldr: KnapSpec adapts speculative draft layers to context length and hardware, achieving reported speedups up to 1.47 times without extra training.

title: KnapSpec: Self-Speculative Decoding via Adaptive Layer Selection as a Knapsack Problem

abstract: The cost of simulator evaluations is a key practical bottleneck for Simulation Based Inference (SBI). In hierarchical settings with shared global parameters and exchangeable site-level parameters and observations, this structure can be exploited to improve simulation efficiency. Existing hierarchical SBI approaches factorise the posterior yet still simulate across multiple sites per training sample; We instead explore likelihood factorisation (LF) to train from single-site simulations. In LF sampling we learn a per-site (factorised) likelihood and then assemble synthetic multi-site observations to amortise inference for the full hierarchical posterior. Building on this, we propose Tokenised Flow Matching for Posterior Estimation (TFMPE), a tokenised flow matching approach that supports function-valued observations through likelihood factorisation. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce a benchmark for hierarchical SBI. We validate TFMPE on this benchmark and on realistic infectious disease and computational fluid dynamics models, finding well-calibrated posteriors while reducing computational cost.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference estimates unknown parameters using data generated by a simulator, but simulator evaluations can be costly. This paper focuses on hierarchical problems with shared global parameters and exchangeable site-level parameters and observations. That repeated structure offers an opportunity to reduce how much simulation is needed for training.

The approach learns a likelihood for an individual site from single-site simulations. It then assembles synthetic observations for multiple sites to train inference for the full hierarchical posterior. This differs from existing hierarchical approaches that factorize the posterior but still simulate multiple sites for each training example. The proposed Tokenised Flow Matching for Posterior Estimation uses this likelihood factorization and supports function-valued observations.

The authors introduce a benchmark for hierarchical inference and evaluate the method on it, alongside realistic infectious-disease and computational-fluid-dynamics models. They report well-calibrated posterior distributions with reduced computational cost. The contribution makes the shared, exchangeable structure useful at the simulation stage, allowing single-site training information to support uncertainty estimates for the larger hierarchical system.
summary.tldr: Tokenised flow matching uses likelihoods learned from single-site simulations to estimate hierarchical posteriors with lower computational cost.

title: Tokenised Flow Matching for Hierarchical Simulation Based Inference

abstract: Prediction-powered inference is a recent methodology for the safe use of black-box ML models to impute missing data, strengthening inference of statistical parameters. However, many applications require strong properties besides valid inference, such as privacy, robustness or validity under continuous distribution shifts; deriving prediction-powered methods with such guarantees is generally an arduous process, and has to be done case by case. In this paper, we resolve this issue by connecting prediction-powered inference with conformal prediction: by performing imputation through a calibrated set-predictor, we attain validity while achieving additional guarantees in a natural manner. We instantiate our procedure for the inference of means, Z- and M-estimation, as well as e-values and e-value-based procedures. Furthermore, in the case of e-values, ours is the first general prediction-powered procedure that operates off-line. We demonstrate these advantages by applying our method on private and time-series data. Both tasks are nontrivial within the standard prediction-powered framework but become natural under our method.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference uses machine learning predictions to fill in missing data and strengthen statistical inference. Valid inference alone may be insufficient when an application also needs privacy, robustness, or validity under changing distributions. Building these additional guarantees separately for each statistical procedure can require substantial new methodological work.

This paper connects prediction-powered inference to conformal prediction by imputing through a calibrated set predictor. Representing predictions as calibrated sets supplies a route to validity while accommodating additional guarantees. The authors instantiate the approach for means, Z-estimation, M-estimation, e-values, and procedures based on e-values, showing that the connection applies to several forms of statistical inference.

For e-values, the authors introduce what they describe as the first general prediction-powered procedure that operates offline. They also demonstrate the framework on private data and time-series data, two settings that are difficult within the standard approach. The contribution is a reusable construction for extending prediction-powered methods, with the examples illustrating how calibration can make added requirements more natural to incorporate.
summary.tldr: Calibrated set predictions extend prediction-powered inference to additional guarantees and statistical procedures, including offline e-value methods.

title: Extending Prediction-Powered Inference through Conformal Prediction

abstract: Auto-bidding is a core component of real-time advertising systems, where decisions must optimize long-term performance under budget and cost constraints, while online exploration is prohibitively risky. Offline reinforcement learning and, more recently, Transformer-based sequence modeling have shown promise for learning bidding policies from logged data, but their unimodal and purely parametric formulations often collapse multiple effective bidding strategies into suboptimal averaged actions and perform unreliably under sparse or long-tail traffic. To mitigate these limitations, we propose DRIVE (Distributional and Retrieval-Augmented Bidding with Value Evaluation), a unified Transformer-based framework that decouples candidate action generation from decision making for offline auto-bidding. DRIVE combines distributional action modeling, retrieval-augmented candidate generation from high-quality historical decisions, and value-based evaluation to select the most promising bid at inference time. Extensive experiments on AuctionNet and additional offline reinforcement learning benchmarks demonstrate that DRIVE consistently improves bidding performance and generalizes well across multiple Transformer–based methods.

paragraphs: Automated advertising bids must account for long-term outcomes while respecting budget and cost constraints. Learning directly through online experimentation can be prohibitively risky, motivating policies trained from historical records. The paper identifies a problem with approaches that compress several effective bidding strategies into one averaged action, especially when traffic is sparse or unusual.

DRIVE separates proposing bids from choosing among them. Its Transformer-based framework models a distribution of actions, retrieves candidate bids from high-quality historical decisions, and then evaluates the candidates by value. At inference time, the system selects the most promising bid from those proposals. This gives candidate generation access to both learned patterns and concrete historical decisions.

Experiments on AuctionNet and additional offline reinforcement-learning benchmarks show consistent improvements in bidding performance. The authors also report that the approach works across multiple Transformer-based methods. The result supports treating bid selection as a comparison among plausible alternatives, with retrieval supplementing the model’s learned action distribution when purely parametric predictions may be unreliable.
summary.tldr: DRIVE improves offline bidding by generating diverse and retrieved candidate bids, then selecting among them using value estimates.

title: DRIVE: Distributional and Retrieval-Augmented Bidding with Value Evaluation

abstract: Conventional dynamic SLAM approaches typically treat dynamic objects as outliers based on pre-defined categories, creating perceptual blind spots that limit the comprehensive environmental perception required for embodied agents. Although integrating Gaussian Splatting into SLAM enables holistic scene representation, it introduces an optimization paradox: without categorical priors, flexible dynamic primitives rapidly overfit static residuals. This phenomenon undermines the self-supervised error signals necessary for distinguishing motion. In response, we present De4D-SLAM, a novel framework designed for decoupled 4D reconstruction from monocular video. Our approach features a Gradient-Isolated Decoupling strategy, which leverages static reconstruction residuals to supervise a Spatially-Aware Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (SA-KAN), ensuring robust, category-agnostic motion segmentation. Additionally, we propose a Flow-Induced Initialization prior to stabilize the non-convex optimization of 4D Gaussian primitives using dense optical flow. Extensive evaluations on the TUM and Bonn benchmarks demonstrate that De4D-SLAM achieves competitive performance in both tracking and dynamic reconstruction, successfully reconciling the tension between robust localization and high-fidelity 4D mapping.

This phenomenon undermines the self-supervised error signals necessary for distinguishing motion. In response, we present De4D-SLAM, a novel framework designed for decoupled 4D reconstruction from monocular video. Our approach features a Gradient-Isolated Decoupling strategy, which leverages static reconstruction residuals to supervise a Spatially-Aware Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (SA-KAN), ensuring robust, category-agnostic motion segmentation. Additionally, we propose a Flow-Induced Initialization prior to stabilize the non-convex optimization of 4D Gaussian primitives using dense optical flow. Extensive evaluations on the TUM and Bonn benchmarks demonstrate that De4D-SLAM achieves competitive performance in both tracking and dynamic reconstruction, successfully reconciling the tension between robust localization and high-fidelity 4D mapping.

paragraphs: De4D-SLAM tackles camera tracking and scene reconstruction from a single camera when objects can move. Conventional methods often discard moving objects using predefined categories, leaving parts of the environment poorly represented. Gaussian scene representations can include both stationary and moving content, but their flexible moving components can also fit errors that actually belong to the static scene.

That unwanted fitting removes the reconstruction errors needed to identify genuine motion. De4D-SLAM separates the relevant gradient signals so static reconstruction residuals can supervise a spatially aware Kolmogorov-Arnold network for motion segmentation. This allows motion detection without relying on object categories. A second component uses dense optical flow to initialize the changing Gaussian representation and stabilize its difficult optimization.

Evaluations on TUM and Bonn report competitive camera tracking and dynamic reconstruction. These findings support the framework’s effort to preserve reliable localization while also reconstructing a scene that changes over time. Its central contribution is managing how static and dynamic components learn, so their flexibility does not destroy the evidence used to distinguish them.
summary.tldr: De4D-SLAM separates static and dynamic learning signals to support camera tracking and changing-scene reconstruction without object-category priors.

title: De4D-SLAM: Gradient-Isolated Static-Dynamic Decoupling for Monocular SLAM in Dynamic Environments

abstract: Neuromorphic event cameras possess superior temporal resolution, power efficiency, and dynamic range compared to traditional cameras. However, their asynchronous and sparse data format poses a significant challenge for conventional deep learning methods. Most existing methods either densify events into frames, sacrificing their sparse asynchronous nature, or use irregular models that are less compatible with GPU acceleration. Inspired by word-to-vector models, we propose event2vec, a novel representation that allows Transformers to process events directly. We demonstrate the effectiveness of event2vec on the DVS Gesture, ASL-DVS, and DVS-Lip benchmarks, showing that event2vec is remarkably parameter-efficient, features high throughput and low latency, and achieves high accuracy even with an extremely low number of events or low spatial resolutions. These results show that sparse asynchronous event data can be directly integrated into high-throughput Transformer architectures, offering an efficient paradigm for real-time neuromorphic vision. The code is provided at https://github.com/Intelligent-Computing-Lab-Panda/event2vec.
