paragraphs: Event2Vec addresses the mismatch between event cameras and conventional deep learning pipelines. These cameras provide sparse, asynchronous observations with strong temporal resolution, power efficiency, and dynamic range. Converting events into dense frames loses their original sparse timing structure, while models designed for irregular data can be less compatible with GPU acceleration.

Inspired by word-to-vector representations, the paper introduces a vector representation that lets Transformers process events directly. The key idea is to make the event format usable within a high-throughput architecture while retaining direct access to event data. This connects the camera’s unusual output format to a model family suited to efficient computation.

Evaluations on DVS Gesture, ASL-DVS, and DVS-Lip report parameter efficiency, high throughput, and low latency. The method also achieves high accuracy when only very few events or low spatial resolutions are available. Together, these findings support direct event representations as a practical route toward efficient neuromorphic vision, including settings where the available visual observations are especially sparse.
summary.tldr: Event2Vec represents camera events directly as vectors, enabling efficient Transformer processing even with sparse or low-resolution observations.

title: Event2Vec: Processing neuromorphic events directly by representations in vector space

abstract: Reconstructing high-fidelity RAW sensor data from processed RGB images is a fundamental yet ill-posed problem, plagued by irreversible information loss and complex non-linear ISP transformations. While generative models offer high-quality reconstruction, they suffer from prohibitive computational costs. Conversely, dominant regression-based methods are fast but susceptible to incoherent observational deviations, often yielding over-smoothed predictions that drift from the authentic signal manifold. To reconcile this trade-off, we propose SHADE, a Single-step Homogeneous Aligned DEterministic flow framework. We validate that, unlike point-to-point regression, the single-step deterministic flow captures global transport trends and enables intrinsic robustness against input perturbations. Furthermore, we introduce Homogeneous Representation Alignment to maximize fidelity. By leveraging a homogeneously initialized student-teacher DINO pair, this mechanism enforces alignment within a shared feature space, significantly amplifying the representational capacity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHADE achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks, establishing a new paradigm for accurate and efficient sensor data reconstruction.

paragraphs: Reconstructing RAW sensor data from a processed RGB image requires working backward through transformations that have already discarded information. The paper addresses this inherently ambiguous reconstruction problem. It targets a trade-off in existing methods: generative approaches can produce high-quality results but cost substantial computation, while fast regression methods can smooth away detail and depart from authentic sensor signals.

SHADE uses a deterministic flow that produces a reconstruction in one step. The authors report that this approach captures broader transport patterns between the image representations, rather than relying on point-to-point regression alone. Their analysis also supports robustness to perturbations in the input. A second component aligns representations using a student–teacher DINO pair initialized homogeneously, so both sides work within a shared feature space.

Experiments report state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across multiple benchmarks. The contribution is a combination of efficient generation and feature alignment intended to improve fidelity. Because the original processing loses information irreversibly, these results concern reconstruction quality rather than guaranteed recovery of the exact original sensor measurements.
summary.tldr: SHADE combines a one-step deterministic flow with shared-space feature alignment for accurate, efficient reconstruction of RAW data from RGB images.

title: Bridging RGB and RAW: Single-step Deterministic Flow with Homogeneous Representation Alignment

abstract: Diffusion models have become the foundation of modern generative systems, with most research focusing primarily on improving generation efficiency and output quality. The timestep embedding component is a crucial part of the diffusion pipeline, which provides a temporal conditioning signal to the denoising network, enabling it to adapt its predictions across different noise levels throughout the process. Despite their potential to contain substantial information, timestep embeddings remain underexplored in current research, especially for security risks and reliable provenance. To fill this gap, we introduce Shadow Timestep Embedding (STE), a novel mechanism that investigates the underutilized temporal space for malicious information injection into diffusion models. In particular, when zooming in on the timestep embedding space, we find that different timesteps exhibit distinct representational capabilities that can encode side-channel information. Moreover, such encoded information can be utilized for attack and defense purposes through the scheduler interface. We present a theoretical analysis of timestep embeddings as position-encoding mappings and derive a mutual coherence evaluation that explains the separability of disjoint timestep intervals. Our findings reveal the diffusion model’s timestep as a powerful side channel for carrying dedicated information, motivating new directions for adversarial generative modeling by understanding the temporal dimension.

paragraphs: A diffusion model uses timestep embeddings to tell its denoising network where it is in the generation process and which noise level it should handle. This paper investigates whether that conditioning space can carry additional information. The question matters for both malicious information injection and reliable provenance, beyond the usual focus on image quality and generation speed.

Shadow Timestep Embedding explores this temporal space as a side channel. The authors find that different timesteps have different representational capabilities and can encode auxiliary information. They also show that information encoded there can be used for attack and defense purposes through the scheduler interface, connecting the temporal signal to how generation is controlled.

This provides an account of why distinct temporal regions can support distinguishable representations. The contribution is to identify and analyze an information-bearing channel inside diffusion conditioning, showing that the timestep signal has implications for security and provenance as well as denoising.
summary.tldr: Shadow Timestep Embedding reveals diffusion timestep conditioning as a side channel for auxiliary information with attack and defense applications.

title: Watch Your Step: Information Injection in Diffusion Models via Shadow Timestep Embedding

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced Table Question Answering, where most queries can be answered by extracting information or simple aggregation. However, a common class of real-world queries is implicitly predictive, requiring the inference of unobserved answers from historical patterns rather than mere retrieval. These queries introduce two challenges: recognizing latent intent and reliable predictive reasoning over massive tables. To assess LLMs in such Tabular questiOn answering with implicit Prediction tasks, we introduce TopBench, a benchmark consisting of 779 samples across four sub-tasks, ranging from single-point prediction to decision making, treatment effect analysis, and complex filtering, requiring models to generate outputs spanning reasoning text and structured tables. We evaluate diverse models under both text-based and agentic workflows. Experiments reveal that current models often struggle with intent recognition, defaulting to just lookups. Deeper analysis identifies that accurate intent disambiguation serves as the prerequisite for leading these predictive behaviors. Furthermore, elevating the upper bound of prediction precision requires the integration of more sophisticated modeling or reasoning capabilities.

paragraphs: Some questions about tables ask for answers that are not explicitly recorded. They require predicting unobserved outcomes from historical patterns, even when the wording does not directly request a prediction. TopBench evaluates this distinction, separating ordinary retrieval and aggregation from the harder combination of recognizing predictive intent and reasoning reliably over large tables.

The benchmark contains 779 samples across four subtasks: single-point prediction, decision making, treatment-effect analysis, and complex filtering. Expected outputs include both reasoning text and structured tables. The authors evaluate diverse models using text-based and agentic workflows, examining whether different ways of interacting with tabular data support these implicitly predictive requests.

The experiments find that models often misread intent and default to looking up existing values. Further analysis identifies correct intent disambiguation as a prerequisite for eliciting predictive behavior. It also finds that improving the upper bound of prediction precision requires stronger modeling or reasoning. The benchmark therefore exposes two connected challenges: deciding that prediction is needed and performing that prediction accurately.
summary.tldr: TopBench tests whether models recognize and answer implicitly predictive table questions, revealing frequent confusion between prediction and lookup.

title: TopBench: A Benchmark for Implicit Predictive Reasoning in Tabular Question Answering

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming everyday applications, yet they lag behind in specialized fields, such as cybersecurity, due to a lack of high-quality, domain-specific models and training datasets. To address this gap, we present CyberPal 2.0, a family of cybersecurity-expert small language models (SLMs) ranging from 4B–20B parameters. To train CyberPal 2.0, we generate an enriched chain-of-thought cybersecurity instruction dataset built with our data enrichment and formatting pipeline, SecKnowledge 2.0, which integrates expert-in-the-loop steering of reasoning formats alongside LLM-driven multi-step grounding, yielding higher-fidelity, task-grounded reasoning traces for security tasks. Across diverse cybersecurity benchmarks, CyberPal 2.0 consistently outperforms its baselines and matches or surpasses various open and closed-source frontier models, while remaining a fraction of their size. On core threat-investigation tasks, such as correlating vulnerabilities and bug tickets with weaknesses, our best 20B-parameter model outperforms GPT-4o, o1, o3-mini, and Sec-Gemini v1, ranking first, while our smallest 4B-parameter model ranks second. On core cyber threat intelligence knowledge tasks, our models outperform almost all tested frontier models, ranking second only to Sec-Gemini v1. To foster reproducibility and practical adoption, we will release our models as open source.

The SecKnowledge 2.0 pipeline generates an enriched instruction dataset with chain-of-thought reasoning. Experts steer the formats of those reasoning traces, while language-model-driven multistep grounding helps connect them to the tasks. This combines expert direction with automated data enrichment to improve the fidelity of the material used for training.

summary.tldr: CyberPal 2.0 uses enriched cybersecurity reasoning data to make 4B–20B models competitive with tested frontier models on specialized benchmarks.

title: Toward Cybersecurity-Expert Small Language Models

abstract: We present the first high-probability optimal regret bound for a policy optimization technique applied to the problem of stochastic contextual multi-armed bandit (CMAB) with general offline function approximation. Our algorithm is both efficient and achieves an optimal regret bound of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ K|\mathcal{A}|\log|\mathcal{F}|})$, where $K$ is the number of rounds, $\mathcal{A}$ is the set of arms, and $\mathcal{F}$ is the function class used to approximate the losses. Our results bridge the gap between theory and practice, demonstrating that the widely used policy optimization methods for the contextual bandit problem can achieve a rigorously-proved optimal regret bound. We support our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit learning involves repeatedly choosing among actions using the available context and learning from the resulting losses. This paper asks whether policy optimization, a widely used way to improve decision rules, can achieve an optimal theoretical guarantee in the stochastic version of that problem with general offline function approximation.

The authors present an efficient algorithm whose regret is bounded with high probability by roughly the square root of the number of rounds times the number of actions times the logarithm of the loss-function class size. The notation suppresses additional logarithmic factors. Regret summarizes accumulated loss relative to a benchmark, while the function class represents the candidates used to approximate losses.

The stated advance is the first optimal high-probability regret bound for a policy-optimization technique in this setting. It provides theoretical support for an approach already common in practice, showing that this algorithm can achieve the desired learning rate. An empirical evaluation accompanies the analysis and supports the theoretical results.
summary.tldr: An efficient policy-optimization algorithm achieves an optimal high-probability regret bound for stochastic contextual bandits.

title: Optimal Regret for Policy Optimization in Contextual Bandits

abstract: Learning-based methods have made significant progress in physics simulation, typically approximating dynamics with a monolithic end-to-end optimized neural network. Although these models offer an effective way to simulation, they may lose essential features compared to traditional numerical simulators, such as physical interpretability and reliability. Drawing inspiration from classical simulators that operate in a modular fashion, this paper presents Neural Modular Physics (NMP) for elastic simulation, which combines the approximation capacity of neural networks with the physical reliability of traditional simulators. Beyond the previous monolithic learning paradigm, NMP enables direct supervision of intermediate quantities and physical constraints by decomposing elastic dynamics into physically meaningful neural modules connected through intermediate physical quantities. With a specialized architecture and training strategy, our method transforms the numerical computation flow into a modular neural simulator, achieving improved physical consistency and generalizability. Experimentally, NMP demonstrates superior generalization to unseen initial conditions and resolutions, stable long-horizon simulation, better preservation of physical properties compared to other neural simulators, and greater feasibility in scenarios with unknown underlying dynamics than traditional simulators.

paragraphs: Neural simulators can approximate physical dynamics, but a single end-to-end network may lose some of the interpretability and reliability associated with traditional numerical methods. Neural Modular Physics addresses elastic simulation by organizing learned computation into physically meaningful modules. The design follows the modular organization of classical simulators.

These neural modules communicate through intermediate physical quantities. That structure allows training to supervise intermediate values directly and impose physical constraints within the computational flow. A specialized architecture and training strategy turn the numerical workflow into a modular neural simulator. The approach combines learned approximation with explicit physical organization, making the internal computation more accessible to supervision.

Experiments show better generalization to unseen initial conditions and resolutions, stable long-horizon simulation, and stronger preservation of physical properties than other neural simulators. The paper also reports greater feasibility than traditional simulators when underlying dynamics are unknown. These findings support physical modularity as a useful design principle for learned elastic simulation, with benefits spanning generalization, stability, and the handling of incompletely specified dynamics.
summary.tldr: Neural Modular Physics organizes elastic simulation into physically meaningful learned modules to improve consistency, stability, and generalization.

title: Neural Modular Physics for Elastic Simulation

abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) can reveal implicit objectives such as safety considerations that go beyond task completion. In this work, we focus on the common safety criteria embedded in crowd preference datasets, where different users may express distinct preferences or objectives, yet follow similar safety principles. Our aim is to discover shared safety criteria from crowd preferences and then transfer them to downstream RL tasks to regularize agent behavior and enforce safety. We first show that direct reward combination—optimizing a preference-learned reward model together with downstream task rewards—has inherent limitations. Motivated by this, we propose Safe Crowd Preference-based RL, a hierarchical framework that extracts safety-aligned skills from crowd preferences and composes them via a high-level policy to safely solve downstream tasks. Experiments across safe RL environments and a preliminary LLM-style task with diverse user goals and shared safety constraints demonstrate that our approach substantially lowers safety costs without access to explicit safety rewards, while achieving task performance comparable to oracle methods trained with ground-truth safety signals.

paragraphs: People can prefer different outcomes while sharing principles about which behavior is unsafe. This paper asks whether an agent can recover those common safety criteria from crowd preferences and transfer them to new reinforcement-learning tasks. The intended signal is implicit in people's choices, rather than supplied as an explicit safety reward.

The authors first show limitations of directly combining a reward learned from preferences with a downstream task reward. They then introduce Safe Crowd Preference-based RL, a hierarchical method that extracts skills aligned with shared safety criteria. A higher-level policy composes these skills to pursue the downstream objective, making reusable behavior the vehicle for transferring safety information.

Experiments cover safe reinforcement-learning environments and a preliminary language-model-style task with varied user goals and shared safety constraints. The method substantially reduces safety costs without explicit safety rewards, while reaching task performance comparable to oracle methods trained with ground-truth safety signals. These findings support skill-based transfer when preferences contain common safety principles, with the language-model-style evidence remaining preliminary.
summary.tldr: The method extracts safety-aligned skills from crowd preferences and combines them to reduce safety costs on downstream tasks.

title: Implicit Safety Alignment from Crowd Preferences

abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is the de facto positional encoding in large language models due to its ability to encode relative positions and support length extrapolation. When adapted to vision transformers, the standard axial formulation decomposes two-dimensional spatial positions into horizontal and vertical components, implicitly restricting positional encoding to axis-aligned directions. We identify this directional constraint as a fundamental limitation of the standard axial 2D RoPE, which hinders the modeling of oblique spatial relationships that naturally exist in natural images. To overcome this limitation, we propose Spiral RoPE, a simple yet effective extension that enables multi-directional positional encoding by partitioning embedding channels into multiple groups associated with uniformly distributed directions. Each group is rotated according to the projection of the patch position onto its corresponding direction, allowing spatial relationships to be encoded beyond the horizontal and vertical axes. Across a wide range of vision tasks including classification, segmentation, and generation, Spiral RoPE consistently improves performance. Qualitative analyzes of attention maps further show that Spiral RoPE exhibits more concentrated activations on semantically relevant objects and better respects local object boundaries, highlighting the importance of multi-directional positional encoding in vision transformers.

paragraphs: Spiral RoPE studies how vision transformers encode the positions of image patches. Standard axial two-dimensional rotary embeddings handle horizontal and vertical coordinates separately. The authors identify this restriction to axis-aligned directions as an obstacle to representing oblique spatial relationships that occur naturally within images.

Their extension divides embedding channels into groups associated with uniformly distributed directions. For each group, a patch's position is projected onto the corresponding direction, and that projection determines the rotation. The resulting representation includes spatial relationships along multiple orientations. This directly changes the directional information available in the positional encoding while retaining a rotary construction.

Across classification, segmentation, and image-generation tasks, the authors report consistent performance improvements. Qualitative attention-map analysis also shows more concentrated activity on semantically relevant objects and better adherence to local object boundaries. These observations connect the numerical improvements to changes in where the models attend. Together, the findings support the importance of encoding spatial relationships beyond horizontal and vertical axes in vision transformers.
summary.tldr: Spiral RoPE encodes image positions along multiple directions, improving reported vision-task performance and object-focused attention.

title: Spiral RoPE: Rotate Your Rotary Positional Embeddings in the 2D Plane

abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is a powerful paradigm for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing RLVR methods typically rely on on-policy optimization from scratch, resulting in high sampling costs and inefficient utilization of accumulated experience. As model capabilities and policy behaviors evolve during training, recent attempts to reuse experience via fixed reasoning trajectories further suffer from policy mismatch. Motivated by these limitations, we argue that experience in RLVR should not be reused as fixed reasoning trajectories, but instead expressed in a policy-adaptive manner. In this work, we propose Experience-Augmented Policy Optimization (EAPO), which leverages a prior RL-optimized policy as an action-level experience prior and selectively injects experience at critical decision points during rollout. To ensure stable and unbiased learning from experience-augmented rollouts, EAPO further incorporates an adapted importance sampling scheme. Experiments on using Qwen-2.5-math 7b and Qwen-3-8B on five different benchmarks demonstrate that EAPO consistently improves reasoning performance over state-of-the-art RLVR methods.

paragraphs: Experience-Augmented Policy Optimization addresses inefficient reuse of experience when training language models with verifiable rewards. Generating fresh reasoning attempts can be expensive. Reusing complete earlier reasoning trajectories introduces another problem: as the model changes, those fixed trajectories can become poorly matched to its current behavior.

EAPO instead uses a previously reinforcement-trained policy as an action-level source of experience. During a new rollout, it selectively introduces that experience at critical decision points. This allows prior knowledge to influence a newly generated trajectory rather than requiring the current model to follow an old one wholesale. An adapted importance-sampling scheme accounts for the altered rollout process to support stable, unbiased learning.

Experiments using Qwen-2.5-math 7b and Qwen-3-8B across five benchmarks show consistent reasoning improvements over state-of-the-art RLVR methods. The central contribution is a more adaptable form of experience reuse: the prior policy supplies guidance where decisions matter, while the training procedure accounts for how that guidance changes the data being collected.
summary.tldr: EAPO reuses a previously trained reasoning policy as selective action-level guidance and corrects for its influence during learning.

title: Experience Augmented Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Concept shift occurs when the distribution of labels conditioned on the features changes between domains, which can make even a well-tuned ML model miscalibrated on a new domain. Identifying these shifted features provides unique insight into how feature-label relationships differ between domains, considering the difference may be across a scientifically relevant dimension, such as time, disease status, population, etc. In this paper, we propose SGShift, a method for attributing performance degradation under concept shift in tabular data to a sparse set of shifted features. We frame concept shift as a feature selection task to learn the features that can explain performance differences between models in the source and target domain. This framework enables SGShift to adapt powerful statistical tools such as generalized additive models, knockoffs, and absorption towards identifying these shifted features. We conduct extensive experiments in synthetic and real data across various ML models and find SGShift can identify shifted features much more accurately than baseline methods, requires few samples in the shifted domain, and is robust to complex cases of concept shift.

paragraphs: Concept shift occurs when the relationship between input features and labels changes across domains. A model can therefore become miscalibrated even if it was carefully tuned before the change. This paper asks which features explain the resulting performance degradation, making the shift more interpretable than a single drop in predictive quality.

SGShift turns that question into a feature-selection problem for tabular data. It seeks a sparse set of features that explains performance differences between models in the source and target domains. The framework adapts statistical tools including generalized additive models, knockoffs, and absorption to identify the features involved in the changed relationships.

In synthetic and real-data experiments across several machine-learning models, SGShift identifies shifted features much more accurately than baseline methods. The authors also report that it needs few target-domain samples and remains robust in complex shift scenarios. This matters when domain differences track scientifically meaningful dimensions such as time, population, or disease status: locating the affected features can help characterize how predictive relationships have changed.
summary.tldr: SGShift explains performance degradation under concept shift by selecting a small set of features whose label relationships changed across domains.

title: Explaining Concept Shift with Interpretable Feature Attribution

abstract: Multi-frame infrared small target detection suffers from extreme semantic paucity of targets and representation collapse due to overwhelming class imbalance, resulting in the persistent inability to accurately distinguish point-like targets from dynamic background clutter. To address these issues, we propose CodeMamba, a collaborative dual-stream framework that reframes this task as the complementary mechanisms of background manifold modeling and motion singularity capturing. The implicit stream emphasizes background regularity and anomaly localization, while the explicit stream focuses on motion consistency and spatiotemporal singularity. Finally, we design a Bayesian uncertainty-weighted fusion module that estimates the reliability of each stream by quantifying its observation noise. Extensive experiments on the IRDST and DAUB benchmarks demonstrate that CodeMamba not only outperforms existing methods but also achieves enhanced sensitivity to point-like targets.

paragraphs: Tiny targets in infrared video can look like little more than points, giving a detector very little recognizable object information. Background pixels also greatly outnumber target pixels, which can undermine useful representations. CodeMamba changes the emphasis: it combines learning the background’s regular structure with detecting unusual movement across frames.

The framework has two cooperating streams. The implicit stream models background regularity and identifies departures from it. The explicit stream examines motion consistency and unusual patterns across space and time. These views provide complementary evidence about whether a small signal belongs to a target or to dynamic background clutter, rather than relying primarily on target appearance.

A Bayesian fusion module combines the streams according to their estimated uncertainty. It quantifies observation noise to assess how reliable each stream is, allowing their contributions to reflect that reliability. Experiments on IRDST and DAUB report better performance than existing methods and greater sensitivity to point-like targets. The results support combining background modeling with motion evidence for this difficult detection setting.
summary.tldr: CodeMamba combines background regularity, motion anomalies, and uncertainty-weighted fusion to improve tiny infrared target detection.

title: CodeMamba: Shifting from Target Semantics to Self-Supervised Background Manifold Learning for Singularity Detection in Infrared Sequences

abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems excel at planning, tool use, and role coordination, but their openness and interaction complexity also expose them to jailbreak and adversarial collaboration. Existing defenses fall into two lines: (i) self-verification that asks each agent to pre-filter unsafe instructions before execution, and (ii) external guard modules that police behaviors. The former often underperforms because a standalone agent lacks sufficient capacity to detect cross-agent unsafe chains and delegation-induced risks; the latter increases system overhead and creates a single-point-of-failure—once compromised, system-wide safety collapses, and adding more guards worsens cost and complexity. To solve these challenges, we propose AdvEvo-MARL, a co-evolutionary multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that internalizes safety into task agents. Rather than relying on external guards, AdvEvo-MARL jointly optimizes attackers (which synthesize evolving jailbreak prompts) and defenders (task agents trained to both accomplish their duties and resist attacks) in adversarial learning environments. To stabilize learning and foster cooperation, we introduce a public baseline for advantage estimation: agents within the same functional group share a group-level mean-return baseline, enabling lower-variance updates and stronger intra-group coordination. Across representative attack scenarios, AdvEvo-MARL consistently keeps attack-success rate (ASR) below 20%, whereas baselines reach up to 38.33%, while preserving or even improving task accuracy (up to +3.67%). These results show that safety and utility can be jointly improved without relying on extra guard agents or added system overhead.

This provides a common reference for evaluating actions, supporting lower-variance learning updates and cooperation within functional groups.

These results support the possibility of improving safety and utility together through adversarial training, without adding guard agents to the deployed system.
summary.tldr: AdvEvo-MARL trains attackers and task agents together to improve resistance to jailbreaks while preserving or improving task performance.

title: AdvEvo-MARL: Shaping Internalized Safety through Adversarial Co-Evolution in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Training LLMs as interactive agents for multi-turn decision-making remains challenging, particularly in long-horizon tasks with sparse and delayed rewards, where agents must execute extended sequences of actions before receiving meaningful feedback. Most existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods model LLM agents as flat policies operating at a single time scale, selecting an action at each turn. In sparse-reward settings, this forces the agent to infer long-range dependencies solely from distant end-of-trajectory signals, often leading to inefficient learning and unstable behavior in complex environments. We propose HiPER, a novel Hierarchical Plan–Execute RL framework that jointly models and optimizes high-level subgoal planning and low-level action execution for LLM agents to overcome flat RL’s brittle long-horizon behavior and weak credit assignment under sparse outcome feedback. By maintaining persistent subgoals across multiple turns and explicitly deciding when to switch between them, HiPER introduces structured intermediate decision points that facilitate learning under sparse feedback, converting implicit multi-turn structure into learnable decisions at different time scales. To enable effective training, we introduce Hierarchical Advantage Estimation (HAE), a two-timescale policy gradient method that assigns credit to both action execution and subgoal transitions and achieves variance reduction relative to flat advantage estimation. Empirically, HiPER achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging interactive benchmarks, reaching 97.4% success on ALFWorld (+6.6% over the best prior method) and 83.3% on WebShop, with especially large gains on long-horizon tasks requiring multiple dependent subtasks. These results highlight the importance of explicit hierarchical decomposition for scalable RL training of multi-turn LLM agents.

paragraphs: Interactive language-model agents often need to complete many dependent actions before receiving useful feedback. HiPER addresses this credit-assignment problem by jointly learning high-level subgoal planning and low-level action execution.

The paper reports reduced variance relative to flat advantage estimation.

Gains are especially large on long tasks involving multiple dependent subtasks. These results support making planning boundaries part of the learned policy: the agent can improve both how it pursues a subgoal and how it decides that a different subgoal should take over.
summary.tldr: HiPER improves multi-turn agent learning by jointly training persistent subgoal planning, action execution, and credit assignment across both timescales.

title: HiPER: Hierarchical Plan–Execute RL for Multi-Turn LLM Agents

abstract: Large generative models raise growing concerns about provenance, misinformation, and impersonation. Digital watermarking offers a principled solution, yet extending it to natural language remains challenging due to text discreteness and sensitivity to semantic perturbations. Existing text watermarking methods either operate at the token level requiring white-box access and remaining fragile to paraphrasing, or at the sentence level, which supports black-box deployment but suffers from low Watermark Success Rate (WSR). We show that low WSR in sentence-level watermarking primarily stems from low injection success probability caused by a mismatch between posterior embedding distributions and semantic accept regions. Based on this insight, we propose X-Guard, a geometry-aware sentence-level watermarking framework that improves injection success by jointly optimizing embedding distributions and semantic space partitioning. X-Guard learns a more isotropic embedding space and introduces A$^2$PQ, a centroid-aligned partitioning scheme that approximately equalizes probability mass across regions. Extensive experiments across multiple models, languages, and attack settings demonstrate that X-Guard consistently improves robustness while preserving text fluency and practical deployability.

paragraphs: Sentence-level watermarking offers a way to mark generated text without requiring access to a model’s internal token-generation machinery. However, existing approaches can have low watermark success rates. This paper traces much of that problem to a mismatch between where sentence embeddings are likely to fall and the semantic regions accepted by the watermarking scheme.

X-Guard addresses this mismatch by optimizing both the embedding distribution and the partition of semantic space. It learns a more isotropic representation, making the embedding geometry less uneven across directions. Its A²PQ partitioning scheme aligns regions with centroids and approximately balances their probability mass. These changes aim to make successful watermark injection more likely.

Experiments across multiple models, languages, and attack settings show consistent improvements in robustness while preserving text fluency and practical deployability. The central contribution is a geometric explanation for injection failures and a method that responds to that explanation. It treats reliable watermarking as a joint problem of sentence representation and region design, rather than considering either component alone.
summary.tldr: X-Guard improves sentence-level text watermarking by aligning embedding geometry with semantic regions used for watermark injection.

title: Towards Reliable Marking and Verification of AI-Generated Text via Geometry-aware Sentence-level Watermarking

abstract: Parameter-based knowledge editing updates the internal knowledge of large language models (LLMs) via localized weight modifications and has attracted significant attention. However, most existing methods overlook fundamental theoretical limitations and are rarely evaluated under realistic, practice-oriented settings. In this paper, we first present a theoretical analysis based on the dimensional Collapse Hypothesis, explaining how localized parameter edits can propagate along fragile directions in the representation space, inducing global interference and ultimately causing reasoning collapse. Building on this insight, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation by systematically varying knowledge complexity, number of edits, evaluation dimensions, and baseline methods. Our results show that parameter-based editing methods consistently damage core LLM capabilities. In contrast, a simple retrieval-based baseline achieves consistently stronger performance than all parameter-editing methods across all evaluated conditions. These findings highlight that preserving the fundamental capabilities of LLMs after knowledge editing should be a central concern for future research.

paragraphs: Parameter-based knowledge editing changes selected model weights to update stored knowledge. This paper questions whether such localized changes reliably preserve the model’s wider abilities. Its theoretical analysis builds on the dimensional Collapse Hypothesis, describing how edits can spread through fragile directions in representation space and cause interference beyond the intended update.

That analysis links local weight changes to possible global damage and reasoning collapse. The authors then investigate the issue empirically by varying knowledge complexity, the number of edits, evaluation dimensions, and comparison methods. This connects the proposed mechanism to a broader assessment of model behavior after editing, rather than judging an edit solely by whether it changes the targeted fact.

Across the evaluated conditions, parameter-editing methods consistently damage core capabilities. A simple retrieval-based baseline also performs better than every tested parameter-editing method. These findings support making preservation of general model abilities a central evaluation goal. The reported comparison concerns the tested methods and conditions, while the theoretical explanation specifically rests on the stated hypothesis.
summary.tldr: The paper links localized knowledge edits to broader interference and finds retrieval stronger than all tested parameter-editing methods.

title: Revisiting Parameter-Based Knowledge Editing in Large Language Models: Theoretical Limits and Empirical Evidence

abstract: Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) favor their own outputs when acting as judges, undermining the integrity of automated post-training and evaluation workflows. However, it is difficult to disentangle which behaviors are explained by narcissism versus experimental confounds. Specifically, LLM evaluators may deliver self-preferring verdicts when comparing responses to questions they fail on; these verdicts may not depend on the identity of the author, but on evaluator quality. We correct this by directly comparing the judge’s voting distribution in cases where it evaluates itself versus another model. This evaluator quality baseline reveals that only 51% of examples in previous findings retain statistical significance against this null hypothesis, covering 89.6% of total self-preference probability mass. Finally, we compare the entropy of voting distributions, suggesting uncertainty-driven overlap, and show that our procedure enables more careful documentation against the backdrop of judge-bias research.

paragraphs: When language models judge responses, they sometimes favor answers they produced themselves. This paper examines whether that pattern necessarily reflects a preference for their own authorship. A judge that struggles with a question may also judge its answers poorly, creating apparent self-preference that can be explained by evaluator quality.

The authors introduce a baseline that directly compares the judge’s voting distribution when evaluating itself with its voting distribution when evaluating another model. This comparison tests whether the observed behavior exceeds what the evaluator-quality explanation would predict. It makes the interpretation of self-preference depend on a relevant alternative explanation, rather than on the direction of the verdict alone.

Under this baseline, 51% of examples from previous findings remain statistically significant, accounting for 89.6% of total self-preference probability mass. These figures show that many individual findings weaken while much of the probability mass remains. An additional comparison of voting entropy suggests overlap driven by uncertainty. The procedure supports more careful documentation of judge bias without dismissing the remaining evidence.
summary.tldr: An evaluator-quality baseline weakens many reported self-preference findings while retaining most of their total probability mass.

title: Are LLM Evaluators Really Narcissists? Sanity Checking Self-Preference Evaluations

abstract: Prediction algorithms are increasingly used to inform decisions about humans, but maximizing accuracy—the standard learning objective—is not necessarily optimal for this purpose. Instead, we propose optimizing social welfare, defined as the average gain users receive from correct predictions. Welfare enables to express, and therefore account for, heterogeneity in how much users benefit from accuracy. But since these valuations are private and users can benefit from overreporting them, learning must simultaneously elicit truthful values and optimize welfare with respect to them. To this end, we propose a novel learning algorithm that incorporates a truthful auction. We show how to compute allocations and prices efficiently, and bound the number of paying users—which surprisingly is independent of the sample size. We conclude with experiments on real and synthetic data that demonstrate our algorithm and explore the connections between welfare and accuracy.

paragraphs: A correct prediction can be more valuable to one person than another, so maximizing overall accuracy need not maximize the benefits people receive. This paper proposes social welfare as the learning objective, defined as users’ average gain from correct predictions. That objective explicitly accounts for differences in how much accuracy matters to different users.

The difficulty is that these valuations are private. Users may benefit from exaggerating how much a correct prediction is worth to them, so the learning system must address truthful reporting alongside prediction. The authors introduce a learning algorithm incorporating a truthful auction, connecting the elicitation of values with optimization of welfare.

They show how to compute allocations and prices efficiently and prove a bound on the number of users who pay that does not depend on sample size. Experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrate the algorithm and explore the relationship between welfare and accuracy. The contribution links predictive learning with incentive design, making differences in users’ benefits part of the objective while accounting for strategic reports of those benefits.
summary.tldr: A truthful auction lets a classifier optimize users’ benefits from correct predictions while accounting for privately held valuations.

title: Welfare-Optimal Classification with Accuracy Auctions

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly support culturally sensitive decision making, yet often exhibit misalignment due to skewed pretraining data and the absence of structured value representations. Existing methods can steer outputs, but often lack demographic grounding and treat values as independent, unstructured signals, reducing consistency and interpretability. We propose OG-MAR, an Ontology-Guided Multi-Agent Reasoning framework. OG-MAR summarizes respondent-specific values from the World Values Survey (WVS) and constructs a global cultural ontology by eliciting relations over a fixed taxonomy via competency questions. At inference time, it retrieves ontology-consistent relations and demographically similar profiles to instantiate multiple value-persona agents, whose outputs are synthesized by a judgment agent that enforces ontology consistency and demographic proximity. Experiments on regional social-survey benchmarks across four LLM backbones show that OG-MAR improves cultural alignment and robustness over competitive baselines, while producing more transparent reasoning traces.

paragraphs: Language models used for culturally sensitive decisions can reflect skewed pretraining data and lack an organized representation of values. Existing steering approaches may also omit demographic grounding or treat values as unrelated signals. OG-MAR addresses these issues by combining survey-derived profiles with an ontology that represents relationships among cultural values.

The framework summarizes individual respondents’ values from the World Values Survey. It builds a global ontology by eliciting relationships within a fixed taxonomy through competency questions. During inference, it retrieves compatible value relationships and demographically similar profiles to instantiate several value-persona agents. A judgment agent combines their outputs while enforcing ontology consistency and demographic proximity.

Experiments on regional social-survey benchmarks across four language model backbones show improved cultural alignment and robustness relative to competitive baselines. The framework also produces more transparent reasoning traces. These findings support linking demographic evidence with structured relationships among values, so that the agents’ contributions and the final synthesis follow an explicit representation of the cultural information used.
summary.tldr: OG-MAR combines survey-grounded personas and structured value relationships to improve cultural alignment on regional social-survey benchmarks.

title: Toward Culturally Aligned LLMs through Ontology-Guided Multi-Agent Reasoning

abstract: Teacher-Student Knowledge Transfer (KT) is ubiquitous in modern machine learning, ranging from classical model compression via Knowledge Distillation (KD) to the emergent phenomenon of Weak-to-Strong (W2S) generalization. While existing studies offer isolated insights, a unified theoretical framework explaining the efficacy of KT across these disparate regimes remains lacking. In this work, we establish a unified spectral analysis of SGD dynamics in high-dimensional linear regression, elucidating the efficiency of KT across seemingly disparate regimes. We characterize KT efficiency through two distinct mechanisms: Spectral Horizon Expansion in KD, which enables the capture of statistically inaccessible high-frequency signals, and Spectral Denoising in W2S, where the student acts as a filter for optimization noise. Our framework unifies these phenomena, revealing that the efficacy of transfer is governed by the interplay between implicit regularization and heterogeneous spectral learning speeds over the spectrum.

paragraphs: Knowledge transfer includes both compressing a teacher into a student and training a stronger student from a weaker teacher. This paper develops one theoretical account of these apparently different settings using high-dimensional linear regression. It analyzes stochastic-gradient learning through the spectrum, separating directions of the learning problem that develop at different speeds.

For knowledge distillation, the identified mechanism is spectral horizon expansion: transfer enables the capture of high-frequency signal components that are otherwise statistically inaccessible in the analyzed setting. For weak-to-strong generalization, the mechanism is spectral denoising, where the student filters optimization noise. The two cases therefore benefit from different changes in how signal and noise pass through training.

The unified analysis attributes transfer effectiveness to the interaction between implicit regularization and unequal learning speeds across spectral directions. This makes the training dynamics central to understanding what a student can gain from a teacher. The result is a theoretical explanation within linear regression that connects distillation and weak-to-strong learning through a shared spectral perspective.
summary.tldr: A spectral analysis of linear regression explains knowledge transfer through expanded signal access in distillation and noise filtering in weak-to-strong learning.

title: What Makes a Strong Model? A Unified Spectral Analysis of Knowledge Transfer over High-dimensional Linear Regression

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has shown promise in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) on text-attributed graphs (TAGs). This work reframes CoT-based graph learning through the principle of clustering as reasoning, offering a $k$-means interpretation of how iterative reasoning operates over graph-structured data. We observe that existing graph CoT methods rely on disjoint architectures and fixed graph representations, limiting step-by-step semantic-topological interaction and interpretability. To overcome this limitation, we propose a unified framework named KCoT that integrates CoT reasoning with graph representation learning. Our key theoretical result reveals a formal mathematical correspondence between a Transformer block and the $k$-means algorithm, allowing reasoning to be interpreted as iterative assignment and update steps. Based on this insight, we introduce a Semantic Discriminating Prompt that explicitly formulates these steps as structured CoT reasoning, together with a structure-grounded alignment strategy to fuse topological priors with evolving thought-conditioned representations. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, validating clustering as a principled mechanism for CoT-based graph learning.

paragraphs: Graphs with text attached to their nodes require models to combine language meaning with connection structure. Existing chain-of-thought approaches can keep these parts too separate: reasoning proceeds while the graph representation remains fixed. This paper proposes KCoT, a framework in which reasoning and graph representation learning develop together.

Its theoretical foundation is a formal correspondence between a Transformer block and the assignment-and-update operations of k-means clustering. This provides an interpretation of iterative reasoning as repeatedly organizing information and refining its representation. KCoT turns that interpretation into a Semantic Discriminating Prompt that explicitly structures the reasoning around those operations.

A structure-grounded alignment strategy then combines graph topology with representations that change as reasoning progresses. This matters because the model can bring semantic and structural information together at successive steps, rather than relying on one fixed graph encoding. Experiments on standard benchmarks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the usefulness of this clustering-based design for the evaluated graph-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: KCoT connects Transformer computation to k-means clustering to jointly develop step-by-step reasoning and graph representations.

title: Clustering as Reasoning: A $k$-Means Interpretation of Chain-of-Thought Graph Learning

abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is central to aligning large language models (LLMs) with instruction following and task-specific reasoning. Despite its success, SFT optimizes token-level likelihoods under the implicit assumption that strictly fitting all tokens in expert demonstrations induces the desired downstream behavior. However, in reasoning tasks where correctness is defined by logical validity or final outcomes rather than exact token realizations, this assumption can lead to optimization misalignment. We empirically observe that low-probability tokens in reasoning demonstrations often correspond to realization-specific or stylistic variations, and that reducing their influence during training consistently improves generalization on reasoning benchmarks. Motivated by this insight, we propose the Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss (BLL-Loss), a simple and parameter-free alternative to standard likelihood training that bounds gradient contributions from low-probability tokens while preserving conventional optimization behavior. We provide theoretical insights and extensive empirical results demonstrating that BLL-Loss improves reasoning generalization across diverse model scales and challenging benchmarks.
originalAbstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is central to aligning large language models (LLMs) with instruction following and task-specific reasoning. Despite its success, SFT optimizes token-level likelihoods under the implicit assumption that strictly fitting all tokens in expert demonstrations induces the desired downstream behavior. However, in reasoning tasks where correctness is defined by logical validity or final outcomes rather than exact token realizations, this assumption can lead to optimization misalignment. We empirically observe that low-probability tokens in reasoning demonstrations often correspond to realization-specific or stylistic variations, and that reducing their influence during training consistently improves generalization on reasoning benchmarks. Motivated by this insight, we propose the Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss (BLL-Loss), a simple and parameter-free alternative to standard likelihood training that bounds gradient contributions from low-probability tokens while preserving conventional optimization behavior. We provide theoretical insights and extensive empirical results demonstrating that BLL-Loss improves reasoning generalization across diverse model scales and challenging benchmarks.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning trains language models to reproduce the tokens in expert demonstrations. For reasoning, however, success depends on valid logic or a correct outcome, and multiple wordings may express the same reasoning. This paper investigates whether forcing a close fit to every demonstration token can pull training away from that underlying goal.

The authors observe that tokens assigned low probability often reflect stylistic choices or particular ways of expressing an answer. Reducing their influence improves generalization in the reported reasoning experiments. Based on this observation, Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss limits the gradient contribution of low-probability tokens while retaining conventional optimization behavior elsewhere.

The loss is presented as a simple, parameter-free alternative to standard likelihood training. Theoretical insights and experiments across model scales and challenging benchmarks support improved reasoning generalization. The finding concerns how strongly demonstrations should shape training: some difficult-to-fit wording deserves less influence when exact phrasing is not what determines whether the reasoning succeeds. It does not imply that every low-probability token is unimportant.
summary.tldr: Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss limits the training influence of low-probability demonstration tokens, improving reasoning generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Don’t Force the Fit: Bounded Log-Likelihood Loss for Enhanced Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external tools such as search engines to solve complex, multi-step problems, yet their rollouts are structurally heterogeneous: variations in tool-call number, placement, and outcomes induce distinct behaviors and reward distributions. As a result, policy gradient methods with a single global baseline suffer from cross-stratum bias, an "apples-to-oranges” comparison that distorts credit assignment and impedes exploration. To address this issue, we propose Stratified GRPO. Its core component, Stratified Advantage Normalization (SAN), partitions trajectories into homogeneous strata based on structural properties and computes advantages locally within each stratum, ensuring comparisons only among true peers. We show that SAN eliminates cross-stratum bias, yields conditionally unbiased unit-variance estimates within strata, and preserves the global unbiasedness and unit-variance properties of standard normalization, resulting in a more reliable learning signal. To improve robustness in finite-sample regimes, we further linearly blend SAN with the global estimator. Experiments on factual QA and deep-research agent benchmarks demonstrate that Stratified GRPO consistently outperforms GRPO by up to 12.6 points, achieving higher training rewards, improved training stability, and more effective search policies. These results establish structure-aware advantage normalization as an effective correction for RL of search agents with structurally heterogeneous rollouts.

paragraphs: Search-agent training compares trajectories that may differ in how often tools are called, where calls occur, and what they return. These structural differences produce different reward distributions. The paper argues that a single global baseline can therefore make misleading comparisons, distorting which behavior receives credit and making exploration harder.

Stratified GRPO groups trajectories by structural properties and normalizes advantages within each group. Its Stratified Advantage Normalization component compares structurally similar trajectories, rather than treating all rollouts as equivalent peers. The authors show that it removes cross-stratum bias, produces conditionally unbiased estimates with unit variance within strata, and preserves the global unbiasedness and unit-variance properties of standard normalization.

Experiments on factual question answering and deep-research agent benchmarks report consistent improvements over GRPO, reaching 12.6 points, alongside higher training rewards and improved stability. The findings support accounting for tool-use structure when constructing learning signals, so differences between rollout types do not obscure the quality of behavior within them.
summary.tldr: Stratified GRPO improves search-agent learning by normalizing rewards among structurally similar trajectories and blending that signal with global estimates.

title: Stratified GRPO: Handling Structural Heterogeneity in Reinforcement Learning of LLM Search Agents

abstract: We develop a novel multi-class classification method based on output codes for the problem of classifying a sequence of amino acids into one of many known protein structural classes, called folds. Our method learns relative weights between one-vs-all classifiers and encodes information about the protein structural hierarchy for multi-class prediction. Our code weighting approach significantly improves on the standard one-vs-all method for the fold recognition problem. In order to compare against widely used methods in protein sequence analysis, we also test nearest neighbor approaches based on the PSI-BLAST algorithm. Our code weight learning algorithm strongly outperforms these PSIBLAST methods on every structure recognition problem we consider.

paragraphs: The task in this paper is to assign an amino-acid sequence to one of several known protein structural classes, called folds. The authors develop a multiclass method based on output codes. Its purpose is to combine class-specific predictions in a way that also uses information about relationships among protein structures.

The method learns relative weights for one-versus-all classifiers and encodes the protein structural hierarchy for the final prediction. Learning these weights lets the system adapt how much influence the individual classifiers have. Including the hierarchy also brings structural class relationships into the multiclass decision, alongside the separate class predictions.

For fold recognition, the learned code weighting significantly improves on the standard one-versus-all approach. The authors also compare against nearest-neighbor methods based on PSI-BLAST, a widely used protein-sequence analysis approach. Their algorithm strongly outperforms those methods on every structure-recognition problem considered. These findings support the combination of adaptive classifier weighting and structural hierarchy information within the evaluated recognition tasks.
summary.tldr: Adaptive output-code weights and protein hierarchy information improve fold recognition over the evaluated one-versus-all and PSI-BLAST methods.

title: Multi-class protein fold recognition using adaptive codes

abstract: The detection of faces in images is fundamentally a rare event detection problem. Cascade classifiers provide an efficient computational solution, by leveraging the asymmetry in the distribution of faces vs. non-faces. Training a cascade classifier in turn requires a solution for the following subproblems: Design a classifier for each node in the cascade with very high detection rate but only moderate false positive rate. While there are a few strategies in the literature for indirectly addressing this asymmetric node learning goal, none of them are based on a satisfactory theoretical framework. We present a mathematical characterization of the node-learning problem and describe an effective closed form approximation to the optimal solution, which we call the Linear Asymmetric Classifier (LAC). We first use AdaBoost or AsymBoost to select features, and use LAC to learn a linear discriminant function to achieve the node learning goal. Experimental results on face detection show that LAC can improve the detection performance in comparison to standard methods. We also show that Fisher Discriminant Analysis on the features selected by AdaBoost yields better performance than AdaBoost itself.

paragraphs: Face detection is a rare-event problem: faces occupy a small part of the candidate space compared with non-faces. Cascades exploit this imbalance by applying classifiers in stages. Each stage needs to retain a very high proportion of faces while tolerating a moderate false-positive rate. This paper gives that asymmetric training objective an explicit mathematical characterization.

The proposed Linear Asymmetric Classifier, or LAC, is a closed-form approximation to the optimal solution of the stage-level learning problem. The procedure first selects features with AdaBoost or AsymBoost, then uses LAC to learn a linear discriminant from those features. This connects the final classifier directly to the detection requirements of a cascade stage.

Face-detection experiments show that LAC can improve detection performance relative to standard methods. The authors also find that Fisher Discriminant Analysis applied to AdaBoost-selected features performs better than AdaBoost itself. Together, these results highlight the value of considering feature selection and the final discriminant separately when training classifiers for an asymmetric detection objective.
summary.tldr: LAC directly approximates the asymmetric objective of cascade stages and can improve face detection using features selected by boosting.

title: Linear Asymmetric Classifier for cascade detectors

abstract: We present a new approach to multiple instance learning (MIL) that is particularly effective when the positive bags are sparse (i.e. contain few positive instances). Unlike other SVM-based MIL methods, our approach more directly enforces the desired constraint that at least one of the instances in a positive bag is positive. Using both artificial and real-world data, we experimentally demonstrate that our approach achieves greater accuracy than state-of-the-art MIL methods when positive bags are sparse, and performs competitively when they are not. In particular, our approach is the best performing method for image region classification.
originalAbstract: We present a new approach to multiple instance learning (MIL) that is particularly effective when the positive bags are sparse (i.e. contain few positive instances). Unlike other SVM-based MIL methods, our approach more directly enforces the desired constraint that at least one of the instances in a positive bag is positive. Using both artificial and real-world data, we experimentally demonstrate that our approach achieves greater accuracy than state-of-the-art MIL methods when positive bags are sparse, and performs competitively when they are not. In particular, our approach is the best performing method for image region classification.

paragraphs: Multiple instance learning works with groups of instances, called bags, whose labels provide information about the instances inside them. A positive bag must contain at least one positive instance. This paper focuses on sparse positive bags, where only a few members are positive, making that small amount of positive evidence central to the learning task.

The proposed approach enforces the requirement that at least one instance in a positive bag be positive more directly than other SVM-based multiple instance methods. Its design therefore concentrates on the constraint linking an individual instance to the bag's label. That focus matters when a positive label is supported by only a small portion of the bag.

Experiments on artificial and real-world data show greater accuracy than state-of-the-art multiple instance learning methods when positive bags are sparse. When they are not sparse, the method remains competitive. The authors also report the best image-region classification performance in their evaluation. These results support the method's particular suitability for sparse positive evidence while showing usefulness beyond that setting.
summary.tldr: A multiple instance learning method more directly enforces positive-bag constraints and improves accuracy when positive instances are scarce.

title: Multiple instance learning for sparse positive bags

abstract: Given a sample covariance matrix, we examine the problem of maximizing the variance explained by a particular linear combination of the input variables while constraining the number of nonzero coefficients in this combination. This is known as sparse principal component analysis and has a wide array of applications in machine learning and engineering. We formulate a new semidefinite relaxation to this problem and derive a greedy algorithm that computes a full set of good solutions for all numbers of non zero coefficients, with complexity O(n3 ), where n is the number of variables. We then use the same relaxation to derive sufficient conditions for global optimality of a solution, which can be tested in O(n3 ). We show on toy examples and biological data that our algorithm does provide globally optimal solutions in many cases.

This is known as sparse principal component analysis and has a wide array of applications in machine learning and engineering. We formulate a new semidefinite relaxation to this problem and derive a greedy algorithm that computes a full set of good solutions for all numbers of non zero coefficients, with complexity O(n3 ), where n is the number of variables. We then use the same relaxation to derive sufficient conditions for global optimality of a solution, which can be tested in O(n3 ). paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks a linear combination of variables that explains substantial variance while using only a limited number of nonzero coefficients. The paper starts from a sample covariance matrix and addresses this trade-off across all possible numbers of selected variables. This gives a range of solutions with different levels of sparsity.

The authors formulate a new semidefinite relaxation and derive a greedy algorithm that computes a full collection of good solutions. Its computational complexity is O(n³), where n is the number of variables. Producing the whole path allows the amount of explained variance to be considered alongside how many variables a solution uses.

The same relaxation yields sufficient conditions for a proposed solution to be globally optimal, with checks also costing O(n³). Passing these conditions certifies optimality; their being sufficient does not mean that every optimal solution must pass them. Experiments on toy examples and biological data show globally optimal solutions in many cases. Thus, the method combines practical candidate generation with a way to certify some of its results.
summary.tldr: A cubic-time greedy method generates sparse PCA solutions across sparsity levels, with sufficient conditions that can certify global optimality.

title: Full regularization path for sparse principal component analysis

abstract: Cross-domain collaborative filtering solves the sparsity problem by transferring rating knowledge across multiple domains. In this paper, we propose a rating-matrix generative model (RMGM) for effective cross-domain collaborative filtering. We first show that the relatedness across multiple rating matrices can be established by finding a shared implicit cluster-level rating matrix, which is next extended to a cluster-level rating model. Consequently, a rating matrix of any related task can be viewed as drawing a set of users and items from a user-item joint mixture model as well as drawing the corresponding ratings from the cluster-level rating model. The combination of these two models gives the RMGM, which can be used to fill the missing ratings for both existing and new users. A major advantage of RMGM is that it can share the knowledge by pooling the rating data from multiple tasks even when the users and items of these tasks do not overlap. We evaluate the RMGM empirically on three real-world collaborative filtering data sets to show that RMGM can outperform the individual models trained separately.

paragraphs: Sparse ratings make it difficult to learn recommendation models within a single domain. This paper proposes transferring rating knowledge across related domains through a rating-matrix generative model. The connection between domains is established at the level of implicit user and item clusters, allowing shared rating structure to exist beyond individual users or items.

The model combines a user-item joint mixture model with a cluster-level rating model. A task's rating matrix is described by drawing users and items through the mixture model and drawing their ratings through the shared cluster-level model. This generative account supports filling missing ratings for existing users as well as new users.

A major advantage is that knowledge can be pooled across tasks even when their users and items do not overlap. Relatedness is represented through the shared cluster structure instead of requiring shared identities. Experiments on three real-world collaborative-filtering datasets show that the model can outperform separate models trained for each task. The result supports cross-domain sharing in the evaluated settings without asserting that transfer always improves recommendations.
summary.tldr: A shared cluster-level rating model transfers recommendation knowledge across related domains even when their users and items do not overlap.

title: Transfer learning for collaborative filtering via a rating-matrix generative model

abstract: In global optimization, when the evaluation of the target function is costly, the usual strategy is to learn a surrogate model for the target function and replace the initial optimization by the optimization of the model. Gaussian processes have been widely used since they provide an elegant way to model the fitness and to deal with the exploration-exploitation trade-off in a principled way. Several empirical criteria have been proposed to drive the model optimization, among which is the well-known Expected Improvement criterion. The major computational bottleneck of these algorithms is the exhaustive grid search used to optimize the highly multi modal merit function. In this paper, we propose a competitive ``adaptive grid'' approach, based on a properly derived Cross-Entropy optimization algorithm with mixture proposals. Experiments suggest that 1) we outperform the classical single-Gaussian cross-entropy method when the fitness function is highly multi modal, and 2) we improve on standard exhaustive search in GP-based surrogate optimization.

Several empirical criteria have been proposed to drive the model optimization, among which is the well-known Expected Improvement criterion. The major computational bottleneck of these algorithms is the exhaustive grid search used to optimize the highly multi modal merit function.
