paragraphs: When evaluating a target function is expensive, global optimization often uses a learned surrogate to guide the search. Gaussian processes support this strategy by modeling fitness and helping balance exploration with exploitation. A criterion such as Expected Improvement then guides where the optimization should look next.

The paper focuses on a computational bottleneck inside that process: optimizing a merit function with many distinct peaks through exhaustive grid search. The authors propose an adaptive-grid approach based on a cross-entropy optimization algorithm with mixture proposals. The target of the improvement is thus the search used within surrogate-based optimization.

Experiments suggest two benefits. The mixture approach outperforms classical cross-entropy optimization with a single Gaussian when the fitness function is highly multimodal, and it improves on standard exhaustive search in Gaussian-process surrogate optimization. These are empirical findings tied to the tested settings. The contribution shows how a more adaptive inner optimization procedure can improve the computational strategy used to select evaluations of an expensive target function.
summary.tldr: A mixture cross-entropy search improves the inner optimization of Gaussian-process surrogates in the reported experiments.

title: Surrogating the surrogate: accelerating Gaussian-process-based global optimization with a mixture cross-entropy algorithm

abstract: Direct quantile regression involves estimating a given quantile of a response variable as a function of input variables. We present a new framework for direct quantile regression where a Gaussian process model is learned, minimising the expected tilted loss function. The integration required in learning is not analytically tractable so to speed up the learning we employ the Expectation Propagation algorithm. We describe how this work relates to other quantile regression methods and apply the method on both synthetic and real data sets.
originalAbstract: Direct quantile regression involves estimating a given quantile of a response variable as a function of input variables. We present a new framework for direct quantile regression where a Gaussian process model is learned, minimising the expected tilted loss function. The integration required in learning is not analytically tractable so to speed up the learning we employ the Expectation Propagation algorithm. We describe how this work relates to other quantile regression methods and apply the method on both synthetic and real data sets.

paragraphs: Quantile regression estimates a chosen point in the distribution of a response as a function of the inputs. This allows the prediction target to be a particular quantile, rather than only a central average. The paper develops a direct quantile regression framework using a Gaussian process model.

The model is learned by minimizing expected tilted loss, the objective associated here with estimating the desired quantile. Learning requires an integration that cannot be performed analytically. The authors employ Expectation Propagation to address that computational obstacle and speed up learning. The approximation is thus part of making the proposed probabilistic framework computationally usable.

The paper also explains how the framework relates to other quantile regression methods and applies it to synthetic and real datasets. These applications demonstrate use of the method in both controlled and observed-data settings. The central contribution is the combination of Gaussian process modeling, a quantile-focused learning objective, and an inference procedure that handles the otherwise intractable integration.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process framework estimates response quantiles using expected tilted loss and Expectation Propagation for tractable learning.

title: Gaussian Process Quantile Regression using Expectation Propagation

abstract: In this paper, we propose a new Soft Confidence-Weighted (SCW) online learning scheme, which enables the conventional confidence-weighted learning method to handle non-separable cases. Unlike the previous confidence-weighted learning algorithms, the proposed soft confidence-weighted learning method enjoys all the four salient properties: (i) large margin training, (ii) confidence weighting, (iii) capability to handle non-separable data, and (iv) adaptive margin. Our experimental results show that SCW performs significantly better than the original CW algorithm. When comparing with the state-of-the-art AROW algorithm, we found that SCW in general achieves better or at least comparable predictive performance, but enjoys considerably better efficiency performance (i.e., producing less number of updates and spending less time cost).
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a new Soft Confidence-Weighted (SCW) online learning scheme, which enables the conventional confidence-weighted learning method to handle non-separable cases. Unlike the previous confidence-weighted learning algorithms, the proposed soft confidence-weighted learning method enjoys all the four salient properties: (i) large margin training, (ii) confidence weighting, (iii) capability to handle non-separable data, and (iv) adaptive margin. Our experimental results show that SCW performs significantly better than the original CW algorithm. When comparing with the state-of-the-art AROW algorithm, we found that SCW in general achieves better or at least comparable predictive performance, but enjoys considerably better efficiency performance (i.e., producing less number of updates and spending less time cost).

paragraphs: Confidence-weighted online learning updates a classifier as examples arrive while accounting for confidence in its model. This paper extends that approach to non-separable data, where the desired separation of examples cannot be achieved perfectly. The proposed Soft Confidence-Weighted method, or SCW, is designed to retain useful features of confidence-weighted learning while accommodating that situation.

The method combines four stated properties: large-margin training, confidence weighting, the ability to handle non-separable data, and an adaptive margin. The margin concerns the separation encouraged by the classifier, while confidence weighting brings the model's certainty into learning. Their combination with a soft treatment of separation is the central methodological contribution described in the abstract.

Experiments show significantly better performance than the original confidence-weighted algorithm. Against AROW, SCW generally achieves better or comparable predictive performance and substantially better efficiency, measured through fewer updates and less time. The empirical result therefore concerns both prediction and the work required during learning, with the predictive comparison explicitly qualified as a general tendency.
summary.tldr: Soft Confidence-Weighted learning handles non-separable data while combining adaptive margins and confidence weighting, with favorable predictive and efficiency results.
